context: A thermally conducting, uniform, and homogeneous bar of length L, cross-sectional area A, density ρ, and specific heat at constant pressure c_p is brought to a nonuniform temperature distribution by contact at one end with a hot reservoir at temperature T_H and at the other end with a cold reservoir at temperature T_c. After steady state is established, the bar is removed from the reservoirs, thermally insulated, and kept at constant pressure. Let x denote the coordinate along the bar measured from the cold end. Define the total heat capacity at constant pressure C_p = c_p ρ A L and the final uniform temperature T_f after insulation. Show that the change in entropy of the bar ΔS satisfies
solution:
The initial steady linear temperature profile along the bar is
$$
T(x)=T_c+\frac{T_H-T_c}{L}x
$$
Adiabatic removal at constant pressure implies conservation of total enthalpy
$$
\int_0^L \rho A c_p [T(x)-T_f] dx=0
$$
Therefore the final uniform temperature is
$$
T_f=\frac{T_H+T_c}{2}
$$
The entropy change of the bar is obtained by integrating over slices along x at constant pressure
$$
\Delta S=\rho A c_p \int_0^L \int_{T(x)}^{T_f} \frac{dT}{T} dx
$$
This can be written as
$$
\Delta S=\rho A c_p \left[L\ln T_f-\int_0^L \ln T(x) dx\right]
$$
Compute the integral
$$
\int_0^L \ln\big(T_c+\frac{T_H-T_c}{L}x\big) dx=L \frac{T_H\ln T_H-T_c\ln T_c-(T_H-T_c)}{T_H-T_c}
$$
Substituting and using C_p=c_p \rho A L yields
$$
\Delta S=C_p\left[\ln T_f-\frac{T_H\ln T_H-T_c\ln T_c-(T_H-T_c)}{T_H-T_c}\right]
$$
Equivalently
$$
\Delta S=C_p\left(1+\ln T_f+\frac{T_c}{T_H-T_c}\ln T_c-\frac{T_H}{T_H-T_c}\ln T_H\right)
$$
with
$$
C_p=c_p \rho A L
$$
and
$$
T_f=\frac{T_H+T_c}{2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as: (1) an explicit algebraic expression of the form ΔS = ... written only with the variables C_p, T_H, T_c, and T_f; and (2) an explicit algebraic expression of the form T_f = ... written only with the variables T_H and T_c. Do not introduce any additional variables or numerical values.

grading_standard.formula:
$$
\Delta S=\rho A c_p \left[L\ln T_f-\int_0^L \ln T(x) dx\right]
$$

context: A mixture of n_1 = 1/10 mole of helium with heat-capacity ratio gamma_1 = C_{p1}/C_{v1} = 5/3 and n_2 = 1/5 mole of nitrogen with heat-capacity ratio gamma_2 = C_{p2}/C_{v2} = 7/5 is modeled as an ideal mixture of two ideal gases. The mixture is initially at temperature T_i = 300\unit{K} and volume V_i = 4\unit{L}. The gas is compressed slowly and adiabatically (reversible and adiabatic). Let p_i, V_i, T_i denote the initial pressure, volume, and temperature, and p_f, V_f, T_f the corresponding final values. Let R be the ideal-gas constant. Let C_{v1}, C_{p1} be the molar heat capacities at constant volume and pressure for helium, and C_{v2}, C_{p2} those for nitrogen. Let \Delta S_1 and \Delta S_2 denote the entropy changes of the helium and nitrogen components, respectively. Show that the changes of temperature and pressure during the compression can be described by an intermediate exponent g defined via T_f = T_i (V_i/V_f)^g for the mixture, and determine g and the effective heat-capacity ratio gamma of the mixture in terms of C_{v1}, C_{p1}, C_{v2}, C_{p2}. Then compute the magnitudes of the changes when the volume is reduced by 1%, i.e., when V_f = (99/100) V_i. Report exact expressions and numerical approximations for T_f and p_f.
solution:
The entropy change for each component of an ideal-gas mixture is
$$
\Delta S_1 = n_1 C_{v1} \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i} + n_1 R \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}
$$
$$
\Delta S_2 = n_2 C_{v2} \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i} + n_2 R \ln \frac{V_f}{V_i}
$$
For a reversible adiabatic compression of the mixture, the total entropy change vanishes
$$
\Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2 = 0
$$
This implies the temperature–volume relation for the mixture
$$
T_f = T_i \left(\frac{V_i}{V_f}\right)^g
$$
where the intermediate exponent g is
$$
 g = \frac{(n_1 + n_2) R}{n_1 C_{v1} + n_2 C_{v2}}
$$
The ideal gas law is
$$
 p V = n R T
$$
Using the ideal gas law together with the temperature–volume relation gives the pressure–volume relation
$$
 p_f = p_i \left(\frac{V_i}{V_f}\right)^\gamma
$$
where the effective heat-capacity ratio of the mixture is
$$
 \gamma = \frac{n_1 C_{p1} + n_2 C_{p2}}{n_1 C_{v1} + n_2 C_{v2}}
$$
For helium (monatomic) the molar heat capacities are
$$
 C_{v1} = \frac{3 R}{2}
$$
$$
 C_{p1} = \frac{5 R}{2}
$$
For nitrogen (diatomic, in this temperature range) they are
$$
 C_{v2} = \frac{5 R}{2}
$$
$$
 C_{p2} = \frac{7 R}{2}
$$
The mole numbers are
$$
 n_1 = \frac{1}{10}
$$
$$
 n_2 = \frac{1}{5}
$$
The total mole number is
$$
 n = n_1 + n_2
$$
$$
 n = \frac{3}{10}
$$
Hence the exponents for the mixture are
$$
 g = \frac{6}{13}
$$
$$
 \gamma = \frac{19}{13}
$$
For a 1\% volume reduction the final volume is
$$
 V_f = \frac{99}{100} V_i
$$
The exact temperature change is
$$
 T_f = T_i \left(\frac{100}{99}\right)^{6/13}
$$
The temperature ratio is approximately
$$
 \frac{T_f}{T_i} \approx 1.006
$$
With the given initial temperature this is
$$
 T_i = 300\unit{K}
$$
$$
 T_f \approx 302\unit{K}
$$
The exact pressure change is
$$
 p_f = p_i \left(\frac{100}{99}\right)^{19/13}
$$
The pressure ratio is approximately
$$
 \frac{p_f}{p_i} \approx 1.016
$$
The initial pressure is determined by the ideal gas law
$$
 p_i V_i = n R T_i
$$
so
$$
 p_i = \frac{n R T_i}{V_i}
$$
The initial volume in SI units is
$$
 V_i = 4 \times 10^{-3}\unit{m^3}
$$
Therefore
$$
 p_f = 1.016 \frac{n R T_i}{V_i}
$$
Numerically this is approximately
$$
 p_f \approx 2.0 \times 10^5\unit{N/m^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide your response in two parts as follows: (1) Algebraic relations: State the temperature–volume relation exactly as "T_f = T_i (V_i / V_f)^g" and give the exponent as "g = ..." written only with the symbols n_1, n_2, R, C_{v1}, C_{v2}. Also state the pressure–volume relation as "p_f = p_i (V_i / V_f)^gamma" and give the effective heat-capacity ratio as "gamma = ..." written only with the symbols n_1, n_2, C_{p1}, C_{p2}, C_{v1}, C_{v2}. (2) 1% volume reduction: Using V_f = (99/100) V_i, first write the exact expressions for T_f and p_f by substituting this V_f into the relations above. Then compute and report T_f (in K) and p_f (in N/m^2) as numerical values. Your final answer should express T_f and p_f as numerical values, rounded to the specified number of significant figures. Use T_i = 300 K, V_i = 4 L (convert to m^3), n_1 = 1/10, n_2 = 1/5, R in SI units, and p_i obtained from p_i = (n R T_i)/V_i with n = n_1 + n_2.

The symbol C_1 denotes a positive constant determined by initial conditions and is used to express the adiabatic invariant in the final relation.

subquestions.subproblem: In the big-bang theory of the universe, the radiation energy initially confined in a small region adiabatically expands in a spherically symmetric manner. The radiation cools down as it expands. Derive a relation between the temperature τ and the radius ℛ of the spherical volume of radiation, based purely on thermodynamic considerations.
subquestions.solution: For a quasi-static process the first law is $$dU=T dS-p dV$$ For an adiabatic expansion $$dS=0$$ For a photon gas $$p=\frac{U}{3V}$$ Combining these gives $$\frac{dU}{U}=-\frac{dV}{3V}$$ Integration yields $$U\propto V^{-1/3}$$ With the energy density defined by u=U/V $$u=\frac{U}{V}$$ Therefore $$u\propto V^{-4/3}$$ Using the blackbody relation $$u=a T^4$$ We obtain $$T^4\propto V^{-4/3}$$ For a sphere $$V\propto R^3$$ Hence $$T\propto R^{-1}$$ Introducing the adiabatic invariant constant C_1 $$R T=C_1$$ The entropy follows from the identity $$dS=\frac{dU}{T}+\frac{p}{T} dV$$ Using the differential of U $$dU=V du+u dV$$ And the photon-gas pressure $$p=\frac{u}{3}$$ With the energy density-temperature relation $$u=a T^4$$ Its differential is $$du=4 a T^3 dT$$ Substituting gives $$dS=4 a V T^2 dT+\frac{4}{3} a T^3 dV$$ Integration yields $$S=\frac{4}{3} a T^3 V$$ The radiation constant is $$a=\frac{\pi^2}{15} \frac{k^4}{(\hbar c)^3}$$ Therefore $$S=\frac{4 \pi^2}{45} \frac{k^4}{(\hbar c)^3} T^3 V$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of T = ..., and your response should use only the symbols T, R, and C_1.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the total entropy of a photon gas as a function of its temperature τ, volume V, and the constants k, \hbar, c (SUNY, Buffalo)
subquestions.solution: The total entropy of a photon gas is $$S=\frac{4}{3} a T^3 V$$ With the radiation constant $$a=\frac{\pi^2}{15} \frac{k^4}{(\hbar c)^3}$$ Substitution gives $$S=\frac{4 \pi^2}{45} \frac{k^4}{(\hbar c)^3} T^3 V$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of S = ..., and your response should use only the symbols T, V, k, \hbar, and c (and numerical constants if needed).

grading_standard.formula: $$dS=4 a V T^2 dT+\frac{4}{3} a T^3 dV$$

context: A material with temperature-independent heat capacity C is initially at temperature T_i and is brought to a final temperature T_f by sequentially contacting N heat reservoirs at temperatures T_i + ΔT, T_i + 2 ΔT, ..., T_i + N ΔT = T_f, where ΔT = (T_f − T_i)/N. At step t, with t ∈ {0, 1, ..., N − 1}, the material starts at temperature T_i + t ΔT and is brought to equilibrium with the reservoir at temperature T_i + (t + 1) ΔT. Let ΔS_1(t) denote the entropy change of the material during step t, ΔS_2(t) the entropy change of the reservoir used in step t, and ΔS_t = ΔS_1(t) + ΔS_2(t) the net entropy change in step t. Let ΔS denote the total entropy change of the combined system (material plus all reservoirs) after all N steps. Compute ΔS for finite N. Then evaluate lim_{N → ∞} ΔS for fixed T_f − T_i.
solution:
For step t, the entropy change of the material is
$$
\Delta S_1(t) = \int_{T_i + t \Delta T}^{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T} \frac{C dT}{T}
$$
$$
\Delta S_1(t) = C \ln \frac{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}{T_i + t \Delta T}
$$
The entropy change of the reservoir is
$$
\Delta S_2(t) = - \frac{C \Delta T}{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}
$$
The net entropy change for step t is
$$
\Delta S_t = \Delta S_1(t) + \Delta S_2(t)
$$
$$
\Delta S_t = C \ln \frac{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}{T_i + t \Delta T} - \frac{C \Delta T}{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}
$$
Summing over all steps gives
$$
\Delta S = \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \Delta S_t
$$
$$
\Delta S = C \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i} - C \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \frac{\Delta T}{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}
$$
In the limit of infinitely many reservoirs with fixed T_f − T_i, the sum becomes an integral
$$
\lim_{N \to \infty} \Delta S = C \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i} - C \int_{T_i}^{T_f} \frac{dT}{T}
$$
$$
\int_{T_i}^{T_f} \frac{dT}{T} = \ln \frac{T_f}{T_i}
$$
$$
\lim_{N \to \infty} \Delta S = 0
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: For finite N, your final answer should be given in the form ΔS = ..., written only in terms of C, T_i, T_f, and N (you may use a summation with a dummy index).
Your final answer should express lim_{N→∞} ΔS as a numerical value.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta S_t = C \ln \frac{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}{T_i + t \Delta T} - \frac{C \Delta T}{T_i + (t+1) \Delta T}$$

context: Two finite, identical, solid bodies each have a constant total heat capacity per body C. Their initial temperatures are T_1 and T_2, respectively. They are used as heat sources to drive a heat engine that operates until both bodies reach a common final temperature T_f. Find the maximum total work W_max obtainable from the system. Use SI units: C in \unit{J/K}, T_1, T_2, T_f in \unit{K}, and W, W_max in \unit{J}. Define W as the total work extracted and \Delta S as the total entropy change of the two-body system.
solution:
By energy conservation for the two bodies,
$$
W = C(T_1 - T_f) + C(T_2 - T_f)
$$
$$
W = C(T_1 + T_2 - 2 T_f)
$$
For maximum work, the reversible limit applies, so the total entropy change satisfies
$$
\Delta S = C \ln \frac{T_f}{T_1} + C \ln \frac{T_f}{T_2}
$$
$$
\Delta S = 0
$$
Hence
$$
\ln \frac{T_f}{T_1} + \ln \frac{T_f}{T_2} = 0
$$
$$
\ln \frac{T_f^2}{T_1 T_2} = 0
$$
$$
T_f^2 = T_1 T_2
$$
$$
T_f = \sqrt{T_1 T_2}
$$
Substituting into the energy expression gives the maximum work
$$
W_{\max} = C(T_1 + T_2 - 2 \sqrt{T_1 T_2})
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of W_max = ..., and your response should use only the variables C, T_1, and T_2. Do not include T_f, W, or ΔS in the final expression.

context: A reversible heat engine operates between two reservoirs with temperatures T_1 and T_2, where T_2 > T_1. The cold reservoir at T_1 has effectively infinite thermal capacity, so T_1 remains constant. The warm reservoir initially at T_2 consists of mu moles of gas in a rigid container (constant volume) with molar heat capacity C_v. The engine operates until the warm reservoir cools from T_2 down to T_1. Let T denote the instantaneous temperature of the warm reservoir during the process. Define Q_{ab} as the total heat extracted from the warm reservoir between the initial state at T_2 and the final state at T_1. Let S be the entropy of the warm reservoir and let Delta S be the change in entropy of the warm reservoir over this period. Let W be the total work done by the engine over this period. For the warm reservoir at constant volume, define dQ_{res} as the differential heat added to the warm reservoir (positive into the reservoir), so dQ_{res}=mu C_v dT. Define dQ as the differential heat absorbed by the engine from the warm reservoir (positive into the engine), so dQ=-dQ_{res}. Let dW be the differential work output of the engine. For a reversible engine exchanging heat with the warm reservoir at temperature T and rejecting heat to the cold reservoir at T_1, the relation dW/dQ=1-T_1/T holds.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the heat extracted from the warmer reservoir during this period?
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of Q_ab = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables mu, C_v, T_1, and T_2.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the change of entropy of the warmer reservoir during this period?
subquestions.solution:
Using the thermodynamic relation at constant volume:
$$dS=\frac{dQ_{res}}{T}$$
and
$$dQ_{res}=\mu C_v dT$$
Therefore,
$$\Delta S=\mu C_v \ln \frac{T_1}{T_2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ΔS = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables mu, C_v, T_1, and T_2.

subquestions.subproblem: How much work did the engine do during this period?
subquestions.solution:
For the reversible engine:
$$\frac{dW}{dQ}=1-\frac{T_1}{T}$$
With the warm reservoir at constant volume:
$$dQ=-\mu C_v dT$$
The total work is
$$W=\int dW$$
Thus,
$$W=-\int_{T_2}^{T_1} \left(1-\frac{T_1}{T}\right) \mu C_v dT$$
Evaluating the integral gives
$$W=\mu C_v (T_2-T_1)-\mu C_v T_1 \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of W = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables mu, C_v, T_1, and T_2.

context: Consider an arbitrary heat engine operating between two finite thermal reservoirs. Each reservoir has the same temperature-independent heat capacity c. The cold reservoir has initial temperature T1, the hot reservoir has initial temperature T2 with T2 > T1, and the engine operates until both reservoirs reach the same final temperature T3. Let ΔS denote the total entropy change of the two reservoirs. Let W_max denote the maximum total work output obtainable during this process. Assume the engine exchanges heat only with these two reservoirs and that no other energy exchanges occur.

subquestions.subproblem: Give the argument which shows that T3 > sqrt(T1 T2)
subquestions.solution:
The increase in entropy of the two reservoirs is
$$
\Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_3} c \frac{dT}{T} + \int_{T_2}^{T_3} c \frac{dT}{T}
$$
$$
\Delta S = c \ln \frac{T_3^2}{T_1 T_2}
$$
$$
\Delta S \geq 0
$$
$$
T_3^2 \geq T_1 T_2
$$
$$
T_3 \geq \sqrt{T_1 T_2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single inequality in the form 'T3 ≥ ...', where the right-hand side is expressed solely in terms of T1 and T2. Use only the symbols T1, T2, and T3.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the maximum amount of work obtainable from the engine?
subquestions.solution:
For maximum work the process must be reversible, so
$$
\Delta S = 0
$$
Hence the final common temperature is
$$
T_3 = \sqrt{T_1 T_2}
$$
The total work equals the decrease in total internal energy of the reservoirs, so
$$
W_{max} = c ( T_1 + T_2 - 2 T_3 )
$$
Substituting for T3 gives
$$
W_{max} = c ( T_1 + T_2 - 2 \sqrt{T_1 T_2} )
$$
which can be written as
$$
W_{max} = c ( \sqrt{T_1} - \sqrt{T_2} )^2
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form 'W_max = ...', and it must be expressed solely in terms of c, T1, and T2.

context: This problem concerns a reversible heat engine operating on the closed cycle shown in Fig. 1.22 on a T-s diagram. Here T denotes absolute temperature in \unit{K} and s denotes entropy in \unit{J/K}. Over a complete cycle, Q denotes the total heat absorbed by the engine, W denotes the net work done by the engine, and the thermal efficiency is defined by $$\eta = \frac{W}{Q}$$ From the figure, the rectangular cycle is bounded by the temperatures T = 1000\unit{K} and T = 500\unit{K}, and by the entropies s = 300\unit{J/K} and s = 400\unit{J/K}. For part (b), two equal masses M of the same liquid are mixed in a thermally insulated vessel. Let c_p^{\star} denote the specific heat capacity at constant pressure in \unit{J/(kg K)}. For clarity in the equations below, define the heat capacity of each portion as $$c_p = M c_p^{\star}$$ and note that the total entropy change is the sum $$\Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2$$ Let the initial temperatures be T_1 and T_2, and the final equilibrium temperature be T_3.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the efficiency for a reversible engine operating around the indicated cycle, where T is temperature in \unit{K} and s is the entropy in \unit{J/K}?
subquestions.solution: The heat absorbed by the engine is $$Q = (1000\unit{K} - 500\unit{K}) \frac{400\unit{J/K} + 300\unit{J/K}}{2}$$ $$Q = 175000\unit{J}$$ The net work done is $$W = (1000\unit{K} - 500\unit{K}) \frac{400\unit{J/K} - 300\unit{J/K}}{2}$$ $$W = 25000\unit{J}$$ Thus the efficiency is $$\eta = \frac{W}{Q}$$ $$\eta = 14.3\%$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the thermal efficiency \eta as a numerical value in percent (%). Report your answer to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: A mass M of a liquid at a temperature T_1 is mixed with an equal mass of the same liquid at a temperature T_2. The system is thermally insulated. If c_p is the heat capacity used in the solution, defined by c_p = M c_p^{\star} where c_p^{\star} is the specific heat of the liquid, find the total entropy change and show that the result is always positive.
subquestions.solution: The equilibrium temperature is $$T_3 = \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2}$$ Therefore $$\Delta S_1 = \int_{T_1}^{T_3} \frac{c_p dT}{T}$$ $$\Delta S_1 = c_p \ln \frac{T_3}{T_1}$$ and $$\Delta S_2 = \int_{T_2}^{T_3} \frac{c_p dT}{T}$$ $$\Delta S_2 = c_p \ln \frac{T_3}{T_2}$$ thus $$\Delta S = \Delta S_1 + \Delta S_2$$ $$\Delta S = c_p \ln \frac{(T_1 + T_2)^2}{4 T_1 T_2}$$ Since $$(T_1 + T_2)^2 \ge 4 T_1 T_2$$ we have $$\Delta S \ge 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta S = ... written only in terms of c_p, T_1, and T_2. Include a brief concluding statement indicating the sign of \Delta S in general.

context: Consider one mole of an ideal gas undergoing quasistatic reversible processes unless otherwise stated. Use S for entropy, U for internal energy, Q for the total positive heat absorbed by the gas over a specified path segment (or over the full cycle, as stated), and W for the net work done by the gas over one complete cycle. Use p for pressure, V for volume (equal to molar volume since n = 1 mole), T for temperature, R for the universal gas constant, C_v and C_p for the molar heat capacities at constant volume and constant pressure, and define gamma by gamma = C_p / C_v. For one mole of an ideal gas, the relations p V = R T and U = C_v T hold. In part (a), the initial state is (T_1, V_1) and the final state is (T_2, V_2), and the entropy change is Delta S = S_2 - S_1. In part (b), define the states A = (p_1, V_1), B = (p_2, V_2), and C = (p_2, V_1), and let their temperatures be T_A, T_B, and T_C with T_A = p_1 V_1 / R, T_B = p_2 V_2 / R, and T_C = p_2 V_1 / R. The cycle is A → B adiabatic expansion, B → C isobaric compression at p_2, and C → A isochoric pressure increase at V_1. The efficiency is defined by eta = W / Q, where Q is the total positive heat input over the cycle (on C → A).

subquestions.subproblem:
One mole of an ideal gas is carried from temperature T_1 and molar volume V_1 to temperature T_2 and molar volume V_2. Show that the change in entropy is
$$\Delta S = C_v \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln \frac{V_2}{V_1}$$
subquestions.solution:
From
$$dS = \frac{1}{T} ( dU + p dV )$$
and
$$dU = C_v dT$$
together with
$$p V = R T$$
we obtain
$$\Delta S = C_v \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1} + R \ln \frac{V_2}{V_1}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ΔS = ... , and your response should be written with C_v, R, T_1, T_2, V_1, V_2.

subquestions.subproblem:
An ideal gas is expanded adiabatically from A = ( p_1 , V_1 ) to B = ( p_2 , V_2 ). Then it is compressed isobarically to C = ( p_2 , V_1 ). Finally the pressure is increased to p_1 at constant volume V_1 (i.e., C → A). Show that the efficiency of the cycle is
$$\eta = 1 - \gamma \frac{ V_2 / V_1 - 1 }{ p_1 / p_2 - 1 }$$
where gamma = C_p / C_v.
subquestions.solution:
The work the system does in the cycle is
$$W = \oint p dV$$
and
$$W = \int_{AB} p dV + p_2 ( V_1 - V_2 )$$
Because AB is adiabatic for an ideal gas and C_p = C_v + R, we get
$$\int_{AB} p dV = - \int_{AB} C_v dT$$
and
$$\int_{AB} p dV = - C_v ( T_B - T_A )$$
Using T = p V / R and C_v = R / ( \gamma - 1 ), we obtain
$$\int_{AB} p dV = \frac{1}{1 - \gamma} ( p_2 V_2 - p_1 V_1 )$$
During the CA part of the cycle the gas absorbs heat
$$Q = \int_{CA} T dS$$
and
$$Q = \int_{CA} C_v dT$$
so
$$Q = C_v ( T_A - T_C )$$
Using V = V_1 on CA and T = p V / R, we get
$$Q = \frac{1}{1 - \gamma} V_1 ( p_2 - p_1 )$$
Hence, the efficiency of the engine is
$$\eta = \frac{W}{Q}$$
and finally
$$\eta = 1 - \gamma \frac{ V_2 / V_1 - 1 }{ p_1 / p_2 - 1 }$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of η = ... , and your response should be written with gamma, V_1, V_2, p_1, p_2.

grading_standard.formula: $$\int_{AB} p dV = \frac{1}{1 - \gamma} ( p_2 V_2 - p_1 V_1 )$$

context: (1) A thermodynamic system has entropy S, volume V, internal energy U, and number of particles N related by S = A (N V U)^{1/3}, where A is a positive constant. Let τ denote the absolute temperature T. Use the thermodynamic definitions 1/T = (∂S/∂U)_{V,N} and p/T = (∂S/∂V)_{U,N}. Define the heat capacity at constant volume by c_v = (∂U/∂T)_{V,N}. (2) Two identical bodies consist solely of the material obeying the equation of state from part (1). They have the same N and V, and their initial temperatures are T_1 and T_2. They are brought to a common final temperature T_f by withdrawing heat from the hotter body and inserting some fraction into the colder body, with the remainder appearing as work W delivered to a work reservoir that carries no entropy. For later use, define S(T) and U(T) as the entropy and internal energy of a single body at temperature T (at fixed N and V) for this material. Define T_f^* as the final temperature that maximizes the delivered work, W_max as this maximum work, and C_U = (A/3)^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2}

subquestions.subproblem: Derive a relation among U, N, V, and τ (the absolute temperature).
subquestions.solution:
Use the thermodynamic definition
$$
\frac{1}{T} = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_{V,N}
$$
From S = A (N V U)^{1/3}, compute
$$
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_{V,N} = \frac{A}{3} (N V)^{1/3} U^{-2/3}
$$
Invert to obtain
$$
T = 3 A^{-1} (N V)^{-1/3} U^{2/3}
$$
Solve for U and use τ = T
$$
U = \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} \tau^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of U = ..., and your response should be written using only A, N, V, and τ.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive a relation among the pressure p, N, V, and τ.
subquestions.solution:
Use the thermodynamic definition
$$
\frac{p}{T} = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{U,N}
$$
From S = A (N V U)^{1/3}, compute
$$
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_{U,N} = \frac{A}{3} (N U)^{1/3} V^{-2/3}
$$
Eliminate U using the result of part (a) to obtain
$$
p = \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} N^{1/2} \tau^{3/2} V^{-1/2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of p = ..., and your response should be written using only A, N, V, and τ.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the specific heat at constant volume c_v.
subquestions.solution:
Use the definition
$$
 c_v = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_{V,N}
$$
From U(T) in part (a), obtain
$$
 c_v = \frac{3}{2} \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2} T^{1/2}
$$
With τ = T, write
$$
 c_v = \frac{3}{2} \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2} \tau^{1/2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of c_v = ..., and your response should be written using only A, N, V, and τ.

subquestions.subproblem: (2) What is the range of possible final temperatures T_f?
subquestions.solution:
At fixed N and V for each body, the entropy as a function of temperature is
$$
S(T) = A^{3/2} 3^{-1/2} (N V)^{1/2} T^{1/2}
$$
The second law with a work reservoir that carries no entropy requires
$$
2 S(T_f) \ge S(T_1) + S(T_2)
$$
This gives the lower bound
$$
T_f \ge \left( \frac{\sqrt{T_1} + \sqrt{T_2}}{2} \right)^2
$$
Define the extracted work by
$$
W = U(T_1) + U(T_2) - 2 U(T_f)
$$
Nonnegative delivered work requires
$$
W \ge 0
$$
Using U(T) = \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2} T^{3/2}, the upper bound is
$$
T_f \le \left( \frac{T_1^{3/2} + T_2^{3/2}}{2} \right)^{2/3}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be an inequality for T_f in the form lower_bound ≤ T_f ≤ upper_bound, and your response should be written using only T_f, T_1, and T_2.

subquestions.subproblem: (2) What T_f corresponds to the maximum delivered work, and what is this maximum amount of work? Consider both reversible and irreversible processes.
subquestions.solution:
The extracted work is
$$
W = U(T_1) + U(T_2) - 2 U(T_f)
$$
Maximal work is obtained by minimizing T_f subject to the second law, achieved for a reversible process satisfying
$$
2 S(T_f) = S(T_1) + S(T_2)
$$
Thus the final temperature for maximum work is
$$
T_f^{*} = \left( \frac{\sqrt{T_1} + \sqrt{T_2}}{2} \right)^2
$$
For convenience define
$$
C_U = \left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^{3/2} (N V)^{1/2}
$$
With U(T) = C_U T^{3/2}, the maximum work is
$$
W_{\max} = C_U \left( T_1^{3/2} + T_2^{3/2} - 2 (T_f^{*})^{3/2} \right)
$$
Using T_f^{*}, this equals
$$
W_{\max} = C_U \left( T_1^{3/2} + T_2^{3/2} - \frac{1}{4} ( \sqrt{T_1} + \sqrt{T_2} )^{3} \right)
$$
An equivalent factorized form is
$$
W_{\max} = \frac{3}{4} C_U ( \sqrt{T_1} - \sqrt{T_2} )^{2} ( \sqrt{T_1} + \sqrt{T_2} )
$$
For any irreversible process,
$$
T_f > T_f^{*}
$$
and the delivered work satisfies
$$
W < W_{\max}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two expressions and two inequalities: (i) T_f^{*} = ... written using only T_1 and T_2; (ii) W_{max} = ... written using only C_U, T_1, and T_2; and (iii) the irreversible-process inequalities in the forms T_f > T_f^{*} and W < W_{max}, written using only T_f, T_f^{*}, W, and W_{max}.

context: One kilogram of water is heated by an electrical resistor from 20 \unit{^\circ C} to 99 \unit{^\circ C} at constant atmospheric pressure. Use M for the mass of the water, c for the specific heat at constant pressure, T_1 and T_2 for the initial and final absolute temperatures, respectively, and \Delta T = T_2 - T_1. Let \Delta U denote the change in internal energy of the water, S the entropy, \Delta S the change in entropy of the water, \Omega the number of accessible quantum states with \Omega_1 and \Omega_2 the initial and final values, k the Boltzmann constant, F_\Omega = \Omega_2/\Omega_1 the factor by which the number of accessible states increases, and W_{\max} the maximum mechanical work obtainable by using this water as a heat reservoir to run a reversible engine whose heat sink is at T_1. Use the numerical values M = 1000 \unit{g}, c = 1 \unit{cal/(g K)}, T_1 = 293 \unit{K} (corresponding to 20 \unit{^\circ C}), and T_2 = 372 \unit{K} (corresponding to 99 \unit{^\circ C}). When needed, use the exact conversion 1 \unit{cal} = \frac{523}{125} \unit{J}. Estimate:

subquestions.subproblem: The change in internal energy of the water.
subquestions.solution:
$$\Delta U = M c \Delta T$$
$$\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$$
$$\Delta T = 79 \unit{K}$$
$$\Delta U = 79000 \unit{cal}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \Delta U as a numerical value in calories (cal). Provide your result rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: The entropy change of the water.
subquestions.solution:
$$\Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} \frac{M c}{T} dT$$

The heat capacities (extensive) are defined below. For an ideal gas, the relation c_p = c_v + n R holds. For part b, define T_1 and T_2 as the initial and final temperatures in the house.
$$S=\frac{n}{2}\left[\sigma+5R\ln\frac{U}{n}+2R\ln\frac{V}{n}\right]$$

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate c_p and c_v, the specific heats at constant pressure and volume.
subquestions.solution:
The temperature is determined by
$$\frac{1}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_V$$
From the given S,
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_V=\frac{5nR}{2U}$$
Hence
$$U=\frac{5}{2}nRT$$
Therefore
$$c_v=\left(\frac{dU}{dT}\right)_V$$
$$c_v=\frac{5}{2}nR$$
Using the ideal-gas relation
$$c_p=c_v+nR$$
we obtain
$$c_p=\frac{7}{2}nR$$

context: A perfect gas is defined by the equation of state p V = N k T and by the property that its internal energy U depends only on the absolute temperature T. Here p is the pressure, V is the volume, N is the number of molecules, k is the Boltzmann constant, S is the entropy, and U is the internal energy. Let c_p and c_v denote the heat capacities per molecule at constant pressure and constant volume, respectively. Let gamma = c_p / c_v be constant. Define K_ad as the constant value of p V^gamma along a reversible adiabatic path. For a perfect gas show that:
source: Assume that gamma = c_p / c_v is constant

subquestions.subproblem: Show that c_p = c_v + k, where c_p and c_v are the heat capacities per molecule at constant pressure and constant volume, respectively
subquestions.solution: From the equation of state we have $$p V = N k T$$ From the fundamental relation we have $$T dS = dU + p dV$$ Using the per-molecule definitions $$c_p = \frac{T}{N} \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_p$$ and $$c_v = \frac{T}{N} \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V$$ it follows that $$c_p - c_v = \frac{T}{N} \left[ \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_p - \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V \right]$$ Using the identity $$T \left[ \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_p - \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V \right] = p \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_p$$ we obtain $$c_p - c_v = \frac{1}{N} p \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_p$$ From p V = N k T we have $$\left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_p = \frac{N k}{p}$$ Hence $$c_p - c_v = k$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of c_p = ..., and your response should use only the variables c_p, c_v, and k.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that p V^gamma is constant during a reversible adiabatic expansion
subquestions.solution: For a reversible adiabatic process we have $$T dS = 0$$ For a perfect gas with U depending only on T, we have $$dU = N c_v dT$$ so that $$N c_v dT = - p dV$$ Differentiating the equation of state yields $$p dV + V dp = N k dT$$ Using c_p - c_v = k gives $$p dV + V dp = N \left( c_p - c_v \right) dT$$ Eliminating dT using N c_v dT = - p dV gives $$p dV + V dp = - \frac{c_p - c_v}{c_v} p dV$$ Introducing gamma = c_p / c_v yields $$\gamma p dV + V dp = 0$$ Dividing by p V gives $$d \ln p + \gamma d \ln V = 0$$ Integrating along the adiabatic path gives $$p V^{\gamma} = K_{ad}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of p V^{\gamma} = ..., and your response should use only the symbols p, V, \gamma, and K_{ad}.

grading_standard.formula: $$T \left[ \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_p - \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V \right] = p \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \right)_p$$
$$p dV + V dp = N k dT$$
$$p dV + V dp = N \left( c_p - c_v \right) dT$$
$$p dV + V dp = - \frac{c_p - c_v}{c_v} p dV$$

context: Consider a simple gas. Let c_p and c_v denote the specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume, respectively, defined per unit mass with SI units of J/(kg K). Let C_p and C_v denote the molar heat capacities with SI units of J/(mol K). Let S be the entropy, T the temperature, p the pressure, V the volume, m the mass of the gas sample, n the number of moles, M the molar mass, R the universal gas constant, α the coefficient of thermal expansion, and κ_T the isothermal compressibility. Tasks: 1) Find the approximate numerical value of c_p - c_v for simple gases and explain the physical reason why c_p differs from c_v. 2) Calculate c_p - c_v for an ideal gas, expressing the result both per unit mass and per mole.
solution:
$$
c_p - c_v = 
\frac{1}{m} \Big( T \Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \Big)_p - T \Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \Big)_V \Big)
$$
$$
S(T,p) = S(T, V(T,p))
$$
$$
\Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \Big)_p = \Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \Big)_V + \Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial V} \Big)_T \Big( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \Big)_p
$$
$$
\Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial V} \Big)_T = \Big( \frac{\partial p}{\partial T} \Big)_V
$$
$$
c_p - c_v = \frac{T}{m} \Big( \frac{\partial p}{\partial T} \Big)_V \Big( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \Big)_p
$$
$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{V} \Big( \frac{\partial V}{\partial T} \Big)_p
$$
$$
\kappa_T = -\frac{1}{V} \Big( \frac{\partial V}{\partial p} \Big)_T
$$
$$
\Big( \frac{\partial p}{\partial T} \Big)_V = \frac{\alpha}{\kappa_T}
$$
$$
c_p - c_v = \frac{V T \alpha^2}{m \kappa_T}
$$
For an ideal gas, the material properties are
$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{T}
$$
$$
\kappa_T = \frac{1}{p}
$$
and therefore
$$
c_p - c_v = \frac{n R}{m}
$$
$$
c_p - c_v = \frac{R}{M}
$$
Equivalently, on a molar basis for an ideal gas,
$$
C_p - C_v = R
$$
with the approximate numerical value
$$
R \approx 8.314 \unit{J/(mol K)}
$$
Thus, for many simple gases whose equations of state are close to ideal, c_p - c_v is approximately R/M. The physical reason that c_p > c_v is that, at constant pressure, the gas expands and performs work p dV, so additional heat is required compared with heating at constant volume.

context: A paramagnetic system is placed in a uniform external magnetic field H and is thermally insulated from the surroundings, so the process is adiabatic with constant entropy S. The system is quasi-statically demagnetized from an initial field H_i to a final field H_f=0 while remaining in internal equilibrium. The internal energy is U, the entropy is S, the temperature is T, and the induced magnetization is M. The equation of state for the magnetization is M=a H/T, and the heat capacity at constant H is c_H=b/T^2, where a and b are positive constants. Use dU=T dS+H dM for this magnetic system. Determine how the temperature T changes as H is reduced to zero, and express T(H) and the final temperature T_f in terms of the initial temperature T_i and field H_i. Then, find the initial field strength H_i required so that the final temperature is half of the initial temperature, i.e., T_f=T_i/2. All logarithms are natural logarithms, and the final answers should be written using the variables H_i, H_f, T_i, T_f, a, and b as defined above.
solution:
From the fundamental relation for this magnetic system
$$
dU=T dS+H dM
$$
we have the Maxwell-type relation
$$
\frac{\partial T}{\partial M}\bigg|_S=\frac{\partial H}{\partial S}\bigg|_M
$$
which implies the Jacobian identity
$$
\frac{\partial(T,S)}{\partial(H,M)}=-1
$$
Using Jacobians,
$$
\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\bigg|_S=\frac{\partial(T,S)}{\partial(H,S)}
$$
and
$$
\frac{\partial(T,S)}{\partial(H,S)}=\frac{\partial(H,T)}{\partial(H,S)}\cdot\frac{\partial(H,M)}{\partial(H,T)}\cdot\frac{\partial(T,S)}{\partial(H,M)}
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\bigg|_S=-\frac{\partial T}{\partial S}\bigg|_H\cdot\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\bigg|_H
$$
Using the definition of heat capacity at constant H,
$$
c_H=T\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\bigg|_H
$$
so
$$
\frac{\partial T}{\partial S}\bigg|_H=\frac{T}{c_H}
$$
From the equation of state for magnetization,
$$
M=\frac{a H}{T}
$$
we have
$$
\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\bigg|_H=-\frac{a H}{T^2}
$$
and from the given heat capacity,
$$
c_H=\frac{b}{T^2}
$$
Combining these results gives the adiabatic temperature–field slope
$$
\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\bigg|_S=\frac{a T H}{b}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
\frac{dT}{dH}=\frac{a T H}{b}
$$
so
$$
\frac{dT}{T}=\frac{a}{b}H\,dH
$$
Integrating from an arbitrary H to the final state H_f=0 with temperature T_f yields
$$
\int_{T(H)}^{T_f}\frac{dT}{T}=\frac{a}{\b}\int_{H}^{0}H\,dH
$$
which gives
$$
\ln\frac{T_f}{T(H)}=-\frac{a H^2}{2 b}
$$
Hence the adiabatic demagnetization path is
$$
T(H)=T_f\exp\!\bigg(\frac{a H^2}{2 b}\bigg)
$$
Evaluated at the initial field H_i with initial temperature T_i,
$$
T_i=T_f\exp\!\bigg(\frac{a H_i^2}{2 b}\bigg)
$$
so the final temperature at H_f=0 is
$$
T_f=T_i\exp\!\bigg(-\frac{a H_i^2}{2 b}\bigg)
$$
This shows that the temperature decreases as H is reduced to zero under adiabatic, quasi-static demagnetization. For a factor-of-2 reduction, impose
$$
T_f=\frac{T_i}{2}
$$
which gives
$$
\frac{1}{2}=\exp\!\bigg(-\frac{a H_i^2}{2 b}\bigg)
$$
and therefore the required initial field is
$$
H_i=\sqrt{\frac{2 b}{a}\ln 2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide three explicit algebraic expressions as your final answer: (1) T(H) = ... written only in terms of H, H_i, T_i, a, and b; (2) T_f = ... written only in terms of T_i, H_i, a, and b; and (3) under the condition T_f = T_i/2, give H_i = ... written only in terms of a and b. Do not introduce any additional variables or constants.

context:
A substance has the equation of state relating pressure p, volume V, and temperature T with a constant A. Its internal energy U depends on constants B, n, a reference volume V_0, and a function f(T) of temperature only. Let S denote the entropy. Determine the constants B and n such that S is a state function consistent with the first law of thermodynamics. The equation of state is
$$p=\frac{A T^3}{V}$$
The internal energy is
$$U=B T^n \ln\frac{V}{V_0}+f(T)$$
Here p is the pressure, V is the volume, T is the temperature, A is a constant, U is the internal energy, B and n are constants to be determined, V_0 is a constant reference volume, f(T) depends only on T, and S is the entropy.
solution:
From the first law of thermodynamics in differential form
$$dS=\frac{dU+p dV}{T}$$
Express dS in terms of partial derivatives
$$dS=\left[\frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T+\frac{p}{T}\right] dV+\frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT$$
Compute the partial derivatives
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T=\frac{B T^n}{V}$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V=n B T^{n-1}\ln\frac{V}{V_0}+\frac{df}{dT}$$
Substitute p and the partial derivatives
$$dS=\frac{B T^{n-1}+A T^2}{V} dV+\left[\frac{1}{T}\frac{df}{dT}+n B T^{n-2}\ln\frac{V}{V_0}\right] dT$$
Impose exactness of dS by equating mixed partial derivatives
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{B T^{n-1}+A T^2}{V}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left[\frac{1}{T}\frac{df}{dT}+n B T^{n-2}\ln\frac{V}{V_0}\right]$$
This yields
$$2 A T-B T^{n-2}=0$$
Therefore
$$n=3$$
$$B=2A$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as two expressions in the form n = ... and B = ... . The expression for B must be written only in terms of A, and n should be given as a constant. Do not introduce any variables other than A, n, and B in your final expressions.

grading_standard.formula: $$dS=\left[\frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T+\frac{p}{T}\right] dV+\frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT$$
$$dS=\frac{B T^{n-1}+A T^2}{V} dV+\left[\frac{1}{T}\frac{df}{dT}+n B T^{n-2}\ln\frac{V}{V_0}\right] dT$$
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{B T^{n-1}+A T^2}{V}\right)=\frac{\partial}{\partial V}\left[\frac{1}{T}\frac{df}{dT}+n B T^{n-2}\ln\frac{V}{V_0}\right]$$

$$S=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial T}\bigg|_L$$

$$0=k_T dL+\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L dT$$
$$\delta L=-\frac{1}{k_T}\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L dT$$
$$\delta Q=T dS$$
$$dS=\frac{C_L}{T} dT-\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L dL$$
$$\delta Q=C_L dT+T\frac{\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L\right)^2}{k_T} dT$$
$$k_S=k_T+T\frac{\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L\right)^2}{C_L}$$
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L=\frac{C_L}{T}\frac{dT}{dL}\bigg|_S$$
$$\delta L=-\frac{\delta Q}{T k_S}\frac{dT}{dL}\bigg|_S$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be written explicitly as \delta L = ..., and your response should be written with \delta Q, T, k_S, and (dT/dL)_S.

grading_standard.formula: $$df=\frac{\partial f}{\partial L}\bigg|_T dL+\frac{\partial f}{\partial T}\bigg|_L dT$$

context:
A rubber band in equilibrium has tension t given as a function of its length x and absolute temperature T by the constitutive relation below. Variables and parameters: t = tension, T = absolute temperature, x = length of the band, l_0 = length of the band when t = 0, A = constant, E = internal energy, S = entropy, c_x(x,T) = heat capacity at fixed length x. At the special length x = l_0, the heat capacity is observed to be a constant κ, independent of T; denote this constant by K, i.e., c_x(l_0,T) = K. You may use T_0 as an arbitrary reference temperature, E(T_0) as an integration constant for the energy, and C as an integration constant for the entropy. In part (b), denote the final temperature by T_f. The constitutive relation is
$$
t = A T \left( \frac{x}{l_0} - \frac{l_0^2}{x^2} \right)
$$

subquestions.subproblem: Find, as functions of T and x: (1) (∂E/∂x)_T, (2) (∂ c_x / ∂ x)_T, (3) c_x(x,T), (4) E(x,T), (5) S(x,T).
subquestions.solution:
First law
$$
dE = T dS + t dx
$$
Heat capacity at fixed x
$$
c_x = T \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_x
$$
Energy-temperature relation at fixed x
$$
c_x = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \right)_x
$$
Treat E as a function E(x,T)
$$
dE = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \right)_x dT + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T dx
$$
Hence
$$
dE = c_x dT + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T dx
$$
From the first law
$$
dS = \frac{1}{T} dE - \frac{t}{T} dx
$$
Therefore
$$
dS = \frac{c_x}{T} dT + \frac{1}{T} \left[ \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T - t \right] dx
$$
Equality of mixed partials for E
$$
\frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial x \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial T \partial x}
$$
Equality of mixed partials for S
$$
\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial T \partial x}
$$
Resulting identity
$$
\left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T = t - T \left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial T} \right)_x
$$
Constitutive law
$$
t = A T \left( \frac{x}{l_0} - \frac{l_0^2}{x^2} \right)
$$
Temperature derivative at fixed x
$$
\left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial T} \right)_x = A \left( \frac{x}{l_0} - \frac{l_0^2}{x^2} \right)
$$
Hence
$$
\left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T = 0
$$
Thus
$$
\left( \frac{\partial c_x}{\partial x} \right)_T = 0
$$
Using the condition at x = l_0
$$
c_x(x,T) = K
$$
Energy from c_x
$$
E(T) - E(T_0) = \int_{T_0}^{T} K dT
$$
Therefore
$$
E(T) = K ( T - T_0 ) + E(T_0)
$$
Entropy differential with the above results
$$
dS = \frac{K}{T} dT - A \left( \frac{x}{l_0} - \frac{l_0^2}{x^2} \right) dx
$$
Integration gives
$$
S(x,T) = K \ln T - A \frac{x^2}{2 l_0} - A \frac{l_0^2}{x} + C
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide all five symbolic expressions, clearly labeled (1)–(5), as follows: (1) give (∂E/∂x)_T as a constant (no variables permitted); (2) give (∂ c_x / ∂ x)_T as a constant (no variables permitted); (3) give c_x(x,T) using only K; (4) give E(x,T) in the form E(T) = … using only K, T, T_0, and E(T_0); (5) give S(x,T) using only A, l_0, x, T, K, and the integration constant C.

subquestions.subproblem: The band is stretched adiabatically from x = l_0 to x = (3/2) l_0. Its initial temperature was T_0. What is its final temperature T_f?
subquestions.solution:
Adiabatic process condition
$$
\frac{K}{T} dT - A \left( \frac{x}{l_0} - \frac{l_0^2}{x^2} \right) dx = 0
$$
Integrating from the initial state to the final state
$$
K \ln \frac{T_f}{T_0} = A \left[ \frac{ \left( \frac{3}{2} l_0 \right)^2 }{ 2 l_0 } + \frac{ l_0^2 }{ \frac{3}{2} l_0 } - \frac{ l_0^2 }{ 2 l_0 } - \frac{ l_0^2 }{ l_0 } \right]
$$
Hence
$$
K \ln \frac{T_f}{T_0} = 0.292 A l_0
$$
Therefore
$$
T_f = T_0 \exp \left( \frac{0.292 A l_0}{K} \right)
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form T_f = …, and may only contain T_0, A, l_0, and K (and numerical constants).

grading_standard.formula: $$dE = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \right)_x dT + \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T dx$$
$$\frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial x \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial T \partial x}$$
$$\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial T \partial x}$$
$$\left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} \right)_T = t - T \left( \frac{\partial t}{\partial T} \right)_x$$
$$S(x,T) = K \ln T - A \frac{x^2}{2 l_0} - A \frac{l_0^2}{x} + C$$
$$K \ln \frac{T_f}{T_0} = A \left[ \frac{ \left( \frac{3}{2} l_0 \right)^2 }{ 2 l_0 } + \frac{ l_0^2 }{ \frac{3}{2} l_0 } - \frac{ l_0^2 }{ 2 l_0 } - \frac{ l_0^2 }{ l_0 } \right]$$

context: Definitions and assumptions for both subproblems: p is the pressure, V the volume, N the number of moles, T the absolute temperature (corresponding to the τ symbol in the original statement), and R the universal gas constant. For a monatomic ideal gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is C_v = 3 R / 2. U is the internal energy, S the entropy, and F the Helmholtz free energy. Reference-state constants are U_0 (the internal energy at T = 0), T_0 and V_0 (a chosen reference temperature and volume), and S_0 = S(T_0, V_0). We also define S_0' as the constant of integration that arises when integrating the entropy at unspecified reference values, and F_0 = U_0 - T_0 S_0 as a constant. In part (b), the cylinder has two compartments, a and b, each containing one mole of monatomic ideal gas, so N_a = 1 and N_b = 1. The separating piston is adiabatic and impermeable, the cylinder walls are diathermal, and the entire cylinder is immersed in a large thermal bath at 0\unit{\degree C}. Initial volumes are V_{a i} = 10\unit{L} and V_{b i} = 1\unit{L}, and final volumes are V_{a f} = 6\unit{L} and V_{b f} = 5\unit{L}. The work W is taken as positive if delivered by the system to the surroundings, and dW_a and dW_b denote the differential works delivered by compartments a and b, respectively

subquestions.subproblem: Using the equation of state p V = N R T and the molar specific heat C_v = 3 R / 2 for a monatomic ideal gas, find the Helmholtz free energy F as a function of N, V, and T. Express your result in terms of the reference-state constants T_0, V_0, S_0, U_0, and F_0 defined in the context
subquestions.solution:
For an ideal gas, the internal energy differential is
$$dU = N C_v dT$$
Integrating with respect to T gives
$$U = N C_v T + U_0$$
The entropy differential is
$$dS = \frac{N C_v}{T} dT + \frac{p}{T} dV$$
The ideal-gas equation of state is
$$p V = N R T$$
Hence
$$\frac{p}{T} = \frac{N R}{V}$$
Integrating for a monatomic ideal gas with C_v = \frac{3 R}{2} yields
$$S = \frac{3 N R}{2} \ln T + N R \ln V + S_0'$$
Choosing the reference state at T_0 and V_0 gives
$$S = \frac{3 N R}{2} \ln \frac{T}{T_0} + N R \ln \frac{V}{V_0} + S_0$$
By definition of the Helmholtz free energy,
$$F = U - T S$$
Substituting U and S gives
$$F = \frac{3 N R T}{2} - \left( \frac{3 N R T}{2} \ln \frac{T}{T_0} - N R T \ln \frac{V}{V_0} \right) + F_0$$
with the constant
$$F_0 = U_0 - T_0 S_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form F(N, V, T) = ... , and your response should use only the symbols N, V, T, R, T_0, V_0, and F_0.

subquestions.subproblem: A cylinder is separated into two parts by an adiabatic, impermeable piston. Compartments a and b each contain one mole of a monatomic ideal gas. Initially, V_{a i} = 10\unit{L} and V_{b i} = 1\unit{L}. The cylinder walls are diathermal and the cylinder is immersed in a large thermal bath at 0\unit{\degree C}. The piston is moved reversibly so that the final volumes are V_{a f} = 6\unit{L} and V_{b f} = 5\unit{L}. How much work W is delivered by the system?
subquestions.solution:
Since the bath fixes the temperature, each compartment undergoes an isothermal process, so with dT = 0 we have
$$dF = - p dV$$
The total work delivered by the system is
$$W = \int dW_a + \int dW_b$$
Using W = - \Delta F at fixed T for each compartment gives
$$W = - \int dF_a - \int dF_b$$
Hence
$$W = \left( N_a \ln \frac{V_{a f}}{V_{a i}} + N_b \ln \frac{V_{b f}}{V_{b i}} \right) R T$$
The numerical result is
$$W = 2.6 \times 10^3 \unit{J}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the total work W as a numerical value in joules (J). Use two significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$S = \frac{3 N R}{2} \ln T + N R \ln V + S_0'$$
$$F = \frac{3 N R T}{2} - \left( \frac{3 N R T}{2} \ln \frac{T}{T_0} - N R T \ln \frac{V}{V_0} \right) + F_0$$
$$W = \left( N_a \ln \frac{V_{a f}}{V_{a i}} + N_b \ln \frac{V_{b f}}{V_{b i}} \right) R T$$

context: A resistor with resistance R=100 \unit{\Omega} is held at a constant temperature T=300 \unit{K} by a large thermal reservoir. A constant current I=10 \unit{A} is passed through the resistor for a time t=300 \unit{s}. Define the following quantities: \Delta S_1 is the entropy change of the resistor, \Delta S_2 is the entropy change of the reservoir, \Delta S is the entropy change of the universe (resistor + reservoir), \Delta U is the change in internal energy of the universe, and \Delta F is the change in the Helmholtz free energy of the universe. The electrical energy dissipated in the resistor is given by Q=I^2 R t, and the reservoir is at temperature T throughout.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the change in the entropy of the resistor?
subquestions.solution:
As the temperature of the resistor is constant and its thermodynamic state returns to its initial state, the entropy change of the resistor is zero.
$$\Delta S_1=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔS_1 as a numerical value in J/K.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the change in the entropy of the universe?
subquestions.solution:
The heat that flows from the resistor to the thermal reservoir at temperature T is:
$$Q=I^2 R t$$
$$Q=3\times 10^6 \unit{J}$$
The increase of entropy of the reservoir is:
$$\Delta S_2=\frac{Q}{T}$$
$$\Delta S_2=10^4 \unit{J/K}$$
Thus the total change of entropy of the universe is:
$$\Delta S=\Delta S_1+\Delta S_2$$
$$\Delta S=10^4 \unit{J/K}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔS as a numerical value in J/K.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the change in the internal energy of the universe?
subquestions.solution:
The increase of the internal energy of the universe equals the electrical energy dissipated:
$$\Delta U=3\times 10^6 \unit{J}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔU as a numerical value in J.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the change in the Helmholtz free-energy of the universe?
subquestions.solution:
The change in Helmholtz free energy is:
$$\Delta F=\Delta U-T\Delta S$$
$$\Delta F=0 \unit{J}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔF as a numerical value in J.

context: Blackbody radiation. Consider an isotropic radiation field in a cavity of volume V at absolute temperature T. Let F be the Helmholtz free energy, S the entropy, p the pressure, U(T,V) the total internal energy, and u(T) the energy density defined by U(T,V)=u(T)V. Maxwell's electromagnetic theory implies the radiation pressure relations p = u(T)/3 and p = U(T,V)/(3V). Use the thermodynamic identities dF = -S dT - p dV and dU = T dS - p dV. In solving the differential equation for u(T), let a be the positive constant of integration.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂p/∂T)_V
subquestions.solution:
$$dF = - S dT - p dV$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial T}\right)_V = - S$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right)_T = - p$$
$$\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial V \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial T \partial V}$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form (∂S/∂V)_T = ..., and your response should only involve S, V, T, and p.

subquestions.subproblem: From electromagnetic theory, Maxwell found that the pressure p from an isotropic radiation field equals one third of the energy density u(T): p = u(T)/3 and p = U(T,V)/(3V), where V is the cavity volume. Using the first law and the Maxwell relation from part (a), relate u(T) to T
subquestions.solution:
$$U(T,V) = u(T) V$$
$$dU = T dS - p dV$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T - p$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V$$
$$p = \frac{1}{3} u(T)$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = u(T)$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V = \frac{1}{3} \frac{du}{dT}$$
$$u = \frac{T}{3} \frac{du}{dT} - p$$
$$u = \frac{1}{3} T \frac{du}{dT} - \frac{1}{3} u$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a differential relation between u and T in the form u = ..., and your response should only involve u and T.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that u obeys the equation u = (1/3) T du/dT - (1/3) u
subquestions.solution: $$u = \frac{1}{3} T \frac{du}{dT} - \frac{1}{3} u$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form u = ..., and your response should only involve u and T.

subquestions.subproblem: Solve this equation and obtain Stefan's law relating u and T
subquestions.solution:
$$u = \frac{1}{3} T \frac{du}{dT} - \frac{1}{3} u$$
$$T \frac{du}{dT} = 4 u$$
$$\frac{du}{u} = \frac{4}{T} dT$$
$$\ln u = 4 \ln T + \ln a$$
$$u = a T^4$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form u = ..., and your response should only involve u, T, and a.

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial V \partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial T \partial V}$$
$$\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T - p$$

context:
A thermodynamic system has Gibbs free energy

$$
G(p,T)=R T \ln \frac{a p}{(R T)^{5/2}}
$$

where p is the pressure, T is the absolute temperature, and a and R are constants. Let S denote the entropy and C_p the specific heat at constant pressure. Find C_p.
solution:
The entropy is

$$
S=-(\frac{\partial G}{\partial T})_p
$$

Using the given G(p,T),

$$
S=\frac{5}{2}R-R\ln \frac{a p}{(R T)^{5/2}}
$$

The specific heat at constant pressure is

$$
C_p=T(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T})_p
$$

Therefore,

$$
C_p=\frac{5}{2}R
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of C_p = ..., expressed only in terms of R.

context: Consider a simple compressible substance held at pressure p and absolute temperature T. Let V be the volume and S be the entropy. Define the heat emitted from the system during a reversible process as Q_{em}, with differential dQ_{em} = - T dS. Show that, at constant temperature T, the following holds: (∂Q_{em}/∂p)_T = T (∂V/∂T)_p. Use standard thermodynamic notation, where subscripts on partial derivatives indicate the variable held constant.
solution:
From the Maxwell relation

$$- (\frac{\partial S}{\partial p})_T = (\frac{\partial V}{\partial T})_p$$

Multiplying by T gives

$$- T (\frac{\partial S}{\partial p})_T = T (\frac{\partial V}{\partial T})_p$$

By definition of heat emitted for a reversible process

$$dQ_{em} = - T dS$$

At constant temperature T this implies

$$(\frac{\partial Q_{em}}{\partial p})_T = - T (\frac{\partial S}{\partial p})_T$$

Combining the results yields

$$(\frac{\partial Q_{em}}{\partial p})_T = T (\frac{\partial V}{\partial T})_p$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of (∂Q_em/∂p)_T = [expression], and your response should only involve T, V, and p using standard thermodynamic partial-derivative notation (e.g., (∂V/∂T)_p).

grading_standard.formula: $$- T (\frac{\partial S}{\partial p})_T = T (\frac{\partial V}{\partial T})_p$$

context: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell produces electrical energy W by feeding O2 to one electrode and H2 to the other. The gases react reversibly, isothermally, and isobarically at p = 1 \unit{atm} and T = 298 \unit{K} to form liquid water. The internal resistance of the cell is negligible. Calculate the cell e.m.f. \varepsilon for the formation of 1 \unit{mol} of water. Definitions and data: q is the total electric charge transferred through the external circuit, F is the Faraday constant with F = 96500 \unit{C/mol}, h_O, h_H, h_W are the molar enthalpies at 1 \unit{atm} and 298 \unit{K} for O2, H2, and H2O, respectively, with h_O = 17200 \unit{J/mol}, h_H = 8100 \unit{J/mol}, h_W = -269300 \unit{J/mol}. S_O, S_H, S_W are the corresponding molar entropies with S_O = 201 \unit{J/(mol.K)}, S_H = 128 \unit{J/(mol.K)}, S_W = 66.7 \unit{J/(mol.K)}. \Delta G denotes the Gibbs free energy change of the reaction.
solution:
The overall reaction is
$$
H_2 + \frac{1}{2} O_2 = H_2O
$$
For a reversible isothermal and isobaric cell, the maximum electrical work equals the decrease of Gibbs free energy
$$
-\Delta G = \varepsilon \Delta q
$$
For the reaction basis of forming 1 \unit{mol} of water, the Gibbs free energy change is
$$
\Delta G = (h_W - T S_W) - \left(h_H + \frac{1}{2} h_O - T \left(S_H + \frac{1}{2} S_O\right)\right)
$$
The charge transferred for forming 1 \unit{mol} of water is
$$
\Delta q = 2 F
$$
Therefore, the e.m.f. is
$$
\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2 F} \left[T S_W - h_W - T \left(S_H + \frac{1}{2} S_O\right) + \left(h_H + \frac{1}{2} h_O\right)\right]
$$
Substituting the numerical values gives
$$
\varepsilon = 1.23 \unit{V}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the cell e.m.f. ε as a numerical value in V. Report your answer to 3 significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta G = (h_W - T S_W) - \left(h_H + \frac{1}{2} h_O - T \left(S_H + \frac{1}{2} S_O\right)\right)$$
$$\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2 F} \left[T S_W - h_W - T \left(S_H + \frac{1}{2} S_O\right) + \left(h_H + \frac{1}{2} h_O\right)\right]$$

context: A simple magnetic system is studied under the following condition: at fixed absolute temperature T, when the magnetic field H is changed to H + ΔH, the entropy S changes by an amount ΔS given by the linear relation ΔS = - C H ΔH / T^2, where C is a constant characteristic of the system. Here S denotes entropy, T denotes absolute temperature, H denotes magnetic field, M denotes magnetization, and G denotes the Gibbs free energy. Determine how the magnetization M depends on the temperature T for small H. To fix the integration constant, assume that in this simple system the magnetization vanishes in the high-temperature limit at fixed small H, i.e., lim_{T→∞} M(T,H) = 0. Also sketch the qualitative plot of M versus T for small H (the diagram is shown in Fig. 1.28).
solution:
From the given linear response at fixed T, we have
$$
\Delta S = - \frac{C H \Delta H}{T^2}
$$
Taking the differential limit yields
$$
\left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial H} \right)_T = - \frac{C H}{T^2}
$$
From the Gibbs identity
$$
dG = - S dT - M dH
$$
we obtain the Maxwell relation
$$
\left( \frac{\partial M}{\partial T} \right)_H = \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial H} \right)_T
$$
Therefore
$$
\left( \frac{\partial M}{\partial T} \right)_H = - \frac{C H}{T^2}
$$
Integrating from T to infinity at fixed H gives
$$
M(\infty,H) - M(T,H) = \int_T^{\infty} - \frac{C H}{t^2} dt
$$
Using the high-temperature condition
$$
\lim_{T \to \infty} M(T,H) = 0
$$
yields
$$
M(T,H) = \frac{C H}{T}
$$
For fixed small H, M decreases as 1/T with increasing T, as shown qualitatively in Fig. 1.28
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form M(T,H) = ..., and your response should use only the variables C, H, and T.

context: A certain magnetic salt obeys Curie's law and has a heat capacity per unit volume at constant magnetic field inversely proportional to the square of the absolute temperature. Equivalently, its magnetic susceptibility and total heat capacity at constant field are specified by the relations χ = b/T and c_H = α V/T^2 with α = b + a H^2, where a and b are constants, V is the sample volume, and H is the magnitude of the applied uniform magnetic field. Let μ_0 denote the vacuum permeability. A sample initially at temperature T_i is placed in a magnetic field of strength H and then adiabatically and quasistatically demagnetized to zero field. Use M = χ H for the magnetization M, S for the entropy, and G(T,H) for the Gibbs free energy. Find the final temperature τ.
solution:
For a reversible adiabatic process we have
$$(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T})_H dT + (\frac{\partial S}{\partial H})_T dH = 0$$
From the definition of heat capacity at constant field we use
$$c_H = T (\frac{\partial S}{\partial T})_H$$
From the Gibbs free energy differential we use
$$dG = - S dT - \mu_0 M V dH$$
which implies the Maxwell relation
$$(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H})_T = \mu_0 V (\frac{\partial M}{\partial T})_H$$
With the constitutive relation for magnetization
$$M = \chi H$$
we obtain
$$(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H})_T = \mu_0 V H (\frac{\partial \chi}{\partial T})_H$$
Therefore the adiabatic condition gives
$$\frac{dT}{dH} = - \frac{(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H})_T}{(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T})_H}$$
so that
$$\frac{dT}{dH} = - \frac{\mu_0 V H T}{c_H} \frac{d\chi}{dT}$$
Using Curie's law
$$\chi = \frac{b}{T}$$
we have
$$\frac{d\chi}{dT} = - \frac{b}{T^2}$$
Using the given heat capacity
$$c_H = \frac{\alpha V}{T^2}$$
with
$$\alpha = b + a H^2$$
we obtain the differential equation
$$\frac{dT}{dH} = \frac{\mu_0 b H T}{\alpha}$$
which can be written as
$$\frac{dT}{T} = \frac{\mu_0 b H}{\alpha} dH$$
Integrating from T_i at field H to the final temperature \tau at zero field gives
$$\int_{T_i}^{\tau} \frac{dT}{T} = \mu_0 b \int_{H}^{0} \frac{H}{b + a H^2} dH$$
Evaluating the integrals yields
$$\ln \frac{\tau}{T_i} = \frac{\mu_0 b}{2 a} \ln \frac{b}{b + a H^2}$$
Thus the final temperature is
$$\tau = \left( \frac{b}{b + a H^2} \right)^{\frac{\mu_0 b}{2 a}} T_i$$
