context: In a closed container at the triple point of water, one gram each of ice, liquid water, and water vapor are initially in equilibrium. The pressure is 4.58\unit{mmHg} and the temperature is 1/100\unit{^\circ C}. Then heat Q=60\unit{cal} is added to the system while the total volume of the container is kept constant. Assume ideal-gas behavior for the vapor. Let x, y, z denote, respectively, the final masses of ice, liquid water, and water vapor in grams. Calculate, to within 2\%, the values of x, y, and z. Justify your answer. Use the following data at 1/100\unit{^\circ C}: latent heat of fusion L_{fus}=80\unit{cal/g}, latent heat of vaporization L_{vap}=596\unit{cal/g}, latent heat of sublimation L_{sub}=676\unit{cal/g}, water and ice densities \rho_{water}=\rho_{ice}=1\unit{g/cm^3}, molar mass of water \mu=18\unit{g/mol}, ideal-gas constant R=8.2\times 10^8\unit{m^3 atm/(mol K)}, absolute temperature T=273.16\unit{K}, and pressure p=4.58\unit{mmHg}. You may also note that the volume of the vapor is much larger than the volume of the water or the volume of the ice.
solution:
Let the initial vapor volume be V_0 and the final vapor volume be V. At the new equilibrium, the masses of ice, water, and water vapor are x, y, and z, respectively. Conservation of mass gives
$$
x+y+z=3
$$
Energy accounting at fixed temperature using the vapor as reference gives
$$
(1-x)L_{sub}+(1-y)L_{vap}=Q
$$
with
$$
Q=60\unit{cal}
$$
Constancy of total volume gives
$$
\frac{1-x}{\rho_{ice}}+\frac{1-y}{\rho_{water}}+V_0=V
$$
The ideal-gas relations for the vapor volume per unit mass give
$$
V_0=\frac{RT}{\mu p}
$$
$$
V=\frac{zRT}{\mu p}
$$
with the parameters
$$
\mu=18\unit{g/mol}
$$
$$
p=4.58\unit{mmHg}
$$
$$
T=273.16\unit{K}
$$
$$
R=8.2\times 10^8\unit{m^3 atm/(mol K)}
$$
$$
\rho_{ice}=1\unit{g/cm^3}
$$
$$
\rho_{water}=1\unit{g/cm^3}
$$
$$
L_{sub}=676\unit{cal/g}
$$
$$
L_{vap}=596\unit{cal/g}
$$
Solving these equations yields
$$
x=\frac{1}{4}\unit{g}
$$
$$
y=\frac{7}{4}\unit{g}
$$
$$
z=1\unit{g}
$$
Thus the added 60\unit{cal} effectively converts \frac{3}{4}\unit{g} of ice into \frac{3}{4}\unit{g} of liquid water at constant vapor mass, consistent with L_{sub}-L_{vap}=L_{fus}=80\unit{cal/g}.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express x, y, and z as numerical values in grams. Report each value to 3 significant figures.

context: Determine the ratio r_c = p_c V_c / (R T_c) at the critical point for a gas that obeys the Dieterici equation of state p (V - b) = R T exp(-a / (R T V)). Here p is the pressure, V is the molar volume, T is the temperature, R is the universal gas constant, and a and b are positive constants characteristic of the gas. The critical point (p_c, V_c, T_c) is defined by the conditions (∂p/∂V)_T = 0 and (∂^2 p/∂V^2)_T = 0 evaluated at T = T_c and V = V_c. Report the numerical value of r_c accurately to two significant figures.
solution:
The critical point conditions are
$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\Bigg|_{T}=0
$$
$$
\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial V^2}\Bigg|_{T}=0
$$
From the equation of state p = \frac{R T}{V - b} \exp\big(-\frac{a}{R T V}\big), we obtain
$$
\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\Bigg|_{T}=R T \frac{\frac{a(V-b)}{R T V^2}-1}{(V-b)^2} e^{-\frac{a}{R T V}}
$$
Thus the first critical condition gives
$$
\frac{a(V-b)}{R T V^2}-1=0
$$
Using this result, the second derivative at fixed T is
$$
\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial V^2}\Bigg|_{T}=\frac{a}{(V-b) V^3} \left(\frac{a}{R T V}-2\right) e^{-\frac{a}{R T V}}
$$
Thus the second critical condition gives
$$
\frac{a}{R T V}-2=0
$$
Solving the two critical conditions yields
$$
V_c=2b
$$
$$
R T_c=\frac{a}{4b}
$$
From the equation of state, the desired ratio at general V and T is
$$
\frac{p V}{R T}=\frac{V}{V-b} e^{-\frac{a}{R T V}}
$$
At the critical point this becomes
$$
r_c=\frac{p_c V_c}{R T_c}=2 e^{-2}
$$
Numerically, to two significant figures
$$
r_c\approx 0.27
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express r_c = p_c V_c / (R T_c) as a numerical value to two significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\Bigg|_{T}=R T \frac{\frac{a(V-b)}{R T V^2}-1}{(V-b)^2} e^{-\frac{a}{R T V}}$$
$$\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial V^2}\Bigg|_{T}=\frac{a}{(V-b) V^3} \left(\frac{a}{R T V}-2\right) e^{-\frac{a}{R T V}}$$

context: Consider a charged, thin conducting soap bubble of equilibrium radius r carrying total charge q. Let the electric potential at the bubble surface be φ. The air inside the bubble is phase α with pressure p^α, the air outside is phase β with pressure p^β, and the soap film is phase γ. Let F^α, F^β, and F^γ denote the Helmholtz free energies of phases α, β, and γ, respectively. Define the excess of ambient pressure over internal pressure as Δp = p^β - p^α. Assume the temperature is constant and surface tension is neglected. The bubble is a spherical conductor in Gaussian units, so φ = q/r. Use the minimum free energy condition to find the relation among r, φ, and Δp. You may use V^α = 4π r^3/3, δV^α = 4π r^2 δr, and δV^β = - δV^α.
solution:
We use the minimum free energy principle at constant temperature.

$$
\delta F^\alpha = - p^\alpha \delta V^\alpha
$$

$$
\delta F^\beta = - p^\beta \delta V^\beta
$$

$$
\delta F^\gamma = q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r
$$

$$
V^\alpha = \frac{4\pi r^3}{3}
$$

$$
\delta V^\alpha = 4\pi r^2 \delta r
$$

$$
\delta V^\beta = - \delta V^\alpha
$$

$$
\delta F^\alpha + \delta F^\beta + \delta F^\gamma = 0
$$

$$
- p^\alpha \delta V^\alpha - p^\beta \delta V^\beta + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r = 0
$$

$$
\left(p^\beta - p^\alpha\right) \delta V^\alpha + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r = 0
$$

$$
\left(p^\beta - p^\alpha\right) 4\pi r^2 \delta r + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r = 0
$$

$$
\left(p^\beta - p^\alpha\right) 4\pi r^2 + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} = 0
$$

$$
\Delta p = p^\beta - p^\alpha
$$

$$
\Delta p = - \frac{q}{4\pi r^2} \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r}
$$

$$
\phi = \frac{q}{r}
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} = - \frac{q}{r^2}
$$

$$
\Delta p = \frac{\phi^2}{4\pi r^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of Δp = ..., and your response should be written with r and φ only.

grading_standard.formula: $$- p^\alpha \delta V^\alpha - p^\beta \delta V^\beta + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r = 0$$
$$\left(p^\beta - p^\alpha\right) 4\pi r^2 \delta r + q \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial r} \delta r = 0$$

context: Consider a spherical soap bubble made from a soap film of constant surface tension sigma and filled with air modeled as a perfect gas. Denote the ambient external pressure by p_0 and the temperature by T. Let r be the equilibrium radius of the bubble, m the mass of air inside the bubble, R the universal gas constant, and M the molar mass of air. Let p_1 be the pressure of the air inside the bubble, V_1 the volume of the air inside the bubble, V_2 the volume of the surrounding air displaced, tau the surface area of the soap film, U the total internal energy of the combined system, S its entropy, mu_1 and mu_2 the chemical potentials of air inside and outside the bubble, and N_1 and N_2 the corresponding particle numbers. Use SI units for all quantities: r in \unit{m}, p_0 and p_1 in \unit{Pa}, T in \unit{K}, sigma in \unit{N/m}, R in \unit{J/(mol K)}, M in \unit{kg/mol}, and m in \unit{kg}.

subquestions.subproblem: Find a relation between the equilibrium radius r of the soap bubble and the mass m of air inside it.
subquestions.solution:
The fundamental differential for the combined system is
$$dU = T dS - p_1 dV_1 - p_0 dV_2 + \sigma d\tau + \mu_1 dN_1 + \mu_2 dN_2$$
At equilibrium
$$dU = 0$$
$$dS = 0$$
$$\mu_1 = \mu_2$$
$$dV_1 = - dV_2$$
$$d(N_1 + N_2) = 0$$
Hence
$$(p_1 - p_0) dV_1 = \sigma d\tau$$
Therefore
$$p_1 - p_0 = \sigma \frac{d\tau}{dV_1}$$
For a sphere
$$\frac{d\tau}{dV_1} = \frac{2}{r}$$
Thus
$$p_1 - p_0 = \frac{2\sigma}{r}$$
For the ideal gas inside the bubble
$$p_1 V_1 = \frac{m}{M} R T$$
And the volume of the bubble is
$$V_1 = \frac{4\pi}{3} r^3$$
Combining these results gives
$$m = \frac{4\pi}{3} \frac{M}{R T} r^3 \left(p_0 + \frac{2\sigma}{r}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of m = ..., and your response should be written using only r, p_0, sigma, R, T, and M.

subquestions.subproblem: Solve the relation of part a for the radius r in the limit that the bubble is large. Define precisely what is meant by large.
subquestions.solution:
The large-bubble limit means
$$p_0 \gg \frac{2\sigma}{r}$$
Equivalently
$$r \gg \frac{2\sigma}{p_0}$$
In this limit the relation reduces to
$$m = \frac{4\pi M p_0 r^3}{3 R T}$$
Solving for the radius gives
$$r = \left(\frac{3 R T m}{4\pi M p_0}\right)^{1/3}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide two items: (i) State the precise 'large-bubble' criterion as a single inequality involving only r, p_0, and sigma; (ii) In that limit, give the radius in the form r = ..., expressed only in terms of m, p_0, R, T, and M.

context: Derive the vapor-pressure equation (Clausius-Clapeyron equation) for liquid-vapor equilibrium along the coexistence curve. Let p be the pressure and T the temperature. For each phase i in {1 (vapor), 2 (liquid)}, let mu_i be the chemical potential per mole (molar Gibbs free energy), S_i the molar entropy, and V_i the molar volume. Let L be the latent heat of vaporization per mole, with L = T(S_1 - S_2) at equilibrium. Find dp/dT along the coexistence curve.
solution:
The differentials of the molar chemical potentials of the vapor (phase 1) and liquid (phase 2) satisfy

$$
d\mu_1 = - S_1 dT + V_1 dp
$$

$$
d\mu_2 = - S_2 dT + V_2 dp
$$

At phase equilibrium one has

$$
\mu_1 = \mu_2
$$

Along the coexistence curve this implies

$$
d\mu_1 = d\mu_2
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{S_1 - S_2}{V_1 - V_2}
$$

Using the latent heat per mole

$$
L = T(S_1 - S_2)
$$

one obtains

$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T(V_1 - V_2)}
$$

When the liquid molar volume is much smaller than the vapor molar volume

$$
V_2 \ll V_1
$$

the equation simplifies to

$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T V_1}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of dp/dT = ..., and your response should be written with L, T, V_1, V_2 only.

context: Consider a single-component liquid-vapor system along its coexistence curve. Let T be the temperature, p be the pressure, and mu be the chemical potential per particle. Let S be the entropy per particle and V be the volume per particle. Subscripts L and V denote liquid and vapor phases, respectively, so S_L, V_L are for the liquid and S_V, V_V are for the vapor. Define the heat of vaporization per particle as q = T(S_V - S_L). In part (b), assume the vapor behaves as an ideal gas so that p V_V = k T, where k is the Boltzmann constant, and that the vapor density is much smaller than the liquid density so V_V >> V_L. Assume q is independent of T.

subquestions.subproblem: By equating the chemical potential on the two sides of the liquid-vapor coexistence curve, derive the Clausius-Clapeyron equation in the form dp/dT = q / [T (V_V - V_L)], where q is the heat of vaporization per particle, V_L is the volume per particle in the liquid, and V_V is the volume per particle in the vapor
subquestions.solution: From the first law of thermodynamics for the chemical potential per particle we have $$d \mu = - S d T + V d p$$ At coexistence the chemical potentials of the liquid and vapor are equal, so infinitesimal changes must satisfy $$- S _ { L } d T + V _ { L } d p = - S _ { V } d T + V _ { V } d p$$ It follows that $$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { S _ { V } - S _ { L } } { V _ { V } - V _ { L } }$$ With q defined by $$q = T \left( S _ { V } - S _ { L } \right)$$ we obtain $$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { T \left( V _ { V } - V _ { L } \right) }$$ which is the Clausius-Clapeyron equation
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form dp/dT = ..., and your response should use only the variables q (heat of vaporization per particle), T (temperature), V_V (vapor volume per particle), and V_L (liquid volume per particle).

subquestions.subproblem: Assuming the vapor follows the ideal gas law and has a density much less than that of the liquid, and that the heat of vaporization is independent of T, show that p(T) has the form p(T) = p_0 exp(- q / (k T))
subquestions.solution: For the vapor treated as an ideal gas per particle we have $$p V _ { V } = k T$$ Since the vapor density is much smaller than that of the liquid, we neglect V_L in the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to write $$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { T V _ { V } }$$ Using the ideal gas relation V_V = k T / p, we obtain $$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q p } { k T ^ { 2 } }$$ Equivalently, $$\frac { 1 } { p } \frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { k T ^ { 2 } }$$ Integrating with respect to T yields $$\ln p = - \frac { q } { k T } + C$$ Therefore, with p_0 = e^C, the pressure is $$p \left( T \right) = p _ 0 \exp \left( - \frac { q } { k T } \right )$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form p(T) = ..., and your response should use only the variables T (temperature), q (heat of vaporization per particle), k (Boltzmann constant), and p_0 (constant of integration).

grading_standard.formula: $$d \mu = - S d T + V d p$$
$$- S _ { L } d T + V _ { L } d p = - S _ { V } d T + V _ { V } d p$$
$$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { S _ { V } - S _ { L } } { V _ { V } - V _ { L } }$$
$$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { T \left( V _ { V } - V _ { L } \right) }$$
$$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { T V _ { V } }$$
$$\frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q p } { k T ^ { 2 } }$$
$$\frac { 1 } { p } \frac { d p } { d T } = \frac { q } { k T ^ { 2 } }$$

context: A \unit{g} sample undergoing a liquid–vapor phase change is taken around a very thin reversible rectangular cycle that straddles the coexistence curve, as shown in Fig. 1.34. Let T be the absolute temperature in \unit{K}, p the pressure in \unit{Pa}, ΔT the small temperature difference between the two isotherms, and Δp the small pressure difference between the two isobars. The sample mass is \unit{g}. Let L be the latent heat absorbed by this \unit{g} during isothermal, isobaric vaporization, with units \unit{J}. Let V_1 be the volume of the \unit{g} as saturated liquid and V_2 be the volume of the \unit{g} as saturated vapor, both at temperature T and pressure p, with units \unit{m^3}. Let W denote the total external work done by the system over one cycle, with units \unit{J}. Let Q denote the net heat absorbed over one cycle, with units \unit{J}. Let η be the thermal efficiency defined by η = W/Q_hot, where Q_hot is the heat absorbed from the hot isotherm; for this cycle, Q_hot = L. Assume the cycle is reversible so that its efficiency equals the Carnot efficiency η = ΔT/T in the limit of small ΔT. Show that the slope of the coexistence curve satisfies dT/dp = T(V_2 - V_1)/L.
solution:
In this reversible cycle, the isobaric process along the coexistence line is isothermal. Define Q as the net heat absorbed over one cycle; for a complete cycle, Q equals the net external work W. The efficiency relative to the hot isotherm is
$$
\eta = \frac{Q}{L}
$$
For a reversible cycle that operates between T and T + \Delta T with \Delta T small, the Carnot efficiency is
$$
\eta = \frac{\Delta T}{T}
$$
Therefore,
$$
Q = \frac{\Delta T}{T} L
$$
The external work over the very flat rectangular cycle is
$$
W = \Delta p (V_2 - V_1)
$$
Since the internal energy change over a full cycle is zero, we have
$$
Q = W
$$
Thus,
$$
\frac{\Delta T}{T} L = \Delta p (V_2 - V_1)
$$
Taking the differential limit yields
$$
\frac{dT}{dp} = \lim_{\Delta p \to 0} \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta p}
$$
and therefore
$$
\frac{dT}{dp} = \frac{T (V_2 - V_1)}{L}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form dT/dp = ..., and your response should be written using only the variables T, p, V_1, V_2, and L.

context: Data and goal: The specific latent heat of vaporization of water is L_s = 2.44×10^6\unit{J/kg}. The saturated water vapor density at the boiling point is ρ_2 = 0.598\unit{kg/m^3} at 100\unit{^\circ C}. The density of liquid water is ρ_1 = 1000\unit{kg/m^3}. Assume an isothermal atmosphere with air temperature T_0 = 300\unit{K}. The density of air at 0\unit{^\circ C} and 1\unit{atm} is ρ = 1.29\unit{kg/m^3}. Let z be altitude, p(z) the atmospheric pressure at altitude z, and p(0) the sea-level pressure. Let m be the mean mass of an air molecule, k the Boltzmann constant, and g the gravitational acceleration with g = 9.8\unit{m/s^2}. Let T be the boiling temperature of water at pressure p, and let T(0) denote the boiling temperature at sea level with T(0) = 100\unit{^\circ C}. Define the constant α by α = L_s ρ_1 ρ_2/(ρ_1 − ρ_2). Using these definitions and the relations below, find the sea-level slope S = dT/dz near z = 0, and report S in \unit{^\circ C/km}.
solution:
The barometric formula for an isothermal atmosphere is
$$
p(z)=p(0)\exp\big(-\frac{mgz}{kT_0}\big)
$$
The Clausius-Clapeyron relation using specific volumes written via densities is
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{L_s}{T\big(\frac{1}{\rho_2}-\frac{1}{\rho_1}\big)}
$$
Define
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{\alpha}{T}
$$
with
$$
\alpha=\frac{L_s\rho_1\rho_2}{\rho_1-\rho_2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
L_s=2.44\times 10^6\unit{J/kg}
$$
$$
\rho_1=1000\unit{kg/m^3}
$$
$$
\rho_2=0.598\unit{kg/m^3}
$$
$$
\alpha=1.40\times 10^6\unit{J/m^3}
$$
The desired slope is
$$
\frac{dT}{dz}=\frac{dT}{dp}\frac{dp}{dz}
$$
From Clausius-Clapeyron,
$$
\frac{dT}{dp}=\frac{T}{\alpha}
$$
From the barometric formula,
$$
\frac{dp}{dz}=-\frac{mg}{kT_0}p(z)
$$
Using the ideal-gas relation at sea level,
$$
p(0)=\frac{\rho k T_0}{m}
$$
we obtain near sea level
$$
\frac{dp}{dz}=-\rho g
$$
Therefore,
$$
\frac{dT}{dz}=-\frac{\rho g}{\alpha}T(0)
$$
With ρ=1.29\unit{kg/m^3}, g=9.8\unit{m/s^2}, and T(0)=100\unit{^\circ C},
$$
\frac{dT}{dz}=-0.87\unit{^\circ C/km}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the sea-level slope S = dT/dz at z = 0 as a numerical value in °C/km, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A long vertical cylindrical column is filled with a single substance and placed in a uniform gravitational field of magnitude g. The system is at absolute temperature T. At equilibrium, the part of the column below a certain horizontal level is solid and the part above that level is liquid. Let the solid have density ρ_s and specific volume V_s=1/ρ_s, and let the liquid have density ρ_1 and specific volume V_1=1/ρ_1. When the temperature is lowered by ΔT, with ΔT/T ≪ 1, the solid–liquid interface is observed to move upward by a distance l. Neglect the thermal expansion of the solid and take L to be the latent heat per unit mass for the solid–liquid phase transition. Let p denote pressure. Find an expression for the liquid density ρ_1 in terms of ρ_s, L, g, T, and ΔT.
solution:
By the Clausius–Clapeyron relation
$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T\left(V_1 - V_s\right)}
$$
and with specific volumes expressed via densities
$$
V_1 = \frac{1}{\rho_1}
$$
$$
V_s = \frac{1}{\rho_s}
$$
we obtain
$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T\left(\frac{1}{\rho_1} - \frac{1}{\rho_s}\right)}
$$
When the temperature decreases by ΔT, the interface rises by l. The hydrostatic change of the interface pressure equals the change due to the weight of the solid below, hence
$$
dT = -\Delta T
$$
$$
dp = -\rho_s g l
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\rho_s g l}{\Delta T} = \frac{L}{T\left(\frac{1}{\rho_1} - \frac{1}{\rho_s}\right)}
$$
which gives
$$
\frac{1}{\rho_1} - \frac{1}{\rho_s} = \frac{L\Delta T}{T\rho_s g l}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\frac{1}{\rho_1} = \frac{1}{\rho_s} + \frac{L\Delta T}{T\rho_s g l}
$$
Hence the required density of the liquid is
$$
\rho_1 = \frac{\rho_s}{1 + \frac{L\Delta T}{T g l}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of ρ_1 = ... , and your response should be written only with the symbols ρ_s, L, g, T, ΔT, and l.

context: Definitions and notation for all parts: Let T denote temperature, p denote pressure, and z denote depth below the Earth's surface taken positive downward. Let T_m(p) be the melting temperature at pressure p. Let mu be the chemical potential per unit mass, S the entropy per unit mass, V the specific volume per unit mass, and L the latent heat of fusion per unit mass. Let rho be density with subscripts l and s denoting liquid and solid phases, respectively. Let g be the local gravitational acceleration, assumed approximately constant near the surface. The hydrostatic relation is to be written with dp/dz positive for increasing depth.

subquestions.subproblem: Use simple thermodynamic considerations to obtain a relation between \frac{1}{T_m} \frac{dT_m}{dp}, the logarithmic rate of variation of melting point with change of pressure, the densities of the solid and liquid phases, and the latent heat of melting. You may find it convenient to relate the latent heat to the entropy change.
subquestions.solution: During the phase transition, the equilibrium condition is $$\mu_l = \mu_s$$ Using the thermodynamic identity $$d\mu = -S dT + V dp$$ evaluation along the melting curve T_m(p) gives $$\left(S_l - S_s\right) dT_m = \left(V_l - V_s\right) dp$$ Hence $$\frac{1}{T_m} \frac{dT_m}{dp} = \frac{V_l - V_s}{T_m \left(S_l - S_s\right)}$$ Relating latent heat and entropy change, $$L = T_m \left(S_l - S_s\right)$$ therefore $$\frac{1}{T_m} \frac{dT_m}{dp} = \frac{V_l - V_s}{L}$$ Using V = 1/\rho for each phase gives $$\frac{dT_m}{T_m dp} = \frac{1}{L \rho_l} \left(1 - \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_s}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form (dT_m)/(T_m dp) = ..., and your response should be written with T_m, L, rho_l, rho_s.

subquestions.subproblem: Use simple hydrostatic considerations to relate the pressure gradient within the Earth to the Earth's density and the acceleration of gravity. Assume that the region in question is not at great depth below the surface.
subquestions.solution: Denoting depth by z, the hydrostatic relation is $$\frac{dp}{dz} = \rho g$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form dp/dz = ..., and your response should be written with rho and g.

subquestions.subproblem: Combine the foregoing to calculate the rate of variation of the melting point of silicate rock with increasing depth below the Earth's surface in a region where the average melting point of the rock is 1300 \unit{^\circ C}. Assume a density ratio \rho_{liquid} / \rho_{solid} \approx 0.9 and a latent heat of melting of 100 \unit{cal/g}. Give your answer in degrees C per kilometer.
subquestions.solution: From the above results, $$\frac{dT_m}{dz} = \frac{T_m \, \rho \, g}{L \, \rho_l} \left(1 - \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_s}\right)$$ Approximating \rho \approx \rho_l gives $$\frac{dT_m}{dz} \approx \frac{T_m g}{L} \left(1 - \frac{\rho_l}{\rho_s}\right)$$ Numerically, $$\frac{dT_m}{dz} = 37 \times 10^{-6} \unit{^\circ C/cm}$$ The requested rate expressed per kilometer is $$R_{Tm} = 3.7 \unit{^\circ C/km}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express R_Tm = dT_m/dz as a numerical value in units of ^\circ C/km, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: The vapor pressure p of ammonia, measured in \unit{mmHg}, is given as a function of the absolute temperature T in \unit{K} by the following relations. For solid ammonia: $$\ln p = 23.03 - \frac{3754}{T}$$ For liquid ammonia: $$\ln p = 19.49 - \frac{3063}{T}$$ Define T_0 as the triple-point temperature in \unit{K}, at which the solid and liquid have the same vapor pressure. Define R as the molar ideal gas constant, used numerically as the standard value R \approx 8.314\unit{J/(mol K)} in calculations. Define C as a dimensionless integration constant in the liquid relation. Define V_g and V_l as the molar volumes of the vapor and liquid, respectively, and V as the molar volume of the vapor. Define \Delta V = V_g - V_l. Define L_vap as the latent heat of vaporization (per mole), L_sub as the latent heat of sublimation (per mole), and L_m as the latent heat of melting (per mole). Let S_g, S_l, and S_s denote the molar entropies of the vapor, liquid, and solid at the triple point. These latent heats satisfy $$L_{vap} = T_0\left(S_g - S_l\right)$$ $$L_{sub} = T_0\left(S_g - S_s\right)$$ $$L_m = T_0\left(S_l - S_s\right)$$ All logarithms are natural logarithms

subquestions.subproblem: What is the temperature of the triple point?
subquestions.solution: At the triple point, the vapor pressures of the solid and liquid are equal, so $$23.03 - \frac{3754}{T_0} = 19.49 - \frac{3063}{T_0}$$ Solving for T_0 gives $$T_0 = \frac{3754 - 3063}{23.03 - 19.49}$$ Therefore $$T_0 \approx 195\unit{K}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the triple-point temperature T_0 as a numerical value in kelvin (K), rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the latent heat of vaporization (boiling) at the triple point. Express your answer in cal/mole. (You may approximate the behavior of the vapor by treating it as an ideal gas, and may use the fact that the density of the vapor is negligibly small compared to that of the liquid.)
subquestions.solution: From the liquid relation $$\ln p = C - \frac{3063}{T}$$ we obtain $$\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{3063\,p}{T^2}$$ The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is $$\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L_{vap}}{T\,\Delta V}$$ With \Delta V \approx V and ideal-gas vapor, $$V = \frac{R T}{p}$$ Substituting gives $$L_{vap} = \frac{3063\,p\,V}{T}$$ Using V = R T p^{-1} yields $$L_{vap} = 3063\,R$$ In SI units, $$L_{vap} \approx 2.54\times 10^{4}\unit{J/mol}$$ Converting to calories per mole, $$L_{vap} \approx 6037\unit{cal/mol}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the latent heat of vaporization at the triple point, L_vap, as a numerical value in calories per mole (cal/mol), rounded to 4 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: The latent heat of sublimation at the triple point is 7508 cal/mole. What is the latent heat of melting at the triple point?
subquestions.solution: From the entropy relations at the triple point, $$L_m = L_{sub} - L_{vap}$$ Substituting values gives $$L_m = 7508 - 6037$$ Therefore $$L_m = 1471\unit{cal/mol}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the latent heat of melting at the triple point, L_m, as a numerical value in calories per mole (cal/mol), rounded to 4 significant figures.

context: Liquid helium-4 has a normal boiling point at T_0=4.2\unit{K} under a saturation pressure p_0=1\unit{atm}=760\unit{mmHg}. At a reduced pressure p=1\unit{mmHg}, it boils at T=1.2\unit{K}. Estimate the average molar latent heat of vaporization L of helium-4 over this temperature range. You may take the saturated vapor to behave as an ideal gas, neglect the liquid molar volume compared to the vapor molar volume, and treat L as approximately constant over the interval. Use R for the universal gas constant, V_g for the molar volume of the saturated vapor, and V_l for the molar volume of the saturated liquid.
solution:
According to the Clausius-Clapeyron equation for a phase equilibrium
$$
\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T\left(V_g - V_l\right)}
$$
Neglecting the liquid molar volume relative to the vapor molar volume
$$
\frac{dp}{dT} \approx \frac{L}{T V_g}
$$
Using the ideal-gas equation of state for the saturated vapor
$$
p V_g = R T
$$
Assuming L is approximately constant and combining the relations, integrate between (p_0,T_0) and (p,T)
$$
\int_{p_0}^{p} \frac{dp}{p} = \frac{L}{R} \int_{T_0}^{T} \frac{dT}{T^2}
$$
Carrying out the integrals
$$
\ln \frac{p}{p_0} = \frac{L}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_0} - \frac{1}{T} \right)
$$
Solving for L
$$
L = \frac{R \ln \frac{p}{p_0}}{\frac{1}{T_0} - \frac{1}{T}}
$$
With the given data
$$
T_0 = 4.2\unit{K}
$$
$$
T = 1.2\unit{K}
$$
$$
p_0 = 760\unit{mmHg}
$$
$$
p = 1\unit{mmHg}
$$
$$
R = 8.314\unit{J/(mol K)}
$$
we obtain the average molar latent heat
$$
L \approx 93\unit{J/mol}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the average molar latent heat of vaporization L as a numerical value in units of J/mol. Report your result to 2 significant figures.

context: A working substance undergoes an infinitesimal Carnot cycle in the liquid–gas coexistence region shown in Fig. 1.38 of the p–V diagram. Symbols used throughout: p is the pressure, V is the molar volume, T is the absolute temperature, L is the latent heat of vaporization per mole, and ΔV is the molar volume change between gas and liquid. R is the universal gas constant. For an infinitesimal Carnot cycle operating between isotherms at T and T + dT, the efficiency satisfies dW/Q = dT/T. In part b, liquid helium is considered with its normal boiling point and vapor pressure, and we assume the vapor density is much smaller than the liquid density so that ΔV ≈ V_gas. The target unknown in part b is T_m, the equilibrium temperature of the liquid at the reduced pressure p_m. Use SI units for all quantities; temperature in K and pressure in any consistent units, noting that ratios of pressures are dimensionless.

subquestions.subproblem: The pressure–volume diagram shows two neighboring isotherms in the region of a liquid–gas phase transition. By considering an infinitesimal Carnot cycle between temperatures T and T + dT in the shaded region of the diagram, derive the Clausius–Clapeyron equation relating the vapor pressure and temperature, where L is the latent heat of vaporization per mole and ΔV is the molar volume change between gas and liquid. Show that
subquestions.solution:
From the p–V diagram, the work done by the working substance in the infinitesimal Carnot cycle is
$$dW = dp \Delta V$$
The heat absorbed from the hot reservoir in the cycle is per mole
$$Q = L$$
For an infinitesimal Carnot engine, the efficiency satisfies
$$\frac{dW}{Q} = \frac{dT}{T}$$
Therefore
$$\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L}{T \Delta V}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be an explicit expression for dp/dT in terms of L, T, and ΔV only. Write it in the form 'dp/dT = [expression in L, T, ΔV]'.

subquestions.subproblem:
Liquid helium boils at the temperature T_0 and vapor pressure p_0. The numerical values are
$$T_0 = 4.2\unit{K}$$
$$p_0 = 1\unit{atm}$$
We now pump on the vapor and reduce the pressure to a much smaller value p_m. Assuming that the latent heat L is approximately independent of temperature and that the helium vapor density is much smaller than that of the liquid, calculate the approximate temperature T_m of the liquid in equilibrium with its vapor at pressure p_m. Express your answer in terms of L, T_0, p_0, p_m, and R.
subquestions.solution:
In the coexistence region the molar volume change is
$$\Delta V = V_{gas} - V_{liquid}$$
With vapor much less dense than liquid,
$$\Delta V \approx V_{gas}$$
For an ideal gas per mole,
$$V_{gas} = \frac{R T}{p}$$
Using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives
$$\frac{dp}{dT} = \frac{L p}{R T^2}$$
Integrating between (T_0,p_0) and (T_m,p_m) yields
$$\ln \frac{p_0}{p_m} = \frac{L}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_m} - \frac{1}{T_0} \right)$$
Solving for T_m gives
$$T_m = \frac{T_0}{1 + \frac{R T_0}{L} \ln \frac{p_0}{p_m}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be an explicit formula for T_m expressed solely in terms of L, T_0, p_0, p_m, and R. Write it in the form 'T_m = [expression in L, T_0, p_0, p_m, R]'.

context: The phase boundary between the superconducting and normal phases of a metal in the H_e - T plane is shown in Fig. 1.43, where H_e is the magnitude of the applied external magnetic field and T is the temperature. The relevant thermodynamic variables are T, p, and H_e. The generalized Gibbs potential is G(T,p,H_e), which includes magnetic work. Consider state A in the normal phase and A' in the superconducting phase; each lies on the phase boundary and has the same T, p, and H_e but different entropy and magnetic moment. Let S and M_H denote the entropy and magnetic moment in the normal phase at a boundary point, and let S' and M_H' denote the entropy and magnetic moment in the superconducting phase at the same boundary point. Consider two other states B and B' arbitrarily close to A and A', respectively, such that p_A = p_B and p_{A'} = p_{B'}}. For a long rod-shaped superconducting sample of volume V oriented parallel to the field, the induced magnetic moment in the superconducting state is M_H' = - V H_e/(4 pi), while in the normal state set M_H = 0. Define the latent heat of the phase transition as L = T (S - S'). Define the critical temperature T_c by H_e(T_c) = 0. Define the critical field at zero temperature H_c by H_e(0) = H_c. Define the specific heat at constant pressure and field by C_{p,H_e} = T (partial S/partial T)_{p,H_e}.

subquestions.subproblem: Use this information to derive a Clapeyron-Clausius relation, that is, a relation between the latent heat L of the transition and the slope dH_e/dT of the phase-boundary curve. What is the latent heat at either end of the curve? For a long rod-shaped superconducting sample with volume V oriented parallel to the field, the induced magnetic moment is M_H' = - V H_e/(4 pi); in the normal state, set M_H = 0.
subquestions.solution:
The differential of the generalized Gibbs potential is
$$dG = - S dT + V dp - M_H dH_e$$
Phase equilibrium on the coexistence curve gives
$$G_A = G_{A'}$$
For neighboring states on the curve we have
$$G_B = G_{B'}$$
Thus the differentials satisfy
$$dG = dG'$$
Along the displacement we have
$$dp = 0$$
This yields the slope of the coexistence curve
$$\frac{dH_e}{dT} = - \frac{S' - S}{M_H' - M_H}$$
With the latent heat defined by L = T (S - S') we obtain
$$\frac{dH_e}{dT} = \frac{L}{T (M_H' - M_H)}$$
For the rod-shaped sample in the superconducting phase we use
$$M_H' = - \frac{V H_e}{4 \pi}$$
In the normal phase we set
$$M_H = 0$$
Therefore
$$\frac{dH_e}{dT} = - \frac{4 \pi L}{V H_e T}$$
At the high-temperature end we have
$$H_e(T_c) = 0$$
Hence
$$L = 0$$
At the low-temperature end we have
$$\frac{dH_e}{dT} = 0 \text{ at } T = 0$$
Hence
$$L = 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide your final answer in two parts: (1) a Clapeyron–Clausius-type slope relation written explicitly as dH_e/dT = ... using only the symbols L, T, M_H', and M_H; then, for the long rod-shaped sample, give the reduced form dH_e/dT = ... using only L, T, V, and H_e. (2) State the latent heat at the two endpoints of the coexistence curve as two separate equalities in the forms L(T = T_c) = ... and L(T = 0) = .... Do not include any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the difference in specific heats at constant field and pressure, Delta C = C_{p,H_e}' - C_{p,H_e}, for the two phases? What is the discontinuity in C_{p,H_e} at H_e = 0, T = T_c? What is Delta C at T = 0, H_e = H_c?
subquestions.solution:
From the relation above we have
$$S' - S = \frac{V H_e}{4 \pi} \frac{dH_e}{dT}$$
With C_{p,H_e} = T \frac{dS}{dT} at fixed p and H_e, the specific-heat difference is
$$\Delta C = C_{p,H_e}' - C_{p,H_e}$$
Therefore
$$\Delta C = \frac{V T}{4 \pi} \left[ H_e \frac{d^2 H_e}{dT^2} + \left( \frac{dH_e}{dT} \right)^2 \right]$$
At T = T_c and H_e = 0 we obtain
$$\Delta C = \frac{V T_c}{4 \pi} \left[ \frac{dH_e}{dT} \right]_{T_c}^2$$
At T = 0 and H_e = H_c we obtain
$$\Delta C = \frac{V T}{4 \pi} H_c \left[ \frac{d^2 H_e}{dT^2} \right]_{T = 0}$$
Hence
$$\Delta C = 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide your final answer in three parts: (1) the general specific-heat difference written explicitly as ΔC = ... expressed only with V, T, H_e, dH_e/dT, and d^2H_e/dT^2. (2) The discontinuity at H_e = 0, T = T_c written as ΔC|_{T = T_c, H_e = 0} = ... expressed only with V, T_c, and (dH_e/dT)|_{T_c}. (3) The value at T = 0, H_e = H_c written as ΔC|_{T = 0, H_e = H_c} = ..., with no variables appearing in the final equality.

grading_standard.formula: $$dG = - S dT + V dp - M_H dH_e$$

context: A certain substance is superconducting in the absence of external magnetic fields for temperatures satisfying the following condition. $$T<T_0$$ In the presence of a uniform magnetic field, the system can exist in two thermodynamic phases for temperatures satisfying the following condition. $$T<T_0'$$ Here T is the temperature, T_0 is the zero-field critical temperature, and T_0' is the highest temperature at which two phases can coexist in a magnetic field with T_0'\leq T_0. The two phases are specified as follows. $$B<B_c(T)$$ corresponds to the superconducting phase. $$B>B_c(T)$$ corresponds to the normal phase. Along the coexistence curve in the B–T plane we have the following condition. $$B=B_c(T)$$ The entropies per unit volume of the normal and superconducting phases along the coexistence curve are denoted by S_N(T) and S_s(T). The entropy discontinuity is defined by $$\Delta S=S_N(T)-S_s(T)$$ The critical field is given by $$B_c(T)=B_0\left(1-\frac{T^2}{T_0^2}\right)$$ We adopt Gaussian cgs conventions on the coexistence curve, with magnetizations per unit volume given by $$M_N=0$$ $$M_s=-\frac{B}{4\pi}$$ so that $$\Delta M=M_N-M_s=\frac{B}{4\pi}$$ Define the dimensionless temperature $$\tau=\frac{T}{T_0}$$ For reference in the solution, we will use the Clausius–Clapeyron relation of a p–V system, where p denotes the pressure and V the volume. Compute the entropy jump per unit volume across the coexistence curve as a function of \tau and the other parameters.
solution: By analogy with a p–V system, use the Clausius–Clapeyron relation $$\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta V}$$ For the magnetic system along the coexistence curve this gives $$\frac{dB}{dT}=-\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta M}$$ Using the defined magnetizations, we have $$\Delta M=\frac{B}{4\pi}$$ Hence $$\Delta S=-\Delta M\frac{dB}{dT}$$ Substituting \Delta M gives $$\Delta S=-\frac{B}{4\pi}\frac{dB}{dT}$$ On the coexistence curve we have $$B=B_c(T)$$ Differentiate the given critical field $$\frac{dB}{dT}=-\frac{2B_0}{T_0^2}T$$ Therefore $$\Delta S=\frac{B B_0}{2\pi}\frac{T}{T_0^2}$$ Substitute the coexistence value of B $$\Delta S(T)=\frac{B_0^2}{2\pi}\frac{T}{T_0^2}\left(1-\frac{T^2}{T_0^2}\right)$$ In terms of the dimensionless temperature \tau we have $$\tau=\frac{T}{T_0}$$ Hence $$\Delta S(\tau)=\frac{B_0^2}{2\pi}\frac{\tau}{T_0}\left(1-\tau^2\right)$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of "ΔS(τ) = ...", and your response should be written with B_0, T_0, τ only.

context: A tube of length L extends along the coordinate x with 0 ≤ x ≤ L. Let n(x,t) denote the sugar concentration as a function of position x and time t. The initial concentration at time t=0 is given by the superposition of cosine modes with amplitudes n_0 and n_1 as follows: $$n(x,0)=n_0+n_1\cos\frac{\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{9}\cos\frac{3\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{25}\cos\frac{5\pi x}{L}$$ The concentration n(x,t) obeys the one-dimensional diffusion equation with diffusion constant D, and the tube ends are reflecting so that there is no flux through x=0 and x=L. Here, L is the tube length, x is the position coordinate, t is time, D is the diffusion constant, n_0 is the uniform background concentration, and n_1 sets the amplitudes of the initial cosine modes. In the solution, X(x) and T(t) are the separated spatial and temporal factors, λ is the separation constant introduced by separation of variables, c_k are the Fourier cosine coefficients determined by the initial condition, and k is a positive integer mode number.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the diffusion equation for n(x,t)
subquestions.solution: $$\frac{\partial n(x,t)}{\partial t}=D\frac{\partial^2 n(x,t)}{\partial x^2}$$ $$\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}(0,t)=0$$ $$\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}(L,t)=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Present the governing one-dimensional diffusion PDE for n(x,t) with diffusion constant D and the corresponding no-flux boundary conditions at x=0 and x=L. Write the equations explicitly using only the variables n, x, t, D, and L.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate n(x,t) for t>0
subquestions.solution: $$n(x,t)=X(x)T(t)$$ $$\frac{d^2X}{dx^2}+\lambda X=0$$ $$\frac{dT}{dt}+D\lambda T=0$$ $$\lambda\ne 0$$ $$\frac{dX}{dx}(0)=0$$ $$\frac{dX}{dx}(L)=0$$ $$\lambda=\left(\frac{k\pi}{L}\right)^2$$ $$k=1,2,3,\ldots$$ $$n(x,t)=n_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}c_k e^{-D\left(\frac{k\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{k\pi x}{L}$$ $$n(x,t)=n_0+n_1 e^{-D\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{9} e^{-D\left(\frac{3\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{3\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{25} e^{-D\left(\frac{5\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{5\pi x}{L}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Give your result explicitly as n(x,t) = [expression], written only in terms of the variables x and t and the parameters L, D, n_0, and n_1.

grading_standard.formula: $$n(x,t)=n_0+n_1 e^{-D\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{9} e^{-D\left(\frac{3\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{3\pi x}{L}+\frac{n_1}{25} e^{-D\left(\frac{5\pi}{L}\right)^2 t}\cos\frac{5\pi x}{L}$$

context: Assume an inviscid fluid with negligible heat conductivity so that small disturbances propagate as undamped sound waves. The fluid is described by an equation of state p=p(ρ,S), where p is the pressure, ρ is the mass density, and S is the entropy per unit mass. The fluid velocity field is v(x,t). Small perturbations about a uniform equilibrium state are denoted by primes: v=v', ρ=ρ0+ρ', p=p0+p', with v=0, ρ=ρ0, p=p0 at equilibrium. The sound speed is denoted by v_s, defined as the phase speed of small adiabatic disturbances. In part (b), consider an ideal, noninteracting spin-1/2 Fermi gas at absolute zero temperature T=0 K. Let N be the total particle number, V the volume, n=N/V the number density, m the particle mass, h the Planck constant, and μ0 the zero-temperature chemical potential (Fermi energy).

subquestions.subproblem: With neglect of viscosity and heat conductivity, small disturbances in a fluid propagate as undamped sound waves. Given the relation p=p(ρ,S), where p is pressure, ρ is the mass density, and S is the entropy, derive an expression for the sound wave speed v_s:
subquestions.solution:
The continuity equation is
$$
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0
$$
The momentum equation (Euler equation) is
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho v)+(v\cdot\nabla)(\rho v)+\nabla p=0
$$
For a fluid at rest, v=0, ρ=ρ_0, p=p_0
$$
v=0
$$
$$
\rho=\rho_0
$$
$$
p=p_0
$$
Introduce small disturbances v=v', ρ=ρ_0+ρ', p=p_0+p' and keep only first-order terms
$$
\frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t}+\rho_0\nabla\cdot v'=0
$$
$$
\rho_0\frac{\partial v'}{\partial t}+\nabla p'=0
$$
Take the time derivative of the linearized continuity equation and the divergence of the linearized momentum equation to obtain
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \rho'}{\partial t^2}=\nabla^2 p'
$$
For adiabatic disturbances S=const, so to first order
$$
p'=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S \rho'
$$
Assuming a uniform medium so that \(\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S\) is constant in space, the wave equation becomes
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \rho'}{\partial t^2}=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S \nabla^2 \rho'
$$
Comparing with the standard wave equation \(\frac{\partial^2 \rho'}{\partial t^2}=v_s^2\nabla^2 \rho'\), the sound speed satisfies
$$
v_s^2=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S
$$
This uses the assumption that the compression due to the disturbance is adiabatic with S=const
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_s^2 = ..., and your response should be written with v_s, p, ρ, S.

subquestions.subproblem: As an example of such a fluid, consider a system of identical, noninteracting spin-1/2 particles of mass m at the absolute zero of temperature. The number density is n. Compute the sound speed v_s in such a system.
subquestions.solution:
At T=0 \unit{K}, for a spin-1/2 ideal Fermi gas the pressure can be written as
$$
p=\frac{2}{5}\frac{N\mu_0}{V}
$$
Using ρ=m n=m N/V, one may express p as
$$
p=\frac{h^2}{5 m^2}\left(\frac{3}{8\pi m}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} \rho^{\frac{5}{3}}
$$
From part (a), the sound speed satisfies
$$
v_s^2=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S
$$
For p\propto \rho^{5/3}, this gives
$$
\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho}\right)_S=\frac{5}{3}\frac{p}{\rho}
$$
Substituting the explicit form in terms of N and V yields
$$
v_s=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{h}{m}\left(\frac{3N}{8\pi V}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_s = ..., and your response should be written with N, V, m, h.

context: A gas in equilibrium at pressure p_0 and mass density rho_0 is confined in a rigid cylinder of length L and cross-sectional area A. The right end at x = L is closed and fixed. The left end at x = 0 has a frictionless, massless, movable piston. Use SI units: L in \unit{m}, A in \unit{m^2}, p and p_0 in \unit{Pa}, rho_0 in \unit{kg/m^3}, f and f_0 in \unit{N}, c in \unit{m/s}, u and V in \unit{m/s}, x in \unit{m}, t in \unit{s}, and omega in \unit{rad/s}. In equilibrium, the external force required on the piston is f_0 = p_0 A. Now apply a small harmonic driving force f(t) = f_0 cos(omega t), producing small piston motions and small-amplitude acoustic disturbances in the gas. Let c be the speed of sound and neglect viscosity. Let u(x,t) denote the gas velocity field along the cylinder axis and let V(t) be the piston velocity, defined by V(t) = u(0,t). Let p(x,t) denote the oscillatory pressure field. The boundary conditions for the small oscillations are p(0,t) = f(t)/A and u(L,t) = 0. Define the acoustic wavenumber k by k = omega/c. In the solution, an integration constant lambda will appear; it is determined by the boundary condition at x = L. Compute V(t).
solution:
We linearize the inviscid fluid about equilibrium and use harmonic time dependence with complex amplitudes.
$$
f_0 = p_0 A
$$
$$
f(t) = f_0 \cos(\omega t)
$$
The boundary conditions for the oscillatory fields are
$$
p(0,t) = \frac{f(t)}{A}
$$
$$
\nu(L,t) = 0
$$
Introduce the wavenumber
$$
k = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$
Represent the fields by complex amplitudes
$$
f(t) = \operatorname{Re} \big( f_0 e^{i \omega t} \big)
$$
$$
p(x,t) = \operatorname{Re} \big( \tilde p(x) e^{i \omega t} \big)
$$
$$
\nu(x,t) = \operatorname{Re} \big( \tilde u(x) e^{i \omega t} \big)
$$
A general solution consistent with the wave equation and the boundary condition at x = 0 is
$$
\tilde p(x) = p_0 \cos(k x) + \lambda \sin(k x)
$$
The linearized Euler equation relates pressure and velocity
$$
\rho_0 \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = - \frac{\partial p}{\partial x}
$$
In complex form this gives
$$
i \omega \rho_0 \tilde u(x) = - \frac{d \tilde p}{d x}
$$
Using the relation between the static and driving amplitudes
$$
p_0 = \frac{f_0}{A}
$$
we obtain
$$
\tilde u(x) = \frac{i k}{\omega \rho_0} \big( - p_0 \sin(k x) + \lambda \cos(k x) \big)
$$
Imposing the boundary condition at the closed end
$$
\tilde u(L) = 0
$$
yields
$$
- p_0 \sin(k L) + \lambda \cos(k L) = 0
$$
so
$$
\lambda = p_0 \tan(k L)
$$
Therefore the velocity amplitude at the piston is
$$
\tilde u(0) = \frac{i k}{\omega \rho_0} p_0 \tan(k L)
$$
Using k = \omega/c gives
$$
\tilde u(0) = \frac{i}{c} \frac{p_0}{\rho_0} \tan \frac{\omega L}{c}
$$
Recovering the physical piston velocity V(t) from the real part
$$
V(t) = \operatorname{Re} \big( \tilde u(0) e^{i \omega t} \big)
$$
we obtain
$$
V(t) = - \frac{p_0}{c \rho_0} \tan \frac{\omega L}{c} \sin(\omega t)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of V(t) = ... and your response should be written using only the variables p_0, c, rho_0, L, omega, and t.

context: In granite, day–night temperature variations are significantly damped at a depth of about 10 cm. Let the temperature at depth Δx = 10 cm be constant at T0 (in degrees Celsius). At the time of the daily maximum surface temperature, take the surface temperature to be T1 ≈ T0 + 10 °C. The incident solar radiation intensity on the ground is Q = 1400 W/m^2, which is approximately Q ≈ 3.3 × 10^−2 cal/(s·cm^2). Assume this radiation is completely absorbed within the top Δx = 10 cm of the ground. Using Fourier’s law in one dimension and a linear temperature gradient, estimate the thermal conductivity K of granite and then choose the best option for K from the set {5 × 10^−3, 5 × 10^1, 5 × 10^2, 5 × 10^5} cal/(s·cm·°C). Define ΔT = T1 − T0, and define K_choice as the selected option for K.
solution:
Assume the temperature at depth Δx = 10 cm is constant at T0.

$$
T_1 \approx T_0 + 10 \unit{^\circ C}
$$

The incident solar radiation intensity is

$$
Q = 1400 \unit{W/m^2}
$$

and its approximate value in cgs heat units is

$$
Q \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-2} \unit{cal/(s\cdot cm^2)}
$$

Assuming Q is fully absorbed within the first Δx = 10 cm, Fourier’s law (using a linear gradient) gives the estimate

$$
K = Q \cdot \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta T}
$$

With Δx = 10 cm and ΔT = T_1 - T_0 = 10 °C,

$$
K = 3.3 \times 10^{-2} \times \frac{10}{10} \unit{cal/(s\cdot cm\cdot ^\circ C)}
$$

$$
K = 3.3 \times 10^{-2} \unit{cal/(s\cdot cm\cdot ^\circ C)}
$$

Accounting for reflection from the surface reduces the effective absorbed flux, so the actual K should be smaller than this estimate. Therefore, the best choice is

$$
K_{\text{choice}} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \unit{cal/(s\cdot cm\cdot ^\circ C)}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express K_choice as a numerical value with units, written exactly in the form: K_choice = ... cal/(s·cm·°C).

context: Convection to and from a vertical surface (e.g., a window pane) in still air follows the empirical heat-flux law q = (2/5)×10^{-4} (Δt)^{5/4} in units of cal/s·cm^2, where Δt is the temperature difference between the surface and the adjacent air in °C. The indoor air temperature is 25 °C and the outdoor air temperature is −15 °C. A glass pane of thickness d = 2 mm has thermal conductivity k = 2×10^{-3} cal/(s·cm·°C). Neglect radiation and assume one-dimensional steady conduction through the pane. Define t_1 as the inner surface temperature in °C and t_2 as the outer surface temperature in °C. Let q be the steady heat flux per unit area in cal/s·cm^2. You may analyze a unit area A = 1 cm^2. Find the inner surface temperature t_1.
solution:
Define the steady heat flux per unit area q and the inner and outer surface temperatures t_1 and t_2 in °C. For the outer convection into the outside air at −15 °C, the flux magnitude is
$$
q = \frac{2}{5} \times 10^{-4} (t_2 + 15)^{5/4} \unit{cal/s cm^2}
$$
For the pane thickness conversion
$$
d = 2 \unit{mm}
$$
$$
d = \frac{1}{5} \unit{cm}
$$
Conduction through the pane gives
$$
q = 2 \times 10^{-3} \frac{t_1 - t_2}{\frac{1}{5}} \unit{cal/s cm^2}
$$
For the inner convection into the room air at 25 °C, the flux magnitude is
$$
q = \frac{2}{5} \times 10^{-4} (25 - t_1)^{5/4} \unit{cal/s cm^2}
$$
At steady state these three expressions are equal, so
$$
\frac{2}{5} \times 10^{-4} (t_2 + 15)^{5/4} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \frac{t_1 - t_2}{\frac{1}{5}}
$$
$$
\frac{2}{5} \times 10^{-4} (25 - t_1)^{5/4} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \frac{t_1 - t_2}{\frac{1}{5}}
$$
Solving for t_1 from these equations gives
$$
 t_1 = 5 \unit{\circ C}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express t_1 as a numerical value with units of °C, in the form t_1 = ... °C.

context: The water at the surface of a lake and the air above it are initially in thermal equilibrium at the freezing temperature of water. At time t=0, the air temperature suddenly drops by ΔT. Find the thickness of the ice on the lake as a function of time h(t), expressed in terms of the latent heat per unit volume L/V and the thermal conductivity Λ of ice. Assume ΔT is small enough that the specific heat of ice may be neglected and that heat transfer through the ice is by conduction across a linear temperature gradient. Use the following definitions and SI units: h(t) is the ice thickness in \unit{m}, t is time in \unit{s}, ΔT is the air temperature drop relative to the freezing temperature in \unit{K}, Λ is the thermal conductivity of ice in \unit{W m^{-1} K^{-1}}, L is latent heat in \unit{J}, V is volume in \unit{m^3}, so L/V is the latent heat per unit volume in \unit{J m^{-3}}. Let ΔS denote an arbitrary area element in \unit{m^2}.
solution:
Consider an arbitrary area ΔS on the water surface that is freezing, and let h(t) be the ice thickness at time t. During a small time interval dt, a layer of water of thickness dh and area ΔS freezes. The latent heat released by this volume is equal to the heat conducted through the ice to the air over the same interval. The latent heat released is
$$
\Delta S dh \frac{L}{V}
$$
The conductive heat transferred through the ice is
$$
\Lambda \frac{\Delta T}{h} \Delta S dt
$$
Equating these gives
$$
\Delta S dh \frac{L}{V} = \Lambda \frac{\Delta T}{h} \Delta S dt
$$
Canceling ΔS and rearranging yields
$$
h dh = \frac{\Lambda \Delta T}{L/V} dt
$$
Integrating from 0 to h(t) and from 0 to t with h(0)=0 gives
$$
\int_0^{h(t)} h dh = \frac{\Lambda \Delta T}{L/V} \int_0^t dt
$$
Evaluating the integrals yields
$$
\frac{h^2(t)}{2} = \frac{\Lambda \Delta T}{L/V} t
$$
Solving for h(t) gives the thickness of the ice as a function of time
$$
h(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2 \Lambda \Delta T t}{L/V}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form h(t) = ..., expressed solely in terms of t, ΔT, Λ, and L/V.

context: A sheet of ice 1\unit{cm} thick has frozen over a pond. The upper surface of the ice is at -20\unit{^\circ C}. Assume the ice-water interface is at 0\unit{^\circ C}. Let T be the temperature of the upper surface, T_0 the temperature at the ice-water interface, and z the instantaneous thickness of the ice measured from the upper surface (origin of the z-axis at the upper surface, positive downward). Let \eta=dz/dt be the rate of increase of the ice thickness, j the heat current density through the ice (taken positive downward), \kappa the thermal conductivity of ice, L the latent heat of fusion of ice per unit mass, and \rho the mass density of water/ice. Use steady one-dimensional conduction through the ice and energy balance at the freezing front.

subquestions.subproblem: At what rate is the thickness of the sheet of ice increasing?
subquestions.solution:
The heat current density through the ice of thickness z is
$$j=-\kappa\frac{T-T_0}{z}$$
Energy balance at the freezing front gives
$$\rho L\frac{dz}{dt}=-j$$
Define the growth rate
$$\eta=\frac{dz}{dt}$$
Hence
$$\eta=-\frac{j}{\rho L}$$
and therefore
$$\eta=\frac{\kappa\left(T-T_0\right)}{\rho L z}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \eta = ..., and your response should be written only with \kappa, T, T_0, \rho, L, and z.

subquestions.subproblem: How long will it take for the sheet's thickness to double? Take \kappa=5\times10^{-3}\unit{cal/(cm s ^\circ C)}, L=80\unit{cal/g}, \rho=1\unit{g/cm^3}, T=-20\unit{^\circ C}, and T_0=0\unit{^\circ C}. The initial thickness is z_1=1\unit{cm} and the final thickness is z_2=2\unit{cm}.
subquestions.solution:
From part (a), rearrange to get
$$dt=\frac{\rho L}{\kappa\left(T-T_0\right)}z\,dz$$
Integrating from z_1 to z_2 yields the elapsed time
$$t=\frac{\rho L\left(z_2^2-z_1^2\right)}{2\kappa\left(T-T_0\right)}$$
Let \Delta t denote the time for the thickness to grow from z_1 to z_2. Substituting z_1=1\unit{cm}, z_2=2\unit{cm}, T=-20\unit{^\circ C}, T_0=0\unit{^\circ C}, \kappa=5\times10^{-3}\unit{cal/(cm s ^\circ C)}, L=80\unit{cal/g}, and \rho=1\unit{g/cm^3} gives
$$\Delta t=1.2\times10^{3}\unit{s}$$
$$\Delta t=20\unit{min}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the elapsed time \Delta t as a numerical value in seconds, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A spherical, black asteroid made of rock has been ejected far from the Sun, so solar radiation is negligible. Heat is produced uniformly inside the asteroid by radioactive elements at a rate per unit mass of \(\dot q\). The asteroid has density \(\rho\), thermal conductivity \(k\), and radius \(R\). Assume a steady state and that the asteroid radiates as a blackbody with Stefan–Boltzmann constant \(\sigma\). Let \(T(r)\) be the temperature at radial coordinate \(r\), \(T_s=T(R)\) be the surface temperature, \(T_c=T(0)\) be the central temperature, and \(Q\) be the total power generated and radiated in steady state. Given: \(\dot q=3\times 10^{-14}\unit{cal/(g s)}\), \(\rho=3.5\unit{g/cm^3}\), \(k=5\times 10^{-3}\unit{cal/(cm s K)}\), \(R=100\unit{km}\). Determine \(T_c\) and \(T_s\).
solution:
At steady state, the total radiated power equals the total internal heat generation

$$
Q=4\pi R^2\sigma T_s^4
$$

$$
Q=\frac{4\pi R^3}{3}\rho\dot q
$$

Solving for the surface temperature gives

$$
T_s=\left(\frac{R\rho\dot q}{3\sigma}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}
$$

$$
T_s=22.5\unit{K}
$$

The steady heat conduction equation with uniform internal heating is

$$
\nabla\cdot\left(-k\nabla T\right)=\rho\dot q
$$

With spherical symmetry this reduces to

$$
\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dT}{dr}\right)=-\frac{\rho\dot q}{k}r^2
$$

Integrating and imposing regularity at the center and the boundary condition \(T(R)=T_s\) yields

$$
T(r)=-\frac{\dot q\rho}{6k}\left(r^2-R^2\right)+T_s
$$

Therefore the central temperature is

$$
T_c=\frac{\dot q\rho R^2}{6k}+T_s
$$

$$
T_c=372\unit{K}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T_s and T_c as numerical values in kelvin, each to 3 significant figures. Report them explicitly in the form: 'T_s = ... K, T_c = ... K'.

context: When there is heat flow in a heat-conducting material, entropy increases. Consider a homogeneous heat conductor with thermal conductivity k (SI units \unit{W/(m K)}). Let T(x,t) be the temperature field, u(x,t) the internal energy per unit volume, S(x,t) the entropy per unit volume, and q(x,t) the heat flux vector. Neglect volume expansion so that the local thermodynamic relation du = T dS holds. Denote the local irreversible entropy generation rate per unit volume by \dot S (SI units \unit{W/(m^3 K)}). Given k and the temperature gradient \nabla T, find \dot S in terms of T and \nabla T.
solution:
Neglecting volume expansion gives
$$
du = T dS
$$
Local energy conservation for heat conduction is
$$
\frac{du}{dt} + \nabla \cdot q = 0
$$
Using du = T dS yields
$$
\frac{dS}{dt} = - \frac{\nabla \cdot q}{T}
$$
Rewriting the right-hand side gives
$$
\frac{dS}{dt} = - \nabla \cdot \frac{q}{T} + q \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{T}
$$
Identify the local irreversible entropy generation rate per unit volume as
$$
\dot S = q \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{T}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\dot S = - \frac{\nabla T}{T^2} \cdot q
$$
Fourier's law gives
$$
q = - k \nabla T
$$
Therefore
$$
\dot S = \frac{k}{T^2} \nabla T \cdot \nabla T
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \dot S = ..., and your response should be written using only k, T, and \nabla T.

context: A classical one-dimensional harmonic oscillator with mass m and spring constant k has a fixed total energy E. Let x be the instantaneous displacement from equilibrium, \dot x the velocity, l the oscillation amplitude, and T the period. The initial phase (starting time) is completely unknown, i.e., the observation time is uniformly distributed over one period. Find the probability density function p(x), where p(x) dx is the probability that the mass is found in the interval dx at position x.
solution:
From energy conservation, we have

$$
E = \frac{k}{2} l^2
$$

$$
E = \frac{k}{2} x^2 + \frac{m}{2} \dot x^2
$$

The period is

$$
T = 2 \int_{-l}^{l} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{\frac{2E - k x^2}{m}}}
$$

$$
T = 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}
$$

With uniformly distributed observation time over one period, the probability density satisfies

$$
p(x) dx = \frac{2 dt}{T}
$$

$$
dt = \frac{dx}{|\dot x|}
$$

$$
|\dot x| = \sqrt{\frac{2E - k x^2}{m}}
$$

Hence

$$
p(x) = \frac{1}{\pi} \sqrt{\frac{k}{2E - k x^2}}
$$

This expression applies for |x| \le l, with p(x) = 0 outside that range.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of p(x) = ... for |x| ≤ l, and p(x) = 0 otherwise. Your response should be written with variables x, E, k, and l only.

context: Consider a one-dimensional lattice with lattice constant a (denoted as α in Fig. 2.1). An atom performs a discrete-time random walk on this lattice: in each time step of duration τ, it hops one lattice spacing to the right with probability p and to the left with probability q, where p+q=1. Let N be the number of steps, with N ≫ 1, and let t=Nτ be the elapsed time. The initial position is chosen as x=0, with the x-axis pointing to the right. After N steps, if n of them are rightward, the displacement is x=(2n−N)a. The probability of having n rightward steps is P(n)=C(N,n)p^n q^{N-n}, where C(N,n)=N!/(n!(N−n)!). Denote ensemble averages by an overline, for example, the average position is x̄=overline{x} and the mean-square fluctuation about the mean is overline{(x−x̄)^2}. Let Ψ_t denote the statistical state of the ensemble at time t; it is only a label for the time and does not affect the classical random-walk calculation.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the average position \overline{x} of the atom at the time t=N\tau where N \gg 1
subquestions.solution:
Define the binomial probability for n rightward steps out of N steps as
$$P(n)=\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}p^n q^{N-n}$$
The average position is
$$\overline{x}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}(2n-N)a\,P(n)$$
Introduce the generating function
$$F(p)=(p+q)^N$$
Use the identity
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}n\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}p^n q^{N-n}=p\frac{dF}{dp}$$
Therefore
$$\overline{x}=2ap\frac{d}{dp}(p+q)^N-Na$$
With p+q=1, this gives
$$\overline{x}=Na(p-q)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \overline{x} = ... , and your response should be written with N, a, p, q only.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the mean-square value \overline{(x-\overline{x})^2} at the time \mathbf{\Psi}_t
subquestions.solution:
First compute the second moment
$$\overline{x^2}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}(2n-N)^2 a^2 P(n)$$
Use the derivative identities
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}n(n-1)\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}p^n q^{N-n}=p^2\frac{d^2F}{dp^2}$$
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}n\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}p^n q^{N-n}=p\frac{dF}{dp}$$
With F(p)=(p+q)^N, one obtains
$$\overline{x^2}=4a^2 p^2\frac{d^2}{dp^2}(p+q)^N-4(N-1)a^2 p\frac{d}{dp}(p+q)^N+N^2 a^2$$
Evaluating at p+q=1 yields
$$\overline{x^2}=Na^2\big((N-1)(p-q)^2+1\big)$$
Using \overline{x}=Na(p-q), the variance is
$$\overline{(x-\overline{x})^2}=\overline{x^2}-\overline{x}^2$$
Therefore
$$\overline{(x-\overline{x})^2}=4Na^2 pq$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \overline{(x-\overline{x})^2} = ... , and your response should be written with N, a, p, q only.
