context: For sodium (Na) metal, the conduction electron number density is approximately n = 2.6 × 10^22 per cubic centimeter. Treat the conduction electrons as a free electron gas. Use E_F for the Fermi energy, N for the total number of conduction electrons, V for the sample volume, and n = N/V for the number density. Use \hbar for the reduced Planck constant, m for the electron mass, c for the speed of light, k for the Boltzmann constant, and T for the temperature. In subpart (b), let C denote the electronic specific heat (per unit mass), and let M denote the total electron mass with M = N m_e, where m_e is the electron mass. Use the numerical values where needed: \hbar ≈ 6.58×10^−15 \unit{eV s}, m ≈ 0.511 \unit{MeV/c^2}, m_e ≈ 9.11×10^−31 \unit{kg}, k ≈ 1.38×10^−23 \unit{J/K}, and at room temperature kT ≈ 1/40 \unit{eV}.

subquestions.subproblem: Give an approximate value (in eV) of the Fermi energy E_F in Na.
subquestions.solution:
The Fermi energy is
$$E_F = 
\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \left(3 \pi^2 \frac{N}{V} \right)^{3/2}$$
We substitute
$$\hbar = 6.58 \times 10^{-15} \unit{eV s}$$
$$m = 0.511 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$\frac{N}{V} = 2.6 \times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$
and obtain

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_F as a numerical value in eV, rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Give an approximate value for the electronic specific heat C of Na at room temperature.
subquestions.solution:
The specific heat is
$$C \approx \frac{1}{M} \frac{N}{E_F} k^2 T$$
Using M = N m_e, this becomes
$$C = \frac{k}{m_e} \frac{k T}{E_F}$$
where
$$m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \unit{kg}$$
$$k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \unit{J/K}$$
and at room temperature
$$k T \approx \frac{1}{40} \unit{eV}$$
We substitute E_F and the other quantities in the above expression and obtain
$$C \approx 11.8 \unit{J/(K g)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express C (electronic specific heat per unit mass) as a numerical value in J/(K g), rounded to 3 significant figures.

context:
The free-electron model of the conduction electrons in metals, modeled as a three-dimensional non-interacting spin-1/2 Fermi gas, often gives a good account of the compressibility at zero temperature. You are given the number density n and the Fermi energy ε_F of a non-interacting Fermi gas at zero absolute temperature T=0 \unit{K}. Find the isothermal compressibility κ. Definitions and notation: V is the volume, p is the pressure, E is the total energy, F is the Helmholtz free energy, S is the entropy, N is the total particle number, m is the particle mass, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, k is the wavevector magnitude, k_F is the Fermi wavevector, and ε(k) is the single-particle energy. The spin degeneracy factor is 2. Use the identity
$$
p V=\frac{2}{3}E
$$
The isothermal compressibility is defined by
$$
\kappa=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_T
$$
solution:
At T=0 \unit{K}, the Helmholtz free energy satisfies
$$
F=E-TS
$$
Thus
$$
F=E
$$
The pressure is
$$
p=-\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right)_T
$$
Therefore
$$
p=-\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\right)_T
$$
Using the identity
$$
p V=\frac{2}{3}E
$$
which implies
$$
E=\frac{3}{2}p V
$$
we differentiate at fixed T to obtain
$$
\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}=\frac{3}{2}\left(p+V\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T\right)
$$
Hence
$$
p=-\frac{3}{2}\left(p+V\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T\right)
$$
so
$$
V\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T=-\frac{5}{3}p
$$
The isothermal compressibility is defined by
$$
\kappa=-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_T
$$
and we use
$$
\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial V}\right)_T}
$$
Therefore
$$
\kappa=\frac{3}{5p}
$$
At T=0 \unit{K}, the pressure can be written as
$$
p=\frac{2E}{3V}
$$
with the ground-state energy
$$
E=\frac{2V}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{k<k_F} d^3k\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}
$$
so that
$$
p=\frac{\hbar^2 k_F^5}{15 m \pi^2}
$$
The number of particles is
$$
N=\frac{2V}{(2\pi)^3}\int_{k<k_F} d^3k
$$
Thus
$$
n=\frac{N}{V}
$$
and
$$
n=\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2}
$$
For an ideal Fermi gas,
$$
\varepsilon(k)=\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}
$$
so the Fermi energy is
$$
\varepsilon_F=\frac{\hbar^2 k_F^2}{2m}
$$
Combining the results gives
$$
p=\frac{2}{5}n\varepsilon_F
$$
Finally, substituting into the expression for κ yields
$$
\kappa=\frac{3}{2 n \varepsilon_F}
$$
All results hold at T=0 \unit{K}.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form κ = [expression], expressed solely in terms of n and ε_F, with no other variables or constants.

context: Fermi gas. Consider an ideal Fermi gas of neutral atoms with atomic mass m = 5 × 10^{-24} \unit{g}, nuclear spin I = \frac{1}{2}, and nuclear magnetic moment μ = 2 × 10^{-24} \unit{erg/gauss}. The gas is at temperature T = 0 \unit{K} and is placed in a uniform external magnetic field of magnitude H = 10^{5} \unit{gauss}. Assume the electronic magnetic moment is zero. Let n denote the particle number density and ε_F the Fermi energy of a fully spin-polarized gas. Let ħ be the reduced Planck constant and π the circle constant. Find the largest number density n_max for which the gas can be completely polarized by the field. Give your final answer in the form n_max = ... with units of \unit{atoms/cm^3}.
solution:
For a fully polarized spin-\frac{1}{2} ideal Fermi gas, the Fermi energy is
$$
\varepsilon_F = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \left(6 \pi^2 n\right)^{2/3}
$$
Complete polarization requires the Zeeman splitting to exceed the Fermi energy
$$
\varepsilon_F \leq 2 \mu H
$$
Combining the two relations gives an upper bound on the density
$$
n \leq \frac{1}{6 \pi^2} \left( \frac{4 m \mu H}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2}
$$
The largest density for complete polarization is
$$
n_{\max} = \frac{1}{6 \pi^2} \left( \frac{4 m \mu H}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2}
$$
Numerically, this yields
$$
n_{\max} \approx 2 \times 10^{17} \unit{atoms/cm^3}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form n_max = ... and expressed solely in terms of m, μ, H, ħ, and π. Do not substitute numerical values or introduce any additional symbols. Include the unit atoms/cm^3.

M is the spin contribution to the magnetic moment in a uniform, fixed magnetic field H. μ is the chemical potential, which equals the Fermi energy ε_F at T = 0 K in the degenerate limit. μ_B is the Bohr magneton. k is the Boltzmann constant. The symbol f(ε) denotes the energy-weight function that appears in the Sommerfeld expansion for the observable in question. The "leading exponent" n is defined as follows: if a quantity X satisfies X(T = 0 K) = 0, then X(T) ~ T^n as T → 0; if X(T = 0 K) ≠ 0, then n = 0 and X(T) has a nonzero T = 0 K limit with temperature corrections at higher powers of T. In part (b), M_0 denotes the zero-temperature value of M at the given H, and α is a positive constant determined by band-structure details near ε_F. For each part, report the answer in the form n = ...

subquestions.subproblem: the specific heat at constant volume;
subquestions.solution:
Let the Sommerfeld-expansion weight be
$$f(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{3/2}$$
The specific heat at constant volume is defined by
$$C_v=\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}$$
In a highly degenerate gas, only electrons within an energy window of order kT about the Fermi surface are thermally excited, so the temperature-dependent part of E scales as T^2, which implies
$$C_v\sim T$$
Therefore, the leading exponent is
$$n=1$$

subquestions.subproblem: the spin contribution to the magnetic moment M in a fixed magnetic field H ：
subquestions.solution:
Let the Sommerfeld-expansion weight be
$$f(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{1/2}$$
The low-temperature expansion of the spin magnetization takes the form
$$M(T)\approx M_0\bigl(1-\alpha T^2\bigr)$$
Thus the leading term is temperature independent and
$$n=0$$
At zero temperature
$$T=0\unit{K}$$
The spin-resolved Fermi energies are shifted by the Zeeman energy
$$\varepsilon_{F\uparrow}=\mu+\mu_B H$$
$$\varepsilon_{F\downarrow}=\mu-\mu_B H$$
which produces a net spin magnetic moment parallel to H at T=0, consistent with n=0

final_answer_instructions: For each subquestion, your final answer should be written in the form 'n = ...' as a numerical value (no units). Use an exact integer if applicable.

Let p denote the magnitude of the single-particle momentum used as an integration variable in momentum-space integrals. Let p_+ and p_- be the corresponding Fermi momenta, and E_+ and E_- the corresponding total energies. Let E be the total energy and n = N/V the number density. Let P denote the thermodynamic pressure; in derivatives of the form (partial/partial V)_T, T denotes the temperature. Let M be the magnetization and chi the magnetic susceptibility in the weak-field limit, defined by M = chi H when mu(0) >> mu_B H. Calculate the zero temperature limit of

subquestions.subproblem: the average energy per particle,

$$p_+ = \left( 2 m [ \mu(0) - \mu_B H ] \right)^{1/2}$$
$$p_- = \left( 2 m [ \mu(0) + \mu_B H ] \right)^{1/2}$$

context: Consider a Fermi gas model of a heavy nucleus. Apart from the Pauli principle, the nucleons are assumed to move independently in a sphere of volume V and form a completely degenerate Fermi gas. Let A be the total number of nucleons with A = N + z, where N is the number of neutrons and z is the number of protons. Assume symmetric nuclear matter N = z. Let m be the nucleon mass, p_F the Fermi momentum, h the Planck constant, and ħ = h/(2π). The nuclear volume is V = (4π/3) R_0^3 A with R_0 ≈ 1.4×10^{-13} \unit{cm}. Use the spin-isospin degeneracy factor 4 for nucleons in symmetric matter, and let E_kin denote the total kinetic energy of all nucleons. Compute the kinetic energy per nucleon E_kin/A with this model and give the result in \unit{MeV}.
solution:
In momentum space, the number of single-particle states in the shell [p,p+dp] is
$$
dN = \frac{4 V}{h^3} 4\pi p^2 dp
$$
The total number of nucleons is
$$
A = \int_0^{p_F} dN
$$
Thus
$$
A = \frac{16\pi V}{h^3} \int_0^{p_F} p^2 dp
$$
Therefore
$$
A = \frac{16\pi V}{3 h^3} p_F^3
$$
The total kinetic energy is
$$
E_{kin} = \int_0^{p_F} \frac{p^2}{2 m} dN
$$
Thus
$$
E_{kin} = \frac{16\pi V}{h^3} \int_0^{p_F} \frac{p^4}{2 m} dp
$$
Therefore
$$
E_{kin} = \frac{16\pi V}{10 m h^3} p_F^5
$$
The kinetic energy per nucleon is
$$
\frac{E_{kin}}{A} = \frac{3}{5} \frac{p_F^2}{2 m}
$$
The nuclear volume is
$$
V = \frac{4\pi}{3} R_0^3 A
$$
From the number relation one also has
$$
V = \frac{3 h^3}{16\pi} p_F^{-3} A
$$
Set ħ ≡ h/(2π) = 1 when expressing p_F in terms of R_0
$$
h^3 = (2\pi)^3
$$
Hence
$$
V = \frac{3 (2\pi)^3}{16\pi} p_F^{-3} A
$$
Equating the two expressions for V gives
$$
p_F = R_0^{-1} \left( \frac{9\pi}{8} \right)^{1/3}
$$
Substituting into the energy per nucleon yields
$$
\frac{E_{kin}}{A} = \frac{3}{10} \left( \frac{9\pi}{8} \right)^{2/3} \frac{1}{m R_0^2}
$$
Numerically, with R_0 \approx 1.4\times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}, this gives
$$
\frac{E_{kin}}{A} \approx 16 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the kinetic energy per nucleon E_kin/A as a numerical value in MeV. Report your result to 2 significant figures.

context: At low temperatures, a mixture of ^3He and ^4He atoms forms a liquid that separates into two phases: a concentrated phase (nearly pure ^3He) and a dilute phase (roughly 6.5% ^3He for T ≤ 0.1 \unit{K}). The lighter ^3He floats on top of the dilute phase, and ^3He atoms can cross the phase boundary (see Fig. 2.23). Definitions for use below: T is the absolute temperature in \unit{K}. S_d(T) and S_c(T) denote the entropy per ^3He particle in the dilute and concentrated phases, respectively. At low temperature, the entropy per particle is linear in T and is written as

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose the container in the figure is now connected to external plumbing so that ^3He atoms can be transferred from the concentrated phase to the dilute phase at a rate of N_\bullet atoms per second (as in a dilution refrigerator). For fixed temperature T (denoted by τ in the original statement), how much power W (absorbed as latent heat) can this system absorb? Express your final answer in terms of N_\bullet, T, λ_d, λ_c, T_{Fd}, and T_{Fc}. λ_d and λ_c are dimensionless constants, T_{Fd} and T_{Fc} are effective Fermi temperatures in \unit{K}, N_\bullet has units of \unit{s^{-1}}, and W is measured in \unit{W}.
subquestions.solution:
The absorbed power equals the latent heat carried by ^3He atoms crossing from the concentrated phase to the dilute phase. Using the entropy per particle S_d(T) in the dilute phase and S_c(T) in the concentrated phase, the power is
$$W = N_\bullet \big( S_d(T) - S_c(T) \big) T$$
With the low-temperature forms
$$S_d(T) = \lambda_d \frac{T}{T_{Fd}}$$
$$S_c(T) = \lambda_c \frac{T}{T_{Fc}}$$
we obtain
$$W = N_\bullet T^2 \left( \frac{\lambda_d}{T_{Fd}} - \frac{\lambda_c}{T_{Fc}} \right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form W = ... and must be written solely in terms of N_\bullet, T, λ_d, λ_c, T_{Fd}, and T_{Fc}. Use exactly these symbols and no numerical values.

context: Determine the minimum electron number density n at which a uniform, nonrelativistic, fully degenerate gas of free electrons at T=0 \unit{K} has a Fermi energy large enough to permit the reaction proton + electron + 0.8 \unit{MeV} -> neutron to proceed from left to right. Definitions: n is the electron number density, \varepsilon_F is the electron Fermi energy, m is the electron mass, h is Planck's constant, n_{min} is the minimum electron number density that meets the reaction threshold, m_n is the neutron mass, and \rho_{min} is the estimated minimum mass density of a neutron star. Assume one nucleon per electron so that \rho_{min}=m_n n_{min}.
solution:
At T=0 \unit{K}, the relation between electron number density n and Fermi energy \varepsilon_F is
$$
n=\frac{8\pi}{3}\left(\frac{2m\varepsilon_F}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}
$$
The reaction proceeds when the threshold condition is
$$
\varepsilon_F\geq 0.8\unit{MeV}
$$
Thus the minimum electron number density is
$$
n_{min}=3.24\times 10^{36}\unit{m^{-3}}
$$
The corresponding minimum mass density of a neutron star is given by
$$
\rho_{min}=m_n n_{min}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\rho_{min}=5.4\times 10^{9}\unit{kg/m^3}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express n_min and rho_min as numerical values. Present them as two separate statements: 'n_min = ...' in units of m^-3 and 'rho_min = ...' in units of kg/m^3. Report n_min to 3 significant figures and rho_min to 2 significant figures.

context: Assume that a neutron star is a highly degenerate, non-relativistic Fermi gas of neutrons in a spherically symmetric equilibrium configuration. The gas is held together by the gravitational pull of a heavy object with mass M and radius r_0 at the center of the star. Neglect all interactions among the neutrons. Let r be the radial distance from the center with r>r_0. Let rho(r) denote the neutron mass density, p(r) the pressure, mu the chemical potential, G the Newtonian gravitational constant, and a>0 the constant in the polytropic equation of state p=a rho^{5/3}. Let C denote the integration constant that appears when integrating the hydrostatic equilibrium equation and that will be fixed by the boundary condition rho(r)→0 as r→∞. Calculate the neutron density rho(r) for r>r_0.
solution:
For a non-relativistic degenerate Fermi gas, the density and pressure scale with the chemical potential mu as
$$
\rho \propto \mu^{3/2}
$$
$$
 p \propto \mu^{5/2}
$$
Therefore there exists a constant a>0 such that
$$
 p=a \rho^{5/3}
$$
Hydrostatic equilibrium in the gravitational field of a central mass M gives
$$
\frac{dp}{dr}=-\frac{\rho M G}{r^{2}}
$$
Rewriting,
$$
\frac{dp}{\rho}=M G d\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)
$$
From the equation of state,
$$
 dp=a \frac{5}{3} \rho^{2/3} d\rho
$$
Hence
$$
 a \frac{5}{2} d\left(\rho^{2/3}\right)=M G d\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)
$$
Integrating,
$$
 a \frac{5}{2} \rho^{2/3}=M G \frac{1}{r}+C
$$
The boundary condition \rho(r)\to 0 as r\to \infty implies
$$
 C=0
$$
Thus, for r>r_0,
$$
 \rho(r)=\left[\frac{2 M G}{5 a r}\right]^{3/2}
$$

subquestions.subproblem: The chemical potentials for the fermions.
subquestions.solution:
At equilibrium for gamma <-> e+ + e-, the chemical potentials satisfy $$
\mu_{e^+} + \mu_{e^-} = \mu_\gamma
$$ Since photons have zero chemical potential, $$
\mu_\gamma = 0
$$ Hence $$
\mu_{e^+} + \mu_{e^-} = 0
$$ By particle-antiparticle symmetry, $$
\mu_{e^+} = \mu_{e^-}
$$ Therefore $$
\mu_{e^+} = 0
$$ and $$
\mu_{e^-} = 0
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form mu_{e^-} = ... and mu_{e^+} = ... as numerical values.

subquestions.subproblem: The average number of electron-positron pairs, in the two limits k T >> m_e c^2 and k T << m_e c^2. (You may leave your answers in terms of dimensionless definite integrals.)
subquestions.solution:
In the ultrarelativistic limit k T >> m_e c^2, neglect m_e and take E = c p. Then $$
N_{e^-} = \frac{2 V}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \int d^3 p \frac{1}{e^{\beta c p} + 1}
$$ With the substitution $$
x = \beta c p
$$ we obtain $$
N_{e^-} = \frac{V}{\pi^2} \frac{(k T)^3}{(\hbar c)^3} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{e^x + 1} dx
$$ By symmetry, $$
N_{e^-} = N_{e^+}
$$ In the nonrelativistic limit k T << m_e c^2, the +1 in the Fermi-Dirac denominator can be neglected (Maxwell-Boltzmann regime), and $$
\varepsilon_p = \sqrt{(c p)^2 + (m_e c^2)^2}
$$ $$
\varepsilon_p \approx m_e c^2 + \frac{p^2}{2 m_e}
$$ Thus $$
N_{e^{\pm}} = \frac{2 V}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \int_0^{\infty} e^{- \beta m_e c^2} e^{- \beta \frac{p^2}{2 m_e}} 4 \pi p^2 dp
$$ and $$
N_{e^{\pm}} = 2 V \left( \frac{2 \pi m_e k T}{h^2} \right)^{3/2} e^{- \frac{m_e c^2}{k T}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answers should be given in the forms: (i) For the ultrarelativistic limit k T >> m_e c^2: N_{e^-} = ... and N_{e^+} = ...; (ii) For the nonrelativistic limit k T << m_e c^2: N_{e^-} = ... and N_{e^+} = .... Use only the variables V, T, m_e, h, hbar, c, and k, and you may include a single dimensionless definite integral where appropriate.

Chemical equilibrium requires $$
\mu_{e^+} + \mu_{e^-} = 0
$$ The imposed electron chemical potential is $$

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the net charge of the system in the presence of this imbalance in the limit k T >> mu >> m_e c^2. (Again, your answer may be left in terms of a dimensionless definite integral.)

context: Heat capacity at constant volume. Consider a system in the canonical ensemble with fixed particle number N and volume V at absolute temperature T. Let k be the Boltzmann constant. The system has discrete microstates indexed by n with energies E_n. The canonical partition function is Z, and ensemble averages are denoted by angle brackets ⟨⋯⟩, so that the average energy is ⟨E⟩. The heat capacity at constant volume is defined by C_v=(∂⟨E⟩/∂T)_{N,V}. Using the canonical ensemble with probability weights proportional to exp(−E_n/(kT)), prove that the heat capacity is related to the mean-square fluctuation of the energy by C_v=(1/(k T^2))⟨(E−⟨E⟩)^2⟩. Here E denotes the microstate energy, and all sums run over the microstates n.
solution:
The canonical partition function is
$$
Z=\sum_n \exp(-E_n/(kT))
$$
The ensemble-average energy is
$$
\langle E \rangle=\frac{1}{Z}\sum_n E_n \exp(-E_n/(kT))
$$
Differentiate Z with respect to T
$$
\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}=\sum_n \exp(-E_n/(kT)) \frac{E_n}{k T^2}
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}=\frac{Z}{k T^2}\langle E \rangle
$$
Differentiate \langle E \rangle with respect to T
$$
\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{1}{Z}\frac{1}{k T^2}\sum_n E_n^2 \exp(-E_n/(kT))-\frac{\langle E \rangle}{Z}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}
$$
Recognizing averages gives
$$
\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{1}{k T^2}\langle E^2 \rangle-\frac{\langle E \rangle}{Z}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}
$$
Using the expression for \frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}
$$
\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{1}{k T^2}\langle E^2 \rangle-\frac{\langle E \rangle^2}{k T^2}
$$
By definition of the constant-volume heat capacity
$$
C_v=\left(\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}\right)_{N,V}
$$
Hence
$$
C_v=\frac{1}{k T^2}\langle (E-\langle E \rangle)^2 \rangle
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the explicit algebraic form "C_v = ..." and must be expressed solely using the symbols C_v, k, T, E, and ⟨E⟩ (ensemble-average brackets ⟨⋯⟩ are permitted). Do not introduce any other variables or constants.

$$\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{1}{k T^2}\langle E^2 \rangle-\frac{\langle E \rangle}{Z}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}$$
$$\frac{\partial \langle E \rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{1}{k T^2}\langle E^2 \rangle-\frac{\langle E \rangle^2}{k T^2}$$

Let $U$ be the total internal energy, $U_{min}$ the minimum possible total energy, and $S_{max}$ the maximum possible entropy. Let $E_{mp}$ and $E_{avg}$ denote the most probable and average energies per particle, respectively. Let $C(T)$ be the heat capacity of the system as a function of $T$. For algebraic convenience, define the auxiliary variable $a=\exp(E/kT)$.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the most probable energy of the system? (f）If C(T) is the heat capacity of the system,what is the value o $\int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } \frac { C ( T ) } { T } d T ?$
subquestions.solution:
For $N\gg 1$, the most probable energy equals the average energy to leading order
$$N E_{mp}\approx N E_{avg}$$
The total energy can be written as
$$U=-NE\frac{a-1/a}{a+1+1/a}$$
Equivalently
$$U=-\frac{2NE\sinh(E/kT)}{1+2\cosh(E/kT)}$$
For the heat-capacity integral
$$\int_0^{\infty} \frac{C(T)}{T} dT=\int_0^{\infty} dS$$
$$\int_0^{\infty} dS=S(\infty)-S(0)$$
$$S(\infty)-S(0)=Nk\ln 3$$

context: Consider an ideal classical (Boltzmann) gas of N indistinguishable particles confined in a volume V at absolute temperature T in the extreme relativistic limit. Each particle has energy epsilon related to the magnitude of its momentum p_mom by epsilon = c p_mom, where c is the speed of light. Let h be Planck's constant, k be Boltzmann's constant, and beta = 1/(k T). Find the pressure p, the entropy S, and the specific heat at constant volume C_V of the gas, expressing each as a function of V, T, and N. Define z as the single-particle partition function and Z as the canonical partition function of the gas.
solution:
Let z denote the single-particle partition function, Z the total partition function, p the pressure, S the entropy, U the internal energy, and C_V the specific heat at constant volume. Using beta = 1/(k T) and Stirling's approximation for ln N! in the classical limit, we obtain

$$z = \frac{4 \pi V}{h^3 c^3} \int_0^\infty \varepsilon^2 e^{-\varepsilon/(k T)} d\varepsilon$$

$$z = \frac{8 \pi V}{h^3 c^3} (k T)^3$$

$$Z = \frac{z^N}{N!}$$

$$Z = \frac{1}{N!} \left( \frac{8 \pi V}{h^3 c^3} \right)^N (k T)^{3 N}$$

$$p = \frac{1}{\beta} \frac{\partial}{\partial V} \ln Z$$

$$p = \frac{N k T}{V}$$

$$S = k \left( \ln Z - \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z \right)$$

$$S = N k \left( 3 \ln k T + \ln \frac{8 \pi V}{N h^3 c^3} + 4 \right)$$

$$U = - \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z$$

$$U = 3 N k T$$

$$C_V = 3 N k$$

Use only the following variables in each expression: for p use N, k, T, V; for S use N, k, T, V, h, c; for C_V use N, k. Do not introduce any other symbols or numerical approximations.

context: Vessel 1 has volume V_1 and contains N molecules of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T (denoted as τ in the original statement) and pressure P_1. Vessel 2 has volume V_2 and contains N molecules of the same ideal gas at the same temperature T and pressure P_2. The single-molecule energy as a function of momentum components p_x, p_y, p_z is given by E_k(p_x,p_y,p_z) = \frac{1}{2m}(p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2) + \varepsilon_k, where m is the molecular mass and \varepsilon_k are the internal energy levels of the molecule. Let h be Planck's constant and k be Boltzmann's constant. Let z denote the single-particle partition function, Z the N-particle partition function for indistinguishable particles, F the Helmholtz free energy, S the entropy, and \beta = 1/(kT).

subquestions.subproblem: Evaluate the free energy F = - k T \ln Z, where Z is the partition function and k is Boltzmann's constant. Explicitly display the dependence on the volume V_1. Now consider another vessel, also at temperature \tau, containing the same number of molecules of an identical gas held at pressure P_2
subquestions.solution:
The single-particle partition function is
$$z = \frac{V}{h^3} \sum_k \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-E_k/(kT)} dp_x dp_y dp_z$$
$$z = V \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right)^{3/2} z_0$$
where
$$z_0 = \sum_n e^{-\varepsilon_n/(kT)}$$
Accounting for indistinguishability, the N-particle partition function is
$$Z = \frac{z^N}{N!}$$
$$Z = \frac{V^N}{N!} \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right)^{3N/2} z_0^N$$
The Helmholtz free energy is
$$F = -kT \ln Z$$
$$F = -kT \left( N \ln V + N \ln z_0 + \frac{3N}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) - \ln N! \right)$$
The entropy obtained from Z is
$$S = k \left( \ln Z - \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln Z \right)$$
$$S = Nk \left( \ln \frac{V}{N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + \ln z_0 - \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln z_0 \right)$$
For vessel 1 and vessel 2, respectively,
$$S_1 = Nk \left( \ln \frac{V_1}{N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + S_0 \right)$$
$$S_2 = Nk \left( \ln \frac{V_2}{N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + S_0 \right)$$
where
$$S_0 = \ln z_0 - \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln z_0$$
Thus the total entropy of the two gases before mixing is
$$S = S_1 + S_2$$
$$S = 2Nk \left[ \ln \frac{\sqrt{V_1 V_2}}{N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + S_0 \right]$$
In the expression for F, the dependence on V_1 is made explicit by taking V = V_1 for vessel 1

Using the ideal-gas relations P_1 V_1 = NkT and P_2 V_2 = NkT, one obtains
$$S = 2Nk \left[ \ln \frac{kT}{\sqrt{P_1 P_2}} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + S_0 \right]$$

subquestions.subproblem: The vessels are then connected to permit the gases to mix without doing work. Evaluate explicitly the change in entropy of the system. Check whether your answer makes sense by considering the special case V _ { 1 } = V _ { 2 }
subquestions.solution:
After mixing at constant temperature T, the final entropy is
$$S' = 2Nk \left[ \ln \frac{V_1 + V_2}{2N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) + \frac{5}{2} + S_0 \right]$$
The change in entropy is
$$\Delta S = S' - S$$
$$\Delta S = 2Nk \ln \frac{V_1 + V_2}{2 \sqrt{V_1 V_2}}$$
Equivalently, using P_i V_i = NkT,
$$\Delta S = 2Nk \ln \frac{P_1 + P_2}{2 \sqrt{P_1 P_2}}$$
For the special case V_1 = V_2 (equivalently P_1 = P_2), one finds
$$\Delta S = 0$$

subquestions.subproblem: Consider an ideal gas of N particles of mass m confined to a volume V at temperature T. Using the classical approximation for the partition function and assuming the particles are indistinguishable, calculate the chemical potential mu of the gas.
subquestions.solution:
$$z = \frac{V^N}{N!} \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right)^{\frac{3N}{2}}$$
$$F = -kT \ln z$$
$$pV = NkT$$
$$G = F + pV$$
$$G = -kT \ln z + NkT$$
$$G = NkT \left[ \ln \frac{N}{V} - \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) \right]$$
$$\mu = -kT \left[ \ln \frac{V}{N} + \frac{3}{2} \ln \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right) \right]$$

context: Consider a dilute ideal gas of heteronuclear diatomic molecules. Each molecule consists of two non-identical atoms, and the moment of inertia about an axis through the molecular center of mass perpendicular to the bond is I. The absolute temperature is T (the original symbol τ is identified with T). The Boltzmann constant is k, the Planck constant is h, and the reduced Planck constant is ħ with ħ = h/(2π). The rotational quantum number is J = 0, 1, 2, ... with degeneracy 2J+1 and energy levels ε_J = (ħ^2/(2I)) J(J+1). For one mole of gas, let N denote the number of molecules in the sample (Avogadro's number). Define the single-molecule rotational partition function z_R, the total rotational partition function for one mole z_R^T, the rotational energy per mole E_R, the rotational constant-volume specific heat per mole C_R, and the rotational entropy per mole S_R. You may use β = 1/(k T). Calculate the rotational contributions C_R and S_R in the two limiting cases k T ≫ ħ^2/I and k T ≪ ħ^2/I, keeping the lowest non-zero order terms in each limit. Express all final answers in terms of I, k, T, h, ħ, and N.
solution:
The single-molecule rotational partition function is
$$
z_R = \sum_{J=0}^{\infty} (2J+1) \exp(- \beta \varepsilon_J)
$$
with energy levels
$$
\varepsilon_J = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I} J(J+1)
$$
The total rotational partition function for one mole is
$$
z_R^T = (z_R)^N
$$
The rotational energy per mole is
$$
E_R = - \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln z_R^T
$$
which gives
$$
E_R = - N \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln z_R
$$
The rotational specific heat per mole is
$$
C_R = \frac{\partial E_R}{\partial T}
$$
The rotational entropy per mole is
$$
S_R = N k \ln z_R + \frac{E_R}{T}
$$
High-temperature limit k T ≫ ħ^2/I, equivalently β ħ^2/(2 I) ≪ 1:
$$
\beta \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I} \ll 1
$$
Use the continuum approximation
$$
z_R = \int_0^{\infty} (2J+1) \exp\Big(- \beta \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I} J(J+1)\Big) dJ
$$
which yields
$$
z_R = \frac{2 I k T}{\hbar^2}
$$
Then
$$
E_R = N k T
$$
$$
C_R = N k
$$
$$
S_R = N k \Big( 1 + \ln \frac{2 I k T}{\hbar^2} \Big)
$$
Low-temperature limit k T ≪ ħ^2/I. Keeping only the ground state J=0 and the first excited manifold J=1 gives
$$
z_R \approx 1 + 3 \exp\Big( - \beta \frac{h^2}{4 \pi^2 I} \Big)
$$
Equivalently
$$
z_R \approx 1 + 3 \exp\Big( - \frac{h^2}{4 \pi^2 k T I} \Big)
$$
The energy is
$$
E_R = \frac{3 N \frac{\hbar^2}{I} \exp\Big( - \frac{h^2}{4 \pi^2 I k T} \Big)}{1 + 3 \exp\Big( - \frac{h^2}{4 \pi^2 I k T} \Big)}
$$
and to lowest order
$$
E_R \approx \frac{3 N \hbar^2}{I} \exp\Big( - \frac{h^2}{4 \pi^2 I k T} \Big)
$$
The specific heat is
$$
C_R = \frac{3 N \hbar^4}{I^2 k T^2} \exp\Big( - \frac{\hbar^2}{4 \pi^2 I k T} \Big)
$$
The entropy is
$$

The spins interact only with the applied field. Let M denote the total magnetic moment of the assembly and E its total energy. The absolute temperature is T and k is Boltzmann's constant. Let S denote the entropy and z the total partition function of the system. The heat capacity at constant applied field is C_H. The auxiliary variable a is introduced for convenience. The average magnetic moment per particle in equilibrium is denoted by \bar{\mu}. The inverse temperature is defined by
$$\beta = \frac{1}{k T}$$

subquestions.subproblem: Find the total magnetic moment and the energy, assuming that the system is in thermal equilibrium at temperature T
subquestions.solution:
The total magnetic moment is
$$M = N \bar{\mu}$$
The average magnetic moment per particle is
$$\bar{\mu} = \mu_0 \tanh\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)$$
Therefore
$$M = N \mu_0 \tanh\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)$$
Using E = - M H gives
$$E = - M H$$
so that
$$E = - N \mu_0 H \tanh\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)$$
The heat capacity at constant field is
$$C_H = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial T} \right)_H$$
which evaluates to
$$C_H = N k \frac{\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)^2}{\cosh^2\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)}$$
The partition function of the system is
$$z = \left( a + \frac{1}{a} \right)^N$$
with
$$a = \exp\left( \frac{\mu_0 H}{k T} \right)$$
The entropy can be written as
$$S = k \left( \ln z - \beta \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln z \right)$$
and hence
$$S = N k \left[ \ln \left( e^{\mu_0 H \beta} + e^{- \mu_0 H \beta} \right) - \mu_0 H \beta \tanh \left( \mu_0 H \beta \right) \right]$$

subquestions.subproblem: The entropy \sigma

If the entropy of the spin states is maintained constant, i.e., mu_0 B/(k T) is kept constant, then the temperature of the spin states can be lowered by reducing the magnetic field adiabatically. In the crystal, the decrease in the temperature of the spin states can cool the lattice vibrations by heat transfer, so the whole crystal is cooled by an adiabatic reduction of the magnetic field. The adiabatic relation is $$\frac{T_f}{B_f} = \frac{T_i}{B_i}$$ Therefore the stated result is $$T_f = 10^{-3} \unit{K}$$

context: Curie–Weiss model. Consider a crystal of N atoms (N on the order of 10^{23}) with spin quantum number s = 1/2 and spin projection m_s = ± 1/2. The spin of the i-th atom is denoted by s_i, whose z component (s_i)_z has eigenvalues ± 1/2. The magnetic moment of the i-th atom is μ_i = g μ_B s_i, where g is the Landé g-factor and μ_B = e ħ / 2 m c is the Bohr magneton, with e the magnitude of the electron charge, ħ the reduced Planck constant, m the electron mass, and c the speed of light. The atoms do not interact unless otherwise stated, are in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature T, and are placed in a uniform external magnetic field H directed along the z axis. Let k denote the Boltzmann constant. Define the dimensionless parameter η = g μ_B H / 2 k T. The total partition function of the spin system is z. The Helmholtz free energy is F = - k T ln z. The entropy of the spin system is S. The magnetization is M = ⟨∑_{i=1}^N (μ_i)_z⟩ and the magnetic susceptibility is χ = M / H. In the mean-field approximation for interacting spins, let n be the number of nearest neighbors of each atom and α be a parameter characterizing the interaction strength. The mean field at a site is denoted by H̄ and is defined by g μ_B H̄ = 2 α ⟨∑_{k=1}^N (s_k)_z⟩. For estimates we use ⟨∑_{k=1}^n (s_k)_z⟩ = (n/N) ⟨∑_{k=1}^N (s_k)_z⟩, so that H̄ can be expressed in terms of the total magnetization M. $$z = (2 \cosh \eta)^N$$
$$\eta = \frac{g \mu_B H}{2 k T}$$
$$F = - k T \ln z$$

For the weak field limit η ≪ 1

context: Consider a system of noninteracting free electrons confined in a cubic box of edge length a and volume V=a^3 in a uniform magnetic field B directed along the z axis. Ignore electron spin. Let e>0 be the magnitude of the electron charge, m the electron mass, c the speed of light, h the Planck constant, and \hbar=h/(2\pi). The cyclotron frequency is \omega_c=e B/(m c). The Bohr magneton is \mu_B=e \hbar/(2 m c). Let k be the Boltzmann constant, T the temperature, and \beta=1/(k T). Denote the momentum components by p_x, p_y, and p_z. Landau levels are labeled by l=0,1,2,\dots. Define the fugacity \lambda=\exp(\beta \mu), where \mu is the chemical potential. Define the thermal de Broglie wavelength \lambda_T=h/\sqrt{2 \pi m k T}. Define the dimensionless field parameter x=\mu_B B/(k T) and the Langevin function \mathcal L(x)=\coth x-1/x. Single-particle eigenstates are labeled by u with energies \epsilon_u. Let \Xi denote the grand partition function. Let F denote the Helmholtz free energy and M the magnetization, with M=-(\partial F/\partial B) at fixed T and V. Let \overline N denote the mean particle number and \overline n=\overline N/V the number density. Let \chi_\infty denote the magnetic susceptibility in the high temperature limit, defined by \chi_\infty=M/(V B). Show that Landau quantization affects the calculation of diamagnetism in the high temperature limit by calculating:

subquestions.subproblem: the degeneracy of the quantized energy levels,
subquestions.solution:
Without the magnetic field, the number of states in the interval p_x to p_x+dp_x and p_y to p_y+dp_y is
$$
\frac{a^2}{h^2} dp_x dp_y
$$
In the magnetic field, the single-particle energies are
$$
E_{l,p_z}=\hbar \omega_c \left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{p_z^2}{2 m}
$$
Let g_l denote the degeneracy of Landau level l. The lth Landau level corresponds to an annular region A_1 in the p_x p_y plane defined by
$$
\frac{p_x^2+p_y^2}{2 m}>2 \mu_B B l
$$
$$
\frac{p_x^2+p_y^2}{2 m}<2 \mu_B B (l+1)
$$
Thus
$$
\ng_l=\frac{a^2}{h^2} \iint_{A_1} dp_x dp_y
$$
In polar coordinates p=\sqrt{p_x^2+p_y^2}, the annulus A_1 becomes A_2 defined by
$$
\frac{p^2}{2 m}>2 \mu_B B l
$$
$$
\frac{p^2}{2 m}<2 \mu_B B (l+1)
$$
Hence
$$
\ng_l=\frac{a^2}{h^2} \int_{A_2} 2 \pi p dp
$$
Carrying out the integral gives
$$
\ng_l=\frac{a^2 e B}{h c}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of g_l = ... , and your response should be written with a, e, B, h, c.

subquestions.subproblem: the grand partition function,
subquestions.solution:
The grand partition function satisfies
$$
\ln \Xi=\sum_{u} \ln \left(1+\lambda e^{-\beta \epsilon_u}\right)
$$
Replacing the sum by the sum over Landau levels with degeneracy and the integral over p_z gives
$$
\ln \Xi=\frac{a}{h} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dp_z \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} g_l \ln \left(1+\lambda e^{-\beta \left[\hbar \omega_c \left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{p_z^2}{2 m}\right]}\right)
$$
In the high temperature limit
$$
\lambda \ll 1
$$
Using \ln(1+y)\approx y yields
$$
\ln \Xi=\frac{e B V}{h^2 c} \lambda \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dp_z \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} e^{-\beta \left[2 \mu_B B \left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{p_z^2}{2 m}\right]}
$$
The Gaussian integral is
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\beta p_z^2/(2 m)} dp_z=\frac{h}{\lambda_T}
$$
The geometric series is
$$
\sum_{l=0}^{\infty} e^{-2 \beta \mu_B B \left(l+\frac{1}{2}\right)}=\frac{1}{2 \sinh x}
$$
Therefore
$$
\ln \Xi=\frac{\lambda V}{\lambda_T^3} \frac{x}{\sinh x}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \ln \Xi = ... , and your response should be written with \lambda, V, \lambda_T, x.

subquestions.subproblem: the magnetic susceptibility in the high temperature limit.
subquestions.solution:
The magnetization is
$$
M=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial B}
$$
In the grand canonical ensemble
$$
M=\frac{1}{\beta} \left(\frac{\partial \ln \Xi}{\partial B}\right)_{\mu, T, V}
$$
Using the result for \ln \Xi gives
$$
M=\frac{\lambda V}{\lambda_T^3} \mu_B \left[\frac{1}{\sinh x}-\frac{x \cosh x}{\sinh^2 x}\right]
$$
The mean particle number is
$$
\overline N=\left(\lambda \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda} \ln \Xi\right)_{B, T, V}
$$
Thus
$$
\overline N=\frac{\lambda V}{\lambda_T^3} \frac{x}{\sinh x}
$$
Hence
$$
M=-\overline N \mu_B \mathcal L(x)
$$
with
$$
\mathcal L(x)=\coth x-\frac{1}{x}
$$
For x \ll 1,
$$
\mathcal L(x)=\frac{1}{3} x-\frac{1}{45} x^3+\dots
$$
In the same limit,
$$
\overline N \approx \frac{\lambda V}{\lambda_T^3}
$$
Therefore
$$
M \approx -\overline N \frac{\mu_B^2 B}{3 k T}
$$
The high temperature susceptibility is
$$
\chi_{\infty}=\frac{M}{V B}
$$
Hence
$$
\chi_{\infty}=-\overline n \frac{\mu_B^2}{3 k T}
$$
with
$$
\overline n=\frac{\overline N}{V}
$$

context: Consider a single electromagnetic mode in a perfectly conducting rectangular cavity. The mode has angular frequency ω and is in thermal equilibrium with a heat bath at temperature T. Let n ∈ {0,1,2,...} denote the photon occupation number of this mode. Angle brackets ⟨⋅⟩ denote thermal averages over the canonical ensemble for this single mode (Bose-Einstein statistics with zero chemical potential). Define the fluctuation Δn = n − ⟨n⟩. Introduce the dimensionless parameter λ = ħ ω / (k T), where ħ is the reduced Planck constant and k is the Boltzmann constant. Let z(λ) be the single-mode partition sum. Find the root-mean-square (rms) fluctuation √⟨(Δn)^2⟩ and determine whether it is smaller than the average photon number ⟨n⟩.
solution:
Define
$$
\lambda = \frac{\hbar \omega}{k T}
$$
Introduce the single-mode partition sum
$$
z = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} e^{-n \lambda}
$$
Evaluate the geometric series
$$
z = \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\lambda}}
$$
The average occupation number is
$$
\langle n \rangle = \frac{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n e^{-n \lambda}}{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} e^{-n \lambda}}
$$
Using z, this can be written as
$$
\langle n \rangle = -\frac{1}{z} \frac{dz}{d\lambda}
$$
Hence
$$
\langle n \rangle = \frac{1}{e^{\lambda} - 1}
$$
For the second moment
$$
\langle n^{2} \rangle = \frac{1}{z} \frac{d^{2} z}{d\lambda^{2}}
$$
The variance is
$$
\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle = \langle n^{2} \rangle - \langle n \rangle^{2}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle = - \frac{d\langle n \rangle}{d\lambda}
$$
Therefore
$$
\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle = \frac{e^{\lambda}}{(e^{\lambda} - 1)^{2}}
$$
The root-mean-square fluctuation is
$$
\sqrt{\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle} = \frac{e^{\lambda/2}}{e^{\lambda} - 1}
$$
In terms of \langle n \rangle
$$
\sqrt{\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle} = \langle n \rangle e^{\lambda/2}
$$
Comparison gives
$$
\sqrt{\langle (\Delta n)^{2} \rangle} > \langle n \rangle
$$
Thus the root-mean-square fluctuation exceeds the average number of photons in the mode
final_answer_instructions: Provide two items in your final answer: (1) an explicit expression for the rms fluctuation written exactly as “√⟨(Δn)^2⟩ = …”, with the right-hand side expressed solely in terms of λ (where λ = ħω/(kT)); do not introduce any other variables or constants on the right-hand side. (2) a single comparison inequality between √⟨(Δn)^2⟩ and ⟨n⟩, written using only one of the forms “√⟨(Δn)^2⟩ < ⟨n⟩”, “√⟨(Δn)^2⟩ = ⟨n⟩”, or “√⟨(Δn)^2⟩ > ⟨n⟩”. Here ⟨n⟩ denotes the thermal average photon number, Δn = n − ⟨n⟩ with n ∈ {0,1,2,…} the photon occupation number, ħ is the reduced Planck constant, ω is the angular frequency, k is the Boltzmann constant, and T is the temperature.

context: Consider an adsorbent surface having N sites, each of which can adsorb one gas molecule. This surface is in contact with an ideal gas with chemical potential μ determined by the pressure p and the temperature T. An adsorbed molecule has energy −ε0 compared to one in a free state. Let N1 denote the number of molecules adsorbed on the surface. Let Ξ denote the grand canonical partition function, and let N̄ denote the mean number of adsorbed molecules. Define the covering ratio θ as the ratio of adsorbed molecules to adsorbing sites, θ = N̄/N. For convenience define α = −μ/(k T). Here k is Boltzmann's constant, h is Planck's constant, m is the mass of a gas molecule, n is the number density of the gas, and ε is the kinetic energy integration variable where appropriate.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the grand canonical partition function (sometimes called the grand sum) and the mean number of adsorbed molecules.
subquestions.solution:
With N1 molecules adsorbed on the surface, the number of configurations is
$$C_{N_1}^N = \frac{N!}{N_1!\left(N - N_1\right)!}$$
The grand canonical partition function is
$$\Xi = \sum_{N_1=0}^{N} C_{N_1}^N e^{N_1\left(\mu + \varepsilon_0\right)/(k T)}$$
The closed form of the grand canonical partition function is
$$(1 + e^{\left(\mu + \varepsilon_0\right)/(k T)})^{N}$$
Define
$$\alpha = -\frac{\mu}{k T}$$
The mean number of adsorbed molecules is
$$\overline{N} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \ln \Xi$$
Evaluating the derivative gives
$$\overline{N} = \frac{N e^{\left(\mu + \varepsilon_0\right)/(k T)}}{1 + e^{\left(\mu + \varepsilon_0\right)/(k T)}}$$
The covering ratio is
$$\theta = \frac{\overline{N}}{N}$$
Hence
$$\theta = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\left(\mu + \varepsilon_0\right)/(k T)}}$$
For an ideal gas the chemical potentials are equal, and the ideal gas satisfies
$$\frac{p}{k T} = n$$
The number density in terms of the chemical potential is
$$n = \int_0^{\infty} \frac{2 \pi (2 m)^{3/2}}{h^{3}} \sqrt{\varepsilon} \ e^{\mu/(k T)} e^{-\varepsilon/(k T)} d\varepsilon$$
Evaluating the integral gives
$$e^{\mu/(k T)} = \frac{p}{k T} \left(\frac{h^{2}}{2 \pi m k T}\right)^{3/2}$$
Substituting into the covering ratio yields
$$\theta = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{k T}{p} \left(\frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^{2}}\right)^{3/2} e^{-\varepsilon_0/(k T)}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give both the grand canonical partition function and the mean number of adsorbed molecules in the forms 'Ξ = ...' and 'N̄ = ...', and your response should be written using only the variables N, μ, ε0, k, T.

$$\left(1 + x\right)^{N} = \sum_{N_1=0}^{N} \frac{N!}{N_1!\left(N - N_1\right)!} x^{N_1}$$

$$\theta = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{k T}{p} \left(\frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^{2}}\right)^{3/2} e^{-\varepsilon_0/(k T)}}$$

context:
A classical monatomic gas of N identical point particles occupies volume V at temperature T. The position of particle i is r_i in three-dimensional space, and r_ij = |r_i - r_j| is the scalar separation between particles i and j. The particles interact pairwise via a hard-sphere potential with core diameter a given by the piecewise definition below. The pressure is p. The specific volume per particle is v = V/N. Let k_B denote Boltzmann's constant, N_A Avogadro's number, and R the molar gas constant with R = N_A k_B. The constant-volume heat capacity of the sample is C_V, and the per-particle specific heat is c_V = C_V/N. The internal energy is U(T,V,N). In part (b), the virial expansion is written for one mole so that N = N_A and V is the molar volume. The hard-sphere potential is

$$\phi(r_{ij})=\begin{cases}\infty,& r_{ij}<a\\0,& r_{ij}>a\end{cases}$$

For later use, define the inverse temperature and the Mayer f-function by

$$\beta=\frac{1}{k_B T}$$

$$f(r)=e^{-\beta \phi(r)}-1$$

The second virial coefficient is defined by

$$B_2(T)=-\frac{1}{2}\int f(r) d^3 r$$

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the constant-volume specific heat as a function of temperature T and specific volume v = V/N
subquestions.solution:
For hard spheres the potential energy is zero for all allowed configurations, so the internal energy is purely kinetic by equipartition

$$U(T,V,N)=\frac{3}{2} N k_B T$$

The constant-volume heat capacity is

$$C_V(T,v,N)=\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}$$

Therefore

$$C_V(T,v,N)=\frac{3}{2} N k_B$$

The per-particle specific heat is

$$c_V(T,v)=\frac{C_V}{N}$$

Hence

$$c_V(T,v)=\frac{3}{2} k_B$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of c_V(T, v) = ..., and your response should be written using k_B only.

subquestions.subproblem: The virial expansion for the equation of state is an expansion of pV/(RT) in inverse powers of V:  pV/(RT) = 1 + A_1(T)/V + A_2(T)/V^2 + ... . Compute the virial coefficient A_1(T)
subquestions.solution:
For hard spheres the Mayer function is

$$f(r)=\begin{cases}-1,& r<a\\0,& r>a\end{cases}$$

The definition of the second virial coefficient gives

$$B_2(T)=-\frac{1}{2}\int f(r) d^3 r$$

Evaluate the integral as

$$\int f(r) d^3 r=-\int_{r<a} d^3 r$$

The geometric integral is

$$\int_{r<a} d^3 r=\frac{4\pi}{3} a^3$$

Hence

$$\int f(r) d^3 r=-\frac{4\pi}{3} a^3$$

Therefore

$$B_2(T)=\frac{2\pi}{3} a^3$$

For one mole the virial expansion is

$$\frac{pV}{R T}=1+\frac{A_1(T)}{V}+\ldots$$

The relation between A_1(T) and B_2(T) is

$$\frac{pV}{N k_B T}=1+\frac{B_2(T) N}{V}+\ldots$$

With R=N_A k_B and N=N_A we obtain

$$A_1(T)=B_2(T) N_A$$

Thus

$$A_1(T)=\frac{2\pi}{3} N_A a^3$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of A_1(T) = ..., and your response should be written using N_A and a only.

context: Consider a classical canonical ensemble of N identical point particles, each of mass m, confined to a volume V at absolute temperature T. The position of particle i is r_i in R^3, and r_{ij} = |r_i - r_j| is the distance between particles i and j. The particles interact via the pairwise central potential phi(r_{ij}) = A r_{ij}^{-n} with A > 0 and n > 0. This potential is homogeneous: phi(gamma r) = gamma^{-n} phi(r) for any gamma > 0. Let U denote the total internal energy and p the pressure. Let k be the Boltzmann constant and h the Planck constant. Let Z(T,V) denote the canonical partition function and F(T,V) the Helmholtz free energy. Using scaling arguments applied to the partition function, show that U can be expressed in the form U = a p V + b N k T, where the constants a and b depend only on n. Determine a(n) and b(n).
solution:
Define beta by
$$
\beta = \frac{1}{k T}
$$
The canonical partition function after integrating over momenta is
$$
Z(T,V) = \left( \frac{2 \pi m k T}{h^2} \right)^{\frac{3N}{2}} \int_V \exp\bigg( - \beta \sum_{i<j} \phi(r_{ij}) \bigg) d^{3N} r
$$
Replace T by \lambda T to obtain
$$
Z(\lambda T,V) = \left( \frac{2 \pi m k \lambda T}{h^2} \right)^{\frac{3N}{2}} \int_V \exp\bigg( - \frac{\beta}{\lambda} \sum_{i<j} \phi(r_{ij}) \bigg) d^{3N} r
$$
Use the homogeneity phi(\gamma r) = \gamma^{-n} phi(r) to write
$$
\exp\bigg( - \frac{\beta}{\lambda} \sum_{i<j} \phi(r_{ij}) \bigg) = \exp\bigg( - \beta \sum_{i<j} \phi(\lambda^{1/n} r_{ij}) \bigg)
$$
Change variables r_i' = \lambda^{1/n} r_i to get
$$
d^{3N} r = \lambda^{-\frac{3N}{n}} d^{3N} r'
$$
Under this change of variables the volume transforms as
$$
V \mapsto \lambda^{\frac{3}{n}} V
$$
Hence
$$
Z(\lambda T,V) = \left( \frac{2 \pi m k \lambda T}{h^2} \right)^{\frac{3N}{2}} \lambda^{-\frac{3N}{n}} \int_{\lambda^{3/n} V} \exp\bigg( - \beta \sum_{i<j} \phi(r_{ij}) \bigg) d^{3N} r
$$
Therefore
$$
Z(\lambda T,V) = \lambda^{3N\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n}\right)} Z\big( T, \lambda^{3/n} V \big)
$$
Equivalently
$$
Z\big( \lambda T, \lambda^{-3/n} V \big) = \lambda^{3N\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n}\right)} Z(T,V)
$$
Define the Helmholtz free energy by
$$
F(T,V) = - k T \ln Z(T,V)
$$
Using the scaling of Z gives
$$
F\big( \lambda T, \lambda^{-3/n} V \big) = - k \lambda T \ln Z\big( \lambda T, \lambda^{-3/n} V \big)
$$
Thus
$$
F\big( \lambda T, \lambda^{-3/n} V \big) = - 3 N \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg) k \lambda T \ln \lambda + \lambda F(T,V)
$$
Differentiate with respect to \lambda and set \lambda = 1 to obtain
$$
T \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial T} \bigg)_V - \frac{3}{n} V \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V} \bigg)_T = - 3 N \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg) k T + F
$$
Use the thermodynamic identities
$$
U = F - T \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial T} \bigg)_V
$$
$$
p = - \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V} \bigg)_T
$$
Substitution yields
$$
U = \frac{3}{n} p V + 3 \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg) N k T
$$
Comparing with U = a p V + b N k T gives
$$
a = \frac{3}{n}
$$
$$
b = 3 \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide both constants as explicit functions of n. Your final answer should be given in the form a(n) = ... , b(n) = ... , and your response should use only the variable n.

grading_standard.formula: $$F\big( \lambda T, \lambda^{-3/n} V \big) = - 3 N \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg) k \lambda T \ln \lambda + \lambda F(T,V)$$
$$T \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial T} \bigg)_V - \frac{3}{n} V \bigg( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V} \bigg)_T = - 3 N \bigg( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{n} \bigg) k T + F$$

context: This problem develops Gaussian integrals and applies them to a simple model of thermal expansion for atoms interacting via a Lennard-Jones–type potential. Conventions and definitions: 1) In parts (a) and (b), α>0 and β are real parameters. In part (b), f(x) is a smooth function on the integration interval, and a>0 denotes an integration cutoff of order 1/√α. This a in part (b) is unrelated to the potential-range parameter a used in parts (c) and (d). 2) In parts (c) and (d), U0>0 and a>0 are the parameters of the interatomic potential U(x)=U0[(a/x)^{12}−2(a/x)^6], and x denotes the scalar separation between two atoms constrained to move along the x axis. 3) In part (d), k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is the absolute temperature with kT≪U0. Let x denote the displacement from the equilibrium separation, so the instantaneous separation is a+x and the mean displacement is denoted by \bar{x}(T); the mean interatomic separation is a+\bar{x}(T). The dimensionless coefficient is defined by λ=(1/a)(d\bar{x}/dT). The effective nearest-neighbor potential used for thermal averaging is U_T(x)=U(a+x)+U(a−x). When instructed to extend integration limits to ±∞, the justification is that for kT≪U0 the dominant contributions to the thermal averages arise from small displacements |x|∼√(kT/U_{T_2})≪a where the quadratic term confines fluctuations, so tails are exponentially suppressed. 4) In the final expression for λ in part (d), the symbol U denotes U0.

subquestions.subproblem: Given $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { - \infty } ^ { + \infty } \exp ( - \alpha x ^ { 2 } ) d x = \sqrt { \pi / \alpha } } \end{array}$ ,show that $\int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } { x ^ { 2 } e ^ { - \alpha x ^ { 2 } } d x } = { \frac { \sqrt \pi } { 2 } } { \alpha ^ { - 3 / 2 } } \ , \quad \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } { x ^ { 4 } e ^ { - \alpha x ^ { 2 } } d x } = { \frac { 3 } { 4 } } { \sqrt \pi } { \alpha ^ { - 5 / 2 } } \ .'
subquestions.solution: Define $$I(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\alpha x^2} dx$$ Using the given result, $$I(\alpha)=\sqrt{\pi}\alpha^{-1/2}$$ Differentiate with respect to \alpha $$\frac{dI}{d\alpha}=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 e^{-\alpha x^2} dx$$ Also, $$\frac{dI}{d\alpha}=-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi}\alpha^{-3/2}$$ Hence, $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 e^{-\alpha x^2} dx=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\alpha^{-3/2}$$ Differentiate once more $$\frac{d^2 I}{d\alpha^2}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^4 e^{-\alpha x^2} dx$$ and also $$\frac{d^2 I}{d\alpha^2}=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi}\alpha^{-5/2}$$ Therefore, $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^4 e^{-\alpha x^2} dx=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi}\alpha^{-5/2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present both integrals explicitly in closed form as two equations: ∫_{-∞}^{∞} x^2 e^{-α x^2} dx = ... and ∫_{-∞}^{∞} x^4 e^{-α x^2} dx = .... Your response should be written only in terms of α (and standard constants such as π), with no additional variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Given that ${ \frac { \beta } { \sqrt { \alpha } } } \ll 1$ and that $\scriptstyle a$ is of the order of $\frac { 1 } { \sqrt { \alpha } }$ show $$ \int _ { - a } ^ { a } f ( x ) e ^ { - \alpha \{ x ^ { 2 } + \beta x ^ { 3 } \} } d x \approx \int _ { - a } ^ { a } f ( x ) ( 1 - \alpha \beta x ^ { 3 } ) e ^ { - \alpha x ^ { 2 } } d x \ . $$
subquestions.solution: Factor the exponential as $$e^{-\alpha\{x^2+\beta x^3\}}=e^{-\alpha x^2} e^{-\alpha\beta x^3}$$ For |x|\lesssim a with a of order \alpha^{-1/2} and with \beta/\sqrt{\alpha}\ll 1, the quantity \alpha\beta x^3 is small, so to leading order we use $$e^{-\alpha\beta x^3}\approx 1-\alpha\beta x^3$$ Therefore, $$\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) e^{-\alpha\{x^2+\beta x^3\}} dx\approx\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\left(1-\alpha\beta x^3\right)e^{-\alpha x^2} dx$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the single approximate equality ∫_{-a}^{a} f(x) e^{-α(x^2+β x^3)} dx ≈ ∫_{-a}^{a} f(x) (1 − αβ x^3) e^{-α x^2} dx. Your response should be written only with f, α, β, and a (x appears only as the dummy integration variable). Do not introduce any other symbols.

subquestions.subproblem: Two atoms interact through a potential $$ U ( x ) = U _ { 0 } \left[ \left( \frac { a } { x } \right) ^ { 1 2 } - 2 \left( \frac { a } { x } \right) ^ { 6 } \right] \ , $$ where $\pmb { x }$ is their separation.Sketch this potential.Calculate the value of $\pmb { x }$ for which $U \{ x \}$ is minimum.
subquestions.solution: Compute the derivative $$\frac{dU}{dx}=U_0\left(-12 a^{12} x^{-13}+12 a^6 x^{-7}\right)$$ Set it to zero to locate the extremum $$\frac{dU}{dx}=0$$ Solve for x to obtain $$x=a$$ Hence U(x) attains its minimum at x=a
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should report the location of the minimum as a single equation of the form x_min = ... and your response should be written using a only. The sketch is not part of the automatically graded final answer.

subquestions.subproblem: Given a row of such atoms constrained to move only on the $\scriptstyle x$ axis,each assumed to interact only with its nearest neighbors,use classical statistical mechanics to calculate the mean interatomic separation $\overline { { x } } ( T )$ To do this,expand $\boldsymbol { U }$ about its minimum，keeping as many terms as necessary to obtain the lowest order temperature dependence of $\overline { { x } } ( T )$ Assume that $k T \ll U _ { 0 }$ ，and in the relevant integrals extend the limits of integration to $\pm \infty$ where appropriate.Explain clearly the justification for extending the limits.Also calculate $$ \lambda = \frac { \left( \frac { d \bar { x } } { d T } \right) } { a } \ . $$ .
subquestions.solution: At T=0 the atoms are at their equilibrium separation a. Define the nearest-neighbor effective potential $$U_T(x)=U(a+x)+U(a-x)$$ Expand about x=0 and keep the lowest anharmonic term needed for the temperature dependence $$U_T(x)=U_T(a)+U_{T_2} x^2+U_{T_3} x^3+\cdots$$ For the given U(x), the coefficients are $$U_{T_2}=\frac{72 U_0}{a^2}$$ $$U_{T_3}=-\frac{504 U_0}{a^3}$$ The thermal average of the displacement is $$\bar{x}(T)=\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x e^{-U_T(x)/(kT)} dx}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-U_T(x)/(kT)} dx}$$ For kT\ll U0 we expand to first order in the cubic term and approximate the weight by a Gaussian with curvature U_{T_2} $$\bar{x}(T)\approx\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\left(1-\frac{U_{T_3}}{kT}x^3\right)e^{-(U_{T_2}/(kT))x^2} dx}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-(U_{T_2}/(kT))x^2} dx}$$ Using the Gaussian integrals from part (a) with \alpha=U_{T_2}/(kT), the result is $$\bar{x}(T)=\frac{7 a k T}{96 U_0}$$ Extending the integration limits to \pm\infty is justified because the dominant fluctuations satisfy |x|\sim\sqrt{kT/U_{T_2}}\ll a when kT\ll U0, so contributions from large |x| are exponentially suppressed. Define $$\lambda=\frac{1}{a}\frac{d\bar{x}}{dT}$$ Therefore, $$\lambda=\frac{7 k}{46 U}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide two equations: (1) the mean separation as \bar{x}(T) = ... expressed using only a, k, T, and U0; and (2) the thermal expansion coefficient as λ = ... expressed using only k and U (where U denotes U0 as specified in the problem statement). Do not introduce any other variables.

context: Estimate. Assume air behaves as an ideal diatomic gas with five active degrees of freedom at room temperature. Use the following constants and definitions throughout: N is the number of molecules in the room, N_A = 6.02 × 10^{23} 1/mol is Avogadro's number, R = 8.31 \unit{J/(mol K)} is the gas constant, V_{room} = 50 \unit{m^3} is the volume of an average-sized room, and 1 \unit{m^3} = 1000 \unit{L}. Take the approximate molar volume of air near room conditions as V_{mol} ≈ 23 \unit{L/mol}. For thermodynamics, let E be the energy per mole at absolute temperature T, Q the heat added to warm one mole through a temperature change \Delta T at constant pressure, and C_p the molar heat capacity at constant pressure with C_p = \frac{7}{2} R for air in this temperature range. In parts that involve heat transfer between reservoirs, let T_1 and T_2 be the absolute temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs, respectively, dQ an infinitesimal heat transfer, dW the minimal external work required by a reversible device to transfer dQ between reservoirs, and \Delta W the corresponding finite-work estimate for a small temperature change \Delta T. Where specified, take T_1 = 313 \unit{K} and T_2 = 293 \unit{K}.

subquestions.subproblem: The number of molecules in the air in a room.
subquestions.solution:
Assuming V_{mol} ≈ 23 \unit{L/mol} and V_{room} = 50 \unit{m^3} = 50 × 1000 \unit{L}, the estimated number of molecules N is
$$N \simeq \frac{50 × 1000}{23} × 6.02 × 10^{23}$$
$$N \sim 10^{27}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the total number of molecules as a numerical value in scientific notation, written as N = ..., with no units, rounded to 1 significant figure.

subquestions.subproblem: Their energy,in joules or in ergs,per mole.
subquestions.solution:
The energy per mole for diatomic air is
$$E = \frac{5}{2} R T$$
Substituting R = 8.31 and T = 300 \unit{K} gives
$$E = \frac{5}{2} × 8.31 × 300$$
$$E \approx 6.2 × 10^{3} \unit{J}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the energy per mole as a numerical value in SI units, written as E = ... J, rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: What quantity of heat (in joules or in ergs) must be added to warm one mole of air at 1 atm from 0 ^ { \circ } C to 20 ^ { \circ } C ?
subquestions.solution:
The required heat at constant pressure is
$$Q = C_p \Delta T$$
with
$$C_p = \frac{7}{2} R$$
and
$$\Delta T = 20 \unit{K}$$
Thus
$$Q = \frac{7}{2} R \Delta T$$
$$Q \approx 5.8 × 10^{2} \unit{J}$$
For a reversible device transferring heat between reservoirs, the minimal differential work is
$$dW = \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_2} dQ$$
With
$$T_1 = 313 \unit{K}$$
$$T_2 = 293 \unit{K}$$
and for a small change
$$\Delta W = \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_2} C_p \Delta T$$
using
$$\Delta T = 2 \unit{K}$$
we obtain
$$\Delta W \approx 4 \unit{J}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the heat added as a numerical value in SI units, written as Q = ... J, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: Consider an ideal helium gas contained in a cube at standard temperature and pressure (STP). The cube has side length L, so the area of one wall is S. Let N denote the number of molecular collisions per second on a single wall. Use the following conventions and definitions: L is the cube side length, S is the wall area with S=L^2, p is the gas pressure at STP, T is the gas temperature at STP, k is the Boltzmann constant, m is the mass of one helium atom, n is the number density given by the ideal-gas relation, and \bar v is the mean molecular speed. Take STP here as p≈1×10^5 Pa and T≈300 K. The cube side length is L=10 cm. Estimate, to order of magnitude, N.
solution:
Convert the cube side length to SI units

$$
L=\frac{1}{10} \unit{m}
$$

The area of one wall is

$$
S=L^2
$$

At STP we take

$$
p\approx 1\times 10^{5} \unit{Pa}
$$

and

$$
T\approx 300 \unit{K}

The collision rate on one wall is estimated by

$$
N\approx \frac{1}{6} \bar v n S

where the mean speed is

$$

$$

and the number density is

$$
 n=\frac{p}{kT}

Combining these gives

Here, N is the number of molecular impacts per second on a single wall, S=L^2 is the wall area, p and T are the STP pressure and temperature, k is the Boltzmann constant, and m is the mass of a helium atom.

context: Estimate the mean free path l of a cosmic ray proton in the atmosphere at sea level. Let sigma be the effective nuclear scattering cross section; take sigma=10^{-26} \unit{cm^2}. Report l in centimeters.
solution:
The proton is scattered by interacting with the nuclei of atmospheric molecules.

$$n=\frac{N}{V}$$

$$n=\frac{p}{kT}$$

The mean free path is

Substituting n gives

context: Even though there is a high density of electrons in a metal, the mean inter-electron separation r is roughly 1–3 \unit{Å}, yet electron-electron mean free paths are long, with \lambda_{ee} roughly 10^{4} \unit{Å} at room temperature. State reasons for the long electron-electron collision mean free path and give a qualitative argument for its temperature dependence. Definitions: r is the mean inter-electron separation, \lambda_{ee} is the electron-electron mean free path, n is the total electron number density, n_{eff} is the effective number density of thermally excited electrons near the Fermi surface that can participate in collisions, \varepsilon_{F} is the Fermi energy, k is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature, and \sigma is an effective electron-electron scattering cross section. Write the final temperature dependence explicitly as \lambda_{ee}(T) \propto \dots
solution:
Because the electron gas in a metal is highly degenerate, Pauli exclusion blocks most final states for scattering. Only electrons within an energy window of order k T about the Fermi surface are thermally excited and can participate in electron-electron collisions. The effective number density of such electrons is
$$
n_{eff}=\x0crac{n k T}{\varepsilon_{F}}
$$
The electron-electron mean free path scales inversely with the available target density and the scattering cross section
$$
\lambda_{ee}\propto\frac{1}{n_{eff}\sigma}
$$
Substituting n_{eff} gives
$$
\lambda_{ee}\propto\frac{\varepsilon_{F}}{k T n \sigma}
$$
At fixed n, \varepsilon_{F}, and \sigma, the temperature dependence is
$$
\lambda_{ee}(T)\propto\frac{1}{T}
$$
Qualitatively, as T increases, more electrons are excited into the energy window near the Fermi surface, increasing the number of available scattering partners and final states, which reduces the mean free path.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \lambda_{ee}(T) \propto f(T), and your response should use only the variable T. Include \lambda_{ee}(T) explicitly on the left-hand side and do not introduce any other symbols or constants.

context: Consider a planar random walk (an orthogonalized drunk) that starts at the lamp-post at the origin. Each of the 3 steps is chosen independently and uniformly from the four cardinal directions: due north, due south, due east, or due west. Each step has fixed length L. Let P denote the probability that after 3 steps the walker is within (including on) the circle of radius 2L centered at the origin. Find P.
solution:
The total number of 3-step walks is
$$
N_{total}=4^3
$$
$$
N_{total}=64
$$
The walker is outside the circle of radius 2L only in two patterns: (i) all three steps in the same direction (net distance 3L), and (ii) two steps in one direction and one step in a perpendicular direction (net distance greater than 2L). The counts for these are
$$
N_{straight}=4
$$
$$
N_{perp}=4\times 2\times 3
$$
$$
N_{perp}=24
$$
Hence the total number of outside walks is
$$
N_{out}=N_{straight}+N_{perp}
$$
$$
N_{out}=28
$$
Therefore the desired probability is
$$
P=1-\frac{N_{out}}{N_{total}}
$$
$$
P=\frac{9}{16}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express P as a numerical value.

context: Estimate how long it would take a molecule of air in a room, where the air is macroscopically motionless and of perfectly uniform temperature and pressure, to reach a point a distance L = 5 m away by molecular diffusion. Use the random-walk model, where L is the displacement, l is the mean free path, v is the mean molecular speed, n is the number of collisions, and t is the required time. Take l = 5×10^{-6} m and v = 5×10^{2} m/s.
solution:
As molecular diffusion is a random process, we model the motion as a random walk with mean free path l. The mean-square displacement after n collisions is

$$
L^2 = n l^2
$$

Thus the required time is

$$
t = 
\frac{n l}{v}
$$

Eliminating n gives

$$
t = 
\frac{L^2}{l v}
$$

Given

$$
L = 5\unit{m}
$$

$$
l = 5\times 10^{-6}\unit{m}
$$

$$
v = 5\times 10^{2}\unit{m/s}
$$

Therefore

$$
t = 10^{4}\unit{s}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express t as a numerical value in seconds, in the form 't = ... s'. Round to 1 significant figure.

context: You have just very gently exhaled a helium atom in a room. Using a kinetic-theory random-walk estimate, compute the diffusion time χ_t (in seconds) for the atom to reach, with reasonable probability, some point on a spherical surface of radius R = 1 meter centered at your head. Assumptions and definitions: R is the target radial displacement. l is the mean free path, τ is the mean time between collisions, v is the typical molecular speed, N is the number of collisions, and t is the diffusion time, with the final answer to be reported as χ_t = t. n is the number density of air molecules, σ is an effective helium–air collision cross-section, k is Boltzmann's constant, T is temperature, and p is pressure. context: Scattering. Two hydrogen atoms interact via a short-range potential of range a = 4 × 10^{-10} \unit{m}. For a gas in thermal equilibrium at temperature T, obtain a numerical estimate of the temperature below which the atom-atom scattering is essentially s-wave. Use the criterion for s-wave dominance K a < 2π, where K is the magnitude of the relative wave number and a is the range of the potential. Relate K to temperature by equating the typical relative kinetic energy (1/2) k T to the free-particle kinetic energy h^2 K^2 /(8 π^2 m), where h is Planck's constant, k is Boltzmann's constant, and m is the mass of a hydrogen atom.
solution:
For s-wave scattering, the condition is
$$
K a < 2 \pi
$$
Using the thermal relation for the relative motion,
$$
\frac{1}{2} k T = \frac{h^2 K^2}{8 \pi^2 m}
$$
we get
$$
T < \frac{h^2}{m k a^2}
$$
Numerically, with a = 4 × 10^{-10} \unit{m},
$$
T < 1 \unit{K}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the maximum temperature below which scattering is essentially s-wave as a numerical value in kelvin. Report it in the format: T_max = [value] K, where T_max denotes the threshold temperature for s-wave dominance. Do not include any variables other than T_max, and do not use inequalities.

context: Show that a small object of mass m immersed in a fluid at absolute temperature T undergoes random motion due to molecular collisions. Consider motion along a fixed Cartesian axis with position x(t) and velocity v(t). Define the elapsed time as t>0 and the displacement as Δx. Use k for the Boltzmann constant. Assume linear viscous drag with coefficient γ proportional to the fluid viscosity, and a random force f(t) along the axis with zero mean and delta-correlated fluctuations characterized by a positive constant a (noise strength). The ensemble average over realizations is denoted by ⟨⋅⟩, δ(⋅) denotes the Dirac delta distribution, and t′ is an auxiliary time variable used in correlation functions. Introduce the parameters β=γ/m and F(t)=f(t)/m. The integration symbols s and s′ denote dummy time variables in the time integrals. Prove that the mean-square displacement satisfies the relation below for long times and express the constant λ in terms of γ and k.
solution:
The velocity is defined by
$$
v(t)=\frac{dx}{dt}
$$
The displacement is
$$
\Delta x=x(t)-x(0)
$$
The random force has zero mean and delta correlation
$$
\langle f(t) \rangle=0
$$
$$
\langle f(t) f(t') \rangle=a \delta(t-t')
$$
The Langevin equation is
$$
m \frac{dv}{dt}=-\gamma v+f(t)
$$
With the initial condition
$$
v(0)=0
$$
Define
$$
\beta=\frac{\gamma}{m}
$$
Define also
$$
F(t)=\frac{f(t)}{m}
$$
The solution for the velocity is
$$
v(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\beta(t-s)} F(s) ds
$$
The velocity autocorrelation is
$$
\langle v(t) v(t') \rangle=\frac{a}{m^2} \int_0^t ds \int_0^{t'} ds' e^{-\beta(t-s)} e^{-\beta(t'-s')} \delta(s-s')
$$
Evaluating the integrals gives
$$
\langle v(t) v(t') \rangle=\frac{a}{2 \beta m^2} e^{-\beta |t-t'|}-\frac{a}{2 \beta m^2} e^{-\beta(t+t')}
$$
Setting t'=t yields
$$
\langle v^2(t) \rangle=\frac{a}{2 \beta m^2}-\frac{a}{2 \beta m^2} e^{-2 \beta t}
$$
At thermal equilibrium the equipartition theorem gives
$$
\langle v^2(t) \rangle=\frac{k T}{m}
$$
Comparing at long times t \to \infty yields
$$
\frac{a}{2 \beta m^2}=\frac{k T}{m}
$$
Using \beta=\gamma/m gives
$$
a=2 \gamma k T
$$
The displacement is
$$
\Delta x=\int_0^t v(s) ds
$$
The mean-square displacement is
$$
\langle(\Delta x)^2\rangle=\int_0^t ds \int_0^t ds' \langle v(s) v(s') \rangle
$$
Using the stationary correlation for long times
$$
\langle v(s) v(s') \rangle=\frac{k T}{m} e^{-\beta |s-s'|}
$$
we obtain
$$
\langle(\Delta x)^2\rangle=\frac{2 k T}{\gamma} \Big[ t-\frac{m}{\gamma} \big(1-e^{-\gamma t/m}\big) \Big]
$$
In the long-time limit this becomes
$$
\langle(\Delta x)^2\rangle=\frac{2 k T}{\gamma} t
$$
This can be written as
$$
\langle(\Delta x)^2\rangle=\frac{T t}{\lambda}
$$
with
$$
\lambda=\frac{\gamma}{2 k}
$$
Thus λ is proportional to the fluid viscosity through γ, as required
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ⟨(Δx)^2⟩ = T t / λ, and you must also express λ solely in terms of γ and k. No variables other than ⟨(Δx)^2⟩, T, t, λ, γ, and k should appear in your final expression.
