context: Consider a two-dimensional ideal monatomic gas of N molecules, each of mass M, at temperature T, constrained to move only in the xy plane. The usual volume becomes an area A, and the pressure p is the force per unit length. Let k denote the Boltzmann constant. Let v_x and v_y be the Cartesian components of the molecular velocity in the plane, and let v be the speed. Let f(v) dv denote the total number of molecules with speeds between v and v + dv, and let f dv_x dv_y denote the total number of molecules with velocity components between v_x and v_x + dv_x and between v_y and v_y + dv_y. Let c denote the normalization constant for the component distribution f dv_x dv_y, and let c' denote the normalization constant for the speed distribution f(v) dv; both c and c' are determined by the requirement that the corresponding distribution integrates to N. Let c_v denote the heat capacity at constant area A and c_p the heat capacity at constant pressure p. Let U denote the internal energy and H the enthalpy of the gas. In part (d), let n denote the number of molecules striking unit length of a wall per unit time.

subquestions.subproblem: Give an expression for f(v) dv, the total number of molecules with speeds between v and v + dv. Assume that the classical limit is applicable in considering the behavior of these molecules.
subquestions.solution:
Start from the 2D Maxwell distribution for velocity components
$$f dv_x dv_y = c e^{-\frac{M}{2 k T} (v_x^2 + v_y^2)} dv_x dv_y$$
Transforming to the speed distribution gives
$$f(v) dv = c' v e^{-\frac{M v^2}{2 k T}} dv$$
Normalize via
$$N = \int_0^\infty f(v) dv$$
The normalized speed distribution is
$$f(v) dv = \frac{M N}{k T} v e^{-\frac{M v^2}{2 k T}} dv$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form f(v) dv = ... dv, and your response should use only N, M, k, T, and v.

subquestions.subproblem: Give the equation of state (relating pressure, temperature, etc.).
subquestions.solution: $$p A = N k T$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form p A = ..., and your response should use only p, A, N, k, and T.

subquestions.subproblem: Give the specific heats at constant area (two dimensional analogue of specific heat at constant volume) and at constant pressure.
subquestions.solution:
By equipartition, the internal energy is
$$U = N k T$$
Therefore
$$c_v = \frac{dU}{dT}$$
$$c_v = N k$$
Using the enthalpy relation
$$H = U + p A$$
and the equation of state, we obtain
$$H = 2 N k T$$
Hence
$$c_p = \frac{dH}{dT}$$
$$c_p = c_v + N k$$
$$c_p = 2 N k$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present both relations c_v = ... and c_p = ..., and your response should use only N and k.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive a formula for the number of molecules striking unit length of the wall per unit time. Express your result in terms of N, A, T, M and any other necessary constants.
subquestions.solution:
The 2D Maxwell distribution for velocity components is
$$f dv_x dv_y = \frac{M N}{2 \pi k T} e^{-\frac{M}{2 k T} (v_x^2 + v_y^2)} dv_x dv_y$$
The number of molecules striking unit length per unit time is
$$n = \int_0^\infty \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{v_x}{A} f dv_x dv_y$$
This evaluates to
$$n = \frac{N}{A} \sqrt{\frac{k T}{2 \pi M}}$$
The pressure can be computed from momentum transfer as
$$p = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{2 M v_x^2}{A} f dv_x dv_y$$
which gives
$$p = \frac{N}{A} k T$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form n = ..., and your response should use only N, A, T, M, k, and fundamental constants (such as π) as needed.

grading_standard.formula: $$f dv_x dv_y = c e^{-\frac{M}{2 k T} (v_x^2 + v_y^2)} dv_x dv_y$$
$$f(v) dv = c' v e^{-\frac{M v^2}{2 k T}} dv$$
$$f(v) dv = \frac{M N}{k T} v e^{-\frac{M v^2}{2 k T}} dv$$
$$f dv_x dv_y = \frac{M N}{2 \pi k T} e^{-\frac{M}{2 k T} (v_x^2 + v_y^2)} dv_x dv_y$$

context: A parallel beam of beryllium atoms with mass number A=9 is formed by evaporation from an oven heated to T_b=1000\unit{K} through a small hole. The vacuum chamber contains background gas at room temperature T_bg=300\unit{K}. The beam traverses a path of length L. Symbols used: m is the mass of a Be atom, k is the Boltzmann constant, sigma is the collision cross-section for collisions between a beam atom and a background gas atom, l is the mean free path in the background gas, n is the number density of the background gas, p is the pressure of the background gas, x is a travel distance along the beam, v_x is the component of atomic velocity along the beam direction, f(v_x) is the flux-weighted one-dimensional velocity distribution for an effusive beam, tau is the flight time over distance L for a particle with velocity v_x, bar{\tau} is the mean flight time over distance L, N is the number density of particles in the beam, and p_0 is the pressure on the wall due to the beam where it strikes. Collisions between beam atoms are ignored unless stated otherwise. The constant e denotes the base of natural logarithms

subquestions.subproblem: If the beam atoms are to traverse a 1\unit{m} path length with less than 1/e loss resulting from collisions with background gas atoms at room temperature T_bg=300\unit{K}, what should be the pressure p in the vacuum chamber? Assume a collision cross-section of 10^{-16}\unit{cm^2}, and ignore collisions between beam atoms.
subquestions.solution:
The requirement of less than 1/e loss after traveling distance L is
$$1-e^{-L/l}<\frac{1}{e}$$
This implies
$$L<l\ln\frac{e}{e-1}$$
The number density and mean free path satisfy
$$n=\frac{1}{l\sigma}$$
Hence
$$n<\frac{\ln\frac{e}{e-1}}{L\sigma}$$
With pressure defined by the ideal gas law
$$p=nkT_{bg}$$
we obtain the bound
$$p<\frac{kT_{bg}\ln\frac{e}{e-1}}{L\sigma}$$
Numerical values used are
$$L=1\unit{m}$$
$$\sigma=10^{-16}\unit{cm^2}$$
$$\sigma=10^{-20}\unit{m^2}$$
$$T_{bg}=300\unit{K}$$
Therefore
$$p<0.18\unit{N/m^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the maximum allowable background pressure p (as an upper bound to ensure less than 1/e loss over L=1\unit{m}) as a numerical value in SI units.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the mean time bar{\tau} for the beam atoms to travel one meter? Show how the exact value for bar{\tau} is calculated from the appropriate velocity distribution. Do not evaluate integrals. Make a simple argument to get a numerical estimate for bar{\tau}.
subquestions.solution:
For a particle with x-directed velocity v_x, the flight time over distance L is
$$\tau=\frac{L}{v_x}$$
For an effusive beam with v_x>0, the flux-weighted distribution along x is
$$f(v_x)dv_x\propto v_x e^{-\frac{mv_x^2}{2kT_b}}dv_x$$
The mean transit time is
$$\bar{\tau}=\frac{\int_0^{\infty}\frac{L}{v_x}v_x e^{-\frac{mv_x^2}{2kT_b}}dv_x}{\int_0^{\infty}v_x e^{-\frac{mv_x^2}{2kT_b}}dv_x}$$
Carrying out the Gaussian integrals gives
$$\bar{\tau}=L\sqrt{\frac{\pi m}{2kT_b}}$$
Using the numerical values
$$T_b=1000\unit{K}$$
$$L=1\unit{m}$$
we estimate
$$\bar{\tau}\approx1.3\times10^{-3}\unit{s}$$
Scattering from background gas atoms is neglected
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of $\bar{\tau} = \;\cdots$ and should be written only with the variables $L, m, k, T_b$.

subquestions.subproblem: If the Be atoms stick to the far wall, estimate the pressure p_0 on the wall due to the beam where the beam strikes the wall. Assume the density of particles in the beam is 10^{10}\unit{cm^{-3}}. Compare this result with the pressure from the background gas.
subquestions.solution:
The momentum flux of incident particles gives
$$p_0=N\frac{\int_0^{\infty}m v_x^2 v_x e^{-\frac{mv_x^2}{2kT_b}}dv_x}{\int_0^{\infty}v_x e^{-\frac{mv_x^2}{2kT_b}}dv_x}$$
Therefore
$$p_0=2NkT_b$$
Numerical values used are
$$N=10^{10}\unit{cm^{-3}}$$
$$N=10^{16}\unit{m^{-3}}$$
$$T_b=1000\unit{K}$$
Thus
$$p_0\approx3\times10^{-4}\unit{N/m^2}$$
The comparison with the background gas pressure p from part (a) is
$$p_0\ll p$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the beam-induced wall pressure $p_0$ as a numerical value in SI units.

context:
Estimate, to within an order of magnitude using kinetic theory, the thermal conductivity kappa of a dilute gas in terms of its absolute temperature T, number density n, molecular mass M, molecular collision cross-section sigma, and constant-volume heat capacity per molecule c_v. Assume a steady one-dimensional temperature gradient along the x direction and neglect convection. Consider pressures near atmospheric, temperatures near room temperature, and characteristic dimensions of the order of centimeters to meters. Use SI units. Variable and concept definitions: q is the heat flux, kappa is the thermal conductivity, n is the molecular number density, overline v is the mean molecular speed, l is the mean free path, sigma is the collision cross-section, k is the Boltzmann constant, M is the molecular mass, T is the absolute temperature, Phi is the molecular crossing rate per unit area per unit time, Delta T is the temperature change over one mean free path, Delta E is the energy transported per molecule, and x is the spatial coordinate. For a numerical estimate for air, use the following values
$$
k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \unit{J/K}
$$
$$
M = 29 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \unit{kg}
$$
$$
\sigma = 10^{-20} \unit{m^2}
$$
$$
 c_v = \frac{5}{2} k
$$
$$
T = 300 \unit{K}
$$
solution:
Assume a steady temperature gradient so that molecules carry energy from hotter to colder regions. The molecular crossing rate per unit area per unit time is
$$
\Phi = \frac{n \overline v}{4}
$$
The temperature change over one mean free path is
$$
\Delta T = l \frac{dT}{dx}
$$
The energy transported per molecule is
$$
\Delta E = c_v \Delta T
$$
The heat flux is
$$
q = \Phi \Delta E
$$
Therefore
$$
q = \frac{1}{4} n \overline v c_v l \frac{dT}{dx}
$$
By Fourier's law
$$
q = \kappa \frac{dT}{dx}
$$
Thus the thermal conductivity is
$$
\kappa = \frac{1}{4} n l \overline v c_v
$$
Using kinetic-theory estimates
$$
l = \frac{1}{n \sigma}
$$
$$
\overline v = \sqrt{\frac{3 k T}{M}}
$$
we obtain
$$
\kappa = \frac{c_v}{4 \sigma} \sqrt{\frac{3 k T}{M}}
$$
For air with the given values, the order-of-magnitude estimate is
$$
\kappa = 0.44 \unit{J/(m K)}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express kappa as a numerical value in SI units, reported in the form "kappa = ...", with 2 significant figures.

context:
A propagating plane sound wave in an ideal gas causes periodic temperature variations. Thermal conductivity tends to smooth out these variations, but such waves are often approximated as adiabatic when conductivity is too slow to act significantly over one wavelength. The thermal conductivity coefficient from kinetic theory is
$$
k \approx 1.23 C_v \overline v l
$$
where C_v is the heat capacity per unit volume, \overline v is the mean thermal speed, and l is the mean free path. Let x denote the position along the direction of propagation, \lambda the wavelength, T(x) the instantaneous temperature with mean T_0, amplitude \Delta T, and phase \varphi_0. Let \delta T(x) denote the temperature change caused by thermal conduction relative to the adiabatic oscillation at the same x. Define the fraction conducted away as
$$
f(x)=\frac{\delta T(x)}{\Delta T}
$$
Determine f(x) as a function of \lambda, and state the condition on \lambda under which thermal conductivity is ineffective, meaning that
$$
|f(x)| \ll 1
$$
for all x
solution:
Assume a sinusoidal temperature field along x
$$
T(x)=T_0+\Delta T \cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}+\varphi_0\right)
$$
Approximate the conductive change over a mean free path by
$$
\delta T=-2 l \frac{dT}{dx}
$$
Compute the spatial derivative
$$
\frac{dT}{dx}=-\Delta T \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}+\varphi_0\right)
$$
Substitute into the conductive change
$$
\delta T=\frac{4\pi l}{\lambda} \Delta T \sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}+\varphi_0\right)
$$
Therefore the fraction conducted away is
$$
f(x)=\frac{\delta T}{\Delta T}
$$
$$
f(x)=\frac{4\pi l}{\lambda} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}+\varphi_0\right)
$$
Thermal conductivity is ineffective when
$$
|f(x)| \ll 1
$$
which requires
$$
\lambda \gg l
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two parts: (1) Provide the expression for the fraction conducted away in the form 'f(x) = ...', written only in terms of x, \lambda, l, and \varphi_0 (and fundamental constants if needed). (2) State the condition for thermal conductivity to be ineffective as a single inequality involving only \lambda and l.

context: Give a qualitative argument based on the kinetic theory of gases to show that the coefficient of viscosity of a classical gas is independent of the pressure at constant temperature. Consider a dilute classical gas undergoing steady shear flow along the x direction with macroscopic velocity component v_x(y). Let n be the number density of molecules, m the mass of one molecule, k the Boltzmann constant, T the absolute temperature, l the molecular mean free path, sigma the molecular collision cross section, \bar v the mean molecular speed, f the viscous shear force per unit area (shear stress), J the molecular flux crossing a unit area per unit time through a plane perpendicular to the x direction, and eta the coefficient of viscosity
solution:
For steady shear flow with velocity gradient \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}, the molecular flux is
$$
J = \frac{n \bar v}{4}
$$
The momentum transfer per molecule is
$$
m \Delta v_x
$$
Over a characteristic displacement \Delta y we estimate
$$
\Delta v_x = \Delta y \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}
$$
For an order-of-magnitude estimate with \Delta y \sim l we have
$$
\Delta v_x \sim l \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}
$$
The viscous shear force per unit area is
$$
f = \frac{n m \bar v \Delta v_x}{4}
$$
Substituting the estimate for \Delta v_x gives
$$
f = \frac{1}{4} n m \bar v l \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}
$$
By Newton's law of viscosity
$$
f = \eta \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}
$$
Therefore
$$
\eta = \frac{n m \bar v l}{4}
$$
For a dilute gas the mean free path satisfies
$$
l \approx \frac{1}{n \sigma}
$$
The mean molecular speed is
$$
\bar v = \sqrt{\frac{8 k T}{\pi m}}
$$
Hence
$$
\eta = \frac{m}{4 \sigma} \sqrt{\frac{8 k T}{\pi m}}
$$
This expression shows that at fixed T the viscosity \eta is independent of the pressure because it contains no dependence on n, while m and \sigma are molecular constants
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \eta = ..., and your response should be written with T, m, k, \sigma only.

grading_standard.formula: $$f = \frac{1}{4} n m \bar v l \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y}$$

context: Consider a dilute gas of identical molecules with mass m. The mean molecular speed is \overline{v}. The macroscopic average flow velocity has only an x-component u_x that varies with z, written u_x = u_x(z), with |u_x| << \overline{v} and with all gradients small. The number density is n, the molecular diameter is d, and the mean free path is l with l >> d and l << L, where L is a characteristic linear dimension of the containing vessel. The shear stress on a plane whose normal points in the z-direction with traction in the x-direction is denoted by \tau_{xz}. The dynamic viscosity is denoted by \eta. The molecular scattering cross section is \sigma. The absolute temperature is T, the pressure is p, and the center-of-mass energy for a binary collision is E_{cm}. Assume a Maxwellian velocity distribution whenever stated.

subquestions.subproblem: The viscosity \eta is defined as the proportionality constant between the velocity gradient and the stress in the x-direction on an imaginary plane whose normal points in the z-direction. Find an approximate expression for \eta in terms of the parameters given.
subquestions.solution:
The shear stress is
$$\tau_{xz} = \frac{1}{4} n \overline{v} m l \frac{\partial u_x}{\partial z}$$
Thus, the viscosity is
$$\eta = \frac{1}{4} m \overline{v} n l$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \eta = ..., and your response should be written only with m, \overline{v}, n, and l.

subquestions.subproblem: If the scattering of molecules is treated like that of hard spheres, what is the temperature dependence of \eta? The pressure dependence? Assume a Maxwellian distribution in both cases.
subquestions.solution:
The mean free path is
$$l = \frac{1}{n \sigma}$$
From part (a),
$$\eta = \frac{1}{4} m \overline{v} n l$$
Therefore,
$$\eta = \frac{m \overline{v}}{4 \sigma}$$
For a Maxwellian distribution,
$$\overline{v} \propto T^{1/2}$$
Hence,
$$\eta \propto T^{1/2}$$
and \eta is independent of pressure
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as two algebraic proportionalities: \eta \propto T^{...} and \eta \propto p^{...}. Use only the variables T and p in these expressions.

subquestions.subproblem: If the molecular scattering cross section \sigma \propto E_{cm}^{2}, where E_{cm} is the center-of-mass energy of two colliding particles, what is the temperature dependence of \eta? Again assume a Maxwellian distribution.
subquestions.solution:
Given
$$\sigma \propto E_{cm}^{2}$$
For a Maxwellian gas,
$$E_{cm} \propto T$$
Thus,
$$\sigma \propto T^{2}$$
Using
$$\eta = \frac{m \overline{v}}{4 \sigma}$$
and
$$\overline{v} \propto T^{1/2}$$
It follows that
$$\eta \propto T^{-3/2}$$
and \eta is independent of pressure
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single algebraic proportionality in the form \eta \propto T^{...}, using only the variable T.

subquestions.subproblem: Estimate \eta for air at atmospheric pressure (10\unit{dyn/cm^2}) and room temperature. State clearly your assumptions.
subquestions.solution:
Assume: molecular weight of air approximately 30, mean molecular speed \overline{v} approximately equal to the speed of sound, and \sigma \approx 10^{-20} \unit{m^2}. Using
$$\eta = \frac{m \overline{v}}{4 \sigma}$$
the estimate is
$$\eta_{air} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-6} \unit{kg/(m s)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \eta_{air} as a numerical value in SI units (kg/(m s)), rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: Electrical conductivity. Derive an approximate expression for the electrical conductivity σ of a degenerate electron gas of number density n electrons per unit volume. Let n have unit \unit{cm^{-3}}. Use τ for the effective collision time between electrons, e for the magnitude of the electron charge, and m for the electron mass. Consider a uniform electric field E_z applied along the z-axis. Let v_z be the z-component of the electron velocity, Δv_z the change in v_z over a time interval of order τ, and j_z the electrical current density along z. You should use E_k for kinetic energy, E_p for potential energy, E for total energy if needed, though they are not required here.
solution:
For a degenerate electron gas, the occupied states form a Fermi surface whose symmetry yields zero net current in the absence of an external field. Under a uniform electric field E_z along z, the electron gas acquires a drift velocity as a whole. The equation of motion along z is

$$
m \frac{dv_z}{dt} = e E_z
$$

Over a characteristic effective collision time τ, the change in velocity is approximated by

$$
\Delta v_z \approx \tau \frac{dv_z}{dt}
$$

The resulting current density is

$$
j_z = e n \Delta v_z
$$

Substituting the acceleration from the equation of motion gives

$$
j_z \approx \frac{n e^2 \tau}{m} E_z
$$

By definition of electrical conductivity along z,

$$
j_z = \sigma E_z
$$

Therefore, the electrical conductivity is

$$
\sigma = \frac{n e^2 \tau}{m}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of σ = ... , and your response should be written with n, e, τ, and m only.

context: Consider a system of identical charged particles confined to a volume V. Each particle has charge e. The particles are in thermal equilibrium at temperature T in the presence of a uniform electric field E directed along the z-axis. Let k denote the Boltzmann constant. Let u denote the electrostatic potential energy of a particle at height z. Let n(z) denote the particle number density at height z, and let n_0 denote the reference density at z=0, so that n_0=n(0). Let D denote the diffusion coefficient defining the diffusive flux along z by Fick's law J_D=-D dn/dz. Let μ denote the mobility, relating the drift velocity v_d to the field via v_d=μ E. Let J_μ denote the drift flux associated with this mobility. All fluxes are taken along the z-direction.

subquestions.subproblem: Let n(z) be the density of particles at the height z. Use equilibrium statistical mechanics to find the constant of proportionality between \frac{dn}{dz} and n.
subquestions.solution:
The electrostatic potential energy is
$$u=-eEz$$
At equilibrium, the concentration distribution is
$$n(z)=n_0\exp\left(\frac{eEz}{kT}\right)$$
where n_0 is the concentration at z=0. Therefore,
$$\frac{dn(z)}{dz}=\frac{eE}{kT}n(z)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form dn/dz = (...) n(z), and your response should be written with e, E, k, T, n(z) only.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that the particles can be characterized by a diffusion coefficient D. Using the definition of D, find the flux J_D arising from the concentration gradient obtained in part (a).
subquestions.solution:
By Fick's law,
$$J_D=-D\frac{dn(z)}{dz}$$
Using the result from part (a),
$$J_D=-D\frac{eE}{kT}n(z)$$
Substituting the equilibrium density,
$$J_D=-D\frac{eE}{kT}n_0\exp\left(\frac{eEz}{kT}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form J_D = ..., and your response should be written with D, e, E, k, T, n(z) only.

subquestions.solution:
The electrostatic potential energy is
$$u=-eEz$$
At equilibrium, the concentration distribution is
$$n(z)=n_0\exp\left(\frac{eEz}{kT}\right)$$
where n_0 is the concentration at z=0. Therefore,
$$\frac{dn(z)}{dz}=\frac{eE}{kT}n(z)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form dn/dz = (...) n(z), and your response should be written with e, E, k, T, n(z) only.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose the particles are also characterized by a mobility \mu relating their drift velocity to the applied field. Find the particle flux J_\mu associated with this mobility.
subquestions.solution:
The particle flux due to drift is
$$J_\mu=n(z)v_d$$
The drift velocity is
$$v_d=\mu E$$
Hence,
$$J_\mu=\mu En_0\exp\left(\frac{eEz}{kT}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form J_μ = ..., and your response should be written with μ, E, n(z) only.

subquestions.subproblem: By making use of the fact that at equilibrium the particle flux must vanish, establish the Einstein relation between \mu and D: \mu = \frac{e}{k}\frac{D}{T}.
subquestions.solution:
At equilibrium, the total flux vanishes,
$$J_D+J_\mu=0$$
Therefore,
$$\mu=\frac{eD}{kT}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form μ = ..., and your response should be written with e, D, k, T only.

context: Consider a system of degenerate electrons at a low temperature in thermal equilibrium under the simultaneous influence of a number density gradient and an electric field. Use the following definitions throughout: μ is the chemical potential, φ(x) is the electrostatic potential, E is the electric field defined by E = - ∇ φ(x), E_F is the Fermi energy, ε is the single-particle energy, T is the temperature, k is the Boltzmann constant, e is the magnitude of the electron charge, h is the Planck constant, m is the electron mass, p_F is the Fermi momentum, N is the total number of electrons, V is the volume, n = N/V is the electron number density, j is the electric current density, σ is the electrical conductivity, D is the diffusion coefficient, ρ = m n is the mass density, J is the diffusion current density, N_F = dN/dE_F is the density of states at the Fermi surface, and \tilde{\mu} = \mu + e \phi(x) is the electrochemical potential. The operator ∇ denotes the spatial gradient. In thermal equilibrium the electrochemical potential \tilde{\mu} is spatially uniform.

subquestions.subproblem: How is the chemical potential μ related to the electrostatic potential φ(x) and the Fermi energy E_F for such a system?
subquestions.solution:
From the Fermi-Dirac distribution
$$n_\epsilon = \{ \exp[(\epsilon - \mu - e \phi(x)) / k T] + 1 \}^{-1}$$
we obtain
$$E_F = \mu_0 + e \phi(x)$$
with
$$\mu_0 = \mu(T = 0)$$
The total number of electrons is
$$N = 2 \frac{V}{h^3} \frac{4}{3} \pi p_F^3$$
Equivalently
$$N = 2 \frac{V}{h^3} \frac{4}{3} \pi (2 m E_F)^{3/2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single equation in the form 'E_F = ...' and must be written using only E_F, μ_0, e, and φ(x).

subquestions.subproblem: How does E_F depend on the electron density n?
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form 'E_F = ...' and must be written using only n, h, and m.

subquestions.subproblem: Using the condition that the electrochemical potential \tilde{\mu} is spatially uniform in thermal equilibrium and considering both the electric field and the density gradient, derive the expressions for the electric and diffusion currents and obtain relations for D in terms of σ, E_F, N, n, and N_F.
subquestions.solution:
The electric current density under the electric field is
$$j = \sigma E$$
Using E = - \nabla \phi(x) gives
$$j = - \sigma \nabla \phi(x)$$
The diffusion current density is
$$J = - D \nabla \rho$$
with
$$\rho = m n$$
In equilibrium we have
$$\frac{j}{e} = - \frac{J}{m}$$
Hence
$$\frac{\sigma}{e} \nabla \phi(x) = - \frac{D}{m} \nabla \rho$$
Using \nabla \rho = m \nabla n gives
$$\frac{\sigma}{e} \nabla \phi(x) = - D \nabla n$$
The density of states at the Fermi surface is
$$N_F = \frac{dN}{dE_F}$$
For the free electron gas this evaluates to
$$N_F = 4 \pi V (2 m)^{3/2} \frac{E_F^{1/2}}{h^3}$$
The electrochemical potential is
$$\tilde{\mu} = \mu + e \phi(x)$$
In equilibrium we have
$$\nabla \tilde{\mu} = 0$$
Thus
$$\nabla \mu + e \nabla \phi(x) = 0$$
Therefore
$$e \nabla \phi(x) + \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial n} \right)_T \nabla n = 0$$
Hence
$$D = \frac{\sigma}{e^2} \left( \frac{\partial \mu}{\partial n} \right)_T$$
For a degenerate electron gas at low temperature we use \mu \approx E_F to write
$$D \approx \frac{\sigma}{e^2} \frac{\partial E_F}{\partial n}$$
This gives
$$D = \frac{2 \sigma E_F}{3 e^2 N}$$
Equivalently
$$D = \frac{2 \sigma}{3 e^2 n} \left[ \frac{h^3}{4 \pi (2 m)^{3/2}} \frac{N_F}{V} \right]^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (1) the electric current density in the form 'j = ...' using only j, σ, and E; (2) the diffusion current density in the form 'J = ...' using only J, D, and ∇ρ; and (3) four expressions for the diffusion coefficient D: (a) 'D = (σ/e^2)(∂μ/∂n)_T' using only D, σ, e, μ, n, and T; (b) a low-temperature form 'D = (σ/e^2)(∂E_F/∂n)' using only D, σ, e, E_F, and n; (c) 'D = 2σE_F/(3e^2N)' using only D, σ, e, E_F, and N; and (d) an equivalent form using the density of states 'D = ...' expressed only with D, σ, e, n, h, m, N_F, and V (constants like π are allowed).

subquestions.subproblem: Repeat of part (a): state the relation among μ, φ(x), and E_F, and write N in terms of E_F for a degenerate electron gas.
subquestions.solution:
From the Fermi-Dirac distribution
$$n_\epsilon = \{ \exp[(\epsilon - \mu - e \phi(x)) / k T] + 1 \}^{-1}$$
we obtain
$$E_F = \mu_0 + e \phi(x)$$
with
$$\mu_0 = \mu(T = 0)$$
The total number of electrons is
$$N = 2 \frac{V}{h^3} \frac{4}{3} \pi p_F^3$$
Equivalently
$$N = 2 \frac{V}{h^3} \frac{4}{3} \pi (2 m E_F)^{3/2}$$

context: Consider a non-interacting, nonrelativistic Fermi gas of electrons confined by hard-wall boxes in one, two, or three spatial dimensions. Electrons have mass m and charge e. Planck constants satisfy h=2\pi\hbar. The single-particle energy is denoted by E. The density of states N(E) is defined as the number of single-particle states per unit energy interval, including spin degeneracy g_s=2. Geometry and sizes: in one dimension the segment has length L, in two dimensions the square has side L and area A=L^2, in three dimensions the cube has side L and volume V=L^3. Quantum numbers n,n_x,n_y,n_z are positive integers. The Fermi energy is E_F, the Fermi temperature is T_F, the Fermi velocity is v_F, the mean free time between scattering events is \tau_e, and the electron diffusivity is D. The total number of electrons is z and the electron number density is \mu, defined by \mu=z/L in one dimension, \mu=z/A in two dimensions, and \mu=z/V in three dimensions. The radial quantum number at the Fermi surface is n_F. The electrical conductivity is \sigma.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the density of states N(E) as a function of energy (N(E) is the number of states per unit energy interval) for the following cases: 1) The particles are constrained to move only along a line of length L 2) The particles move only on a two dimensional area A 3) The particles move in a three dimensional volume V
subquestions.solution:
1) Motion along length L
The wave eigenfunction is
$$\psi_n(x)=\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$$
with n=1,2,\ldots
The energy levels from the Schr\odinger equation are
$$E_n=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{\pi n}{L}\right)^2$$
Equivalently,
$$n=\frac{2L}{h}\sqrt{2mE}$$
Including spin degeneracy, the total number of states up to n is
$$\overline{N}(n)=2n$$
Thus,
$$N(E)=\frac{d\overline{N}}{dE}$$
Using the chain rule,
$$\frac{d\overline{N}}{dn}=2$$
and
$$\frac{dn}{dE}=\frac{L}{h}\sqrt{\frac{2m}{E}}$$
so
$$N(E)=L\left(\frac{8m}{h^2E}\right)^{1/2}$$
2) Motion in a square of side L with A=L^2
The eigenfunction is
$$\psi_{n_x,n_y}(x,y)=\sin\frac{n_x\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{n_y\pi y}{L}$$
with n_x=1,2,\ldots and n_y=1,2,\ldots
The energy is
$$E(n_x,n_y)=\frac{h^2\left(n_x^2+n_y^2\right)}{8mL^2}$$
Defining n^2=n_x^2+n_y^2, this can be written as
$$E(n)=\frac{h^2n^2}{8mL^2}$$
The number of states between n and n+dn is
$$d\overline{N}=\pi n\,dn$$
Hence,
$$N(E)=\pi n\frac{dn}{dE}$$
Using
$$n=\frac{L\sqrt{8mE}}{h}$$
we obtain
$$N(E)=\frac{4\pi mL^2}{h^2}$$
Equivalently, since A=L^2,
$$N(E)=\frac{4\pi mA}{h^2}$$
3) Motion in volume V with V=L^3
The energy is
$$E(n)=\frac{h^2}{8m}\left(\frac{n}{L}\right)^2$$
with
$$n^2=n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2$$
where n_x=1,2,\ldots, n_y=1,2,\ldots, n_z=1,2,\ldots
The number of states between n and n+dn is
$$d\overline{N}=\pi n^2\,dn$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide three algebraic expressions for the density of states in the formats: N_1D(E) = ..., N_2D = ... (independent of E), and N_3D(E) = .... Use only the following variables for each case: for 1D use E, L, m, h; for 2D use A, m, h; for 3D use E, V, m, h.

subquestions.subproblem: In a Fermi electron gas in a solid when T \ll T_F, scattering by phonons and impurities limits electrical conduction. In this case, the conductivity can be written as $$\sigma=e^2N(E_F)D$$ where e is the electron charge, N(E_F) is the density of states defined above evaluated at the Fermi energy, and D is the electron diffusivity. D is proportional to the product of the square of the Fermi velocity and the mean time, \tau_e, between scattering events, i.e., D\sim v_F^2\tau_e. 1) Give a physical argument for the dependence of the diffusivity on N(E_F). 2) Calculate the dependence of \sigma on the total electron density in each of the three cases listed in part a
subquestions.solution:
1) The mean free time is inversely proportional to the probability of collision, and the latter is proportional to the density of states on the Fermi surface since T\ll T_F and elastic scatterings near the Fermi surface dominate. Thus
$$\tau_e\sim\frac{1}{N(E_F)}$$
Hence
$$D\sim\frac{v_F^2}{N(E_F)}$$
2) Using
$$\sigma=e^2N(E_F)D$$
and the result above,
$$\sigma\sim e^2v_F^2$$
Since for nonrelativistic electrons v_F^2\sim E_F, we have
$$\sigma\sim E_F$$
Let the total number of electrons be z and the electron number density be \mu. Then
$$\mu=\frac{z}{L}$$
for one-dimensional motion,
$$\mu=\frac{z}{A}$$
for two-dimensional motion, and
$$\mu=\frac{z}{V}$$
for three-dimensional motion
In all three cases,
$$E_F=\frac{h^2}{8m}\left(\frac{n_F}{L}\right)^2$$
Moreover,
$$z=2n_F$$
for one-dimensional motion,
$$z=\frac{\pi n_F^2}{2}$$
for two-dimensional motion, and
$$z=\frac{\pi n_F^3}{3}$$
for three-dimensional motion
Therefore,
$$\sigma\sim E_F$$
which implies
$$\sigma\sim\mu^2$$
for one-dimensional motion,
$$\sigma\sim\mu$$
for two-dimensional motion, and
$$\sigma\sim\mu^{2/3}$$
for three-dimensional motion
These results differ greatly from those of the classical theory because only the electrons near the Fermi surface contribute to the conductivity
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer must include both: (1) one concise sentence giving a physical argument describing how the mean free time and the diffusivity depend on the density of states at the Fermi level; and, immediately after, the proportionality relations written as formulas in the forms: \tau_e \propto ..., D \propto v_F^2 .... Use only the symbols \tau_e, D, v_F, N(E_F) in these two formulas. (2) the conductivity–density scalings written exactly as: \"\sigma_{1D} \propto \mu^{...}, \sigma_{2D} \propto \mu^{...}, \sigma_{3D} \propto \mu^{...}\" using only the symbols \sigma and \mu.
